Wicknell Chivayo, the Zimbabwean tycoon who died in a helicopter crash along with his wife Lucy Muteke last week, divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death.
He called himself "Sir Wicknell", a nod to the embellishment that epitomised his lifestyle - and a nickname some used for the 45-year-old who packed enough controversy into his short life to last several lifetimes.
He was relentlessly self-documenting, building much of his public persona on social media, where he posed with piles of cash and announced the cars and money he gave to people whom he considered deserving.
Chivayo delighted in displaying his access to heads of state across Africa and showing off his possessions, conducting video tours of his fleet of expensive cars, mainly Rolls-Royces, with vanity plates, watches and a vast collection of designer shoes.
His admirers saw a fabulously wealthy man sharing his good fortune. His detractors recoiled at the ostentatious displays, questioned the origins of his money and his political connections, and saw his lifestyle as a stark illustration of inequality.
But Chivayo remained tone-deaf to such criticism. As his fortunes rose, he became ever more unapologetic about flaunting his wealth in a country where nearly half the population lives below the international poverty line, according to the World Bank.
"He gave to those few on an island of wealth in a sea of poverty," Pedzisai Ruhanya, director of the Zimbabwe Democracy Institute think-tank, told the BBC, explaining how his donations were mainly to influential people.
He dismissed Chivayo's generosity as grandstanding for the ruling Zanu-PF party - an attempt to ensure the support of key politicians and even church leaders.
Nonetheless, there has been an outpouring of grief, especially from recipients of his largesse, and tributes from politicians, religious leaders and business figures.
Among the mourners gathered at the Chivayos' opulent home in the capital, Harare, ahead of their burial on Thursday, was Cleopas Mukungunugwa, a young and prominent Zanu-PF social media influencer and recipient of two luxury cars from Sir Wicknell.
Standing outside the mansion, where a massive poster of the couple is displayed, he told local media that he was devastated by his patron's death, external, explaining how "Sir Wicknell" often dictated what he should write in his posts.
"He was criticised by many on social media and our goal was to bolster his reputation as a philanthropist," he said.
Chivayo dropped out of high school aged 15 because his family could no longer afford the fees after his father died when he was 10.
His first job was as a wages clerk for a bus company. From there, he moved into his first independent hustle - selling mobile phones and dealing in foreign currency, often on the black market at the height of the country's hyperinflation crisis.
In 2005, he was sentenced to five years in prison for money laundering involving 837,000 South African rand (then worth $137,500, Â£72,000). He served three years at Chikurubi Maximum Prison after two years were suspended.
Details of his career following his release are murky, but he went into the energy business, becoming what one state-run newspaper described as a "tenderpreneur" -making money by getting government contracts.
He headed the firm Intratrek Zimbabwe, which partnered with Chinese electrical giant CHiNT Electric. This was at a time when legislation required all companies in the country to cede economic control to black Zimbabweans, under a policy known as indigenisation.
In 2014, Intratrek was selected to build a 100MW solar power station in the southern town of Gwanda. A contract worth more than $170m was signed the following year. It became one of the biggest controversies of Chivayo's business career.
Zimbabwe Power Company, the state-owned utility that awarded the contract, sought to terminate it when Intratrek failed to deliver, but the courts ultimately ruled that the agreement remained valid.
A parliamentary inquiry later described Intratrek as a "briefcase company" being used as a front to attract investment.
Chivayo acknowledged that Intratrek lacked expertise in solar construction, describing it as the local partner while CHiNT provided the technical muscle.
Intratrek received an advance of more than $5m for the Gwanda solar plant, but it remains unbuilt to this day.
Just weeks before Chivayo's death, Intratrek received a government notice to proceed with the project and was given 24 months to complete it.
As the accusations flew, the businessman just smiled and sweet-talked his way through the maelstrom - even winning over President Emmerson Mnangagwa, who was initially unimpressed by him when he first came to power.
In 2018, Mnangagwa cited Gwanda as a lesson in the dangers of doing business with "fly-by-night briefcase businessmen", adding ominously that "Chikurubi is not full". The state-run Herald newspaper reported that the warning was directed at Chivayo.
Yet within a few years, that relationship transformed into a bromance. In one of several photographs capturing the remarkable informality between them, Chivayo lounges, almost lying, on a sofa beside Mnangagwa, apparently entirely at ease in the president's company.
His access was not confined to Zanu-PF - he also posted photographs with opposition figures, including the late Morgan Tsvangirai and Nelson Chamisa.
But he became a conspicuous presence around Mnangagwa, speaking glowingly of the president and making no secret of his support for Zanu-PF.
He faced allegations over the procurement of materials for the 2023 elections, in which Mnangagwa was voted in for a second term.
Investigations alleged that South African supplier Ren-Form grossly inflated prices and subsequently paid hundreds of millions of rand to a company linked to him. Chivayo denied wrongdoing, and Zimbabwe's anti-corruption commission later said it had found no evidence linking him to procurement fraud. Ren

Moment Nasa scientist Margaret Hamilton receives presidential medal of honour
The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90.
Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering".
And in 2016, she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Honor - the nation's highest civilian honour - by Barack Obama in a ceremony at the White House.
"To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement announcing Hamilton's passing, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream.

Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing", and will operate as a "UK Mission"
"We did not want it to come to this," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar wrote on social media, as he said 20 diplomats and the Consul General would leave Israel while a task force of seven could remain in the building "with a very limited scope of activity".
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband responded that some staff had been "temporarily withdrawn" for security reasons, but stressed the mission will "work with the Palestinian people".
Israel said in September it would shut the consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law.
The UK government had made last-ditch efforts to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate ahead of Thursday's deadline, after the Israeli government said it would close the consulate within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement.
The consulate, which was first established in 1838, handles UK relations with Palestinians in Jerusalem as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.
It is distinct from the UK embassy in Tel Aviv, which is the UK's main diplomatic hub with Israel.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said the country had implemented measures announced on 8 September in response to UK sanctions.
"The British Consulate in Jerusalem is closing its operations today. Accordingly, the sign of the British Consulate in Jerusalem has been removed," he wrote on social media.
However, the British flag could still be seen outside and several staff were seen entering on Thursday morning.
Saar said talks with the UK government had resulted in agreement on certain principles, including that "the consul general and 20 diplomats (including the consul general) are ending their duties and will leave Israel."
But Saar acknowledged that the building is "the property of the British government" and said Israel had authorised "a task force of only seven diplomats with a very limited scope of activity" to operate in the building.
As a result of this agreement with the UK, he said, "no steps will be taken against Israel".
Israeli media had been reporting that the UK had threatened to expel Israeli diplomats from London - raising the prospect of further damaging bilateral relations.
In a written statement on the morning of the deadline, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK does not accept Israel has the right to close the consulate.
"The UK government reiterates its long-standing view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory."
Following discussions with the Israeli government, he said, the building "will not be closing" and will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem from Thursday.
However Miliband said an understanding had not been reached on "necessary assurances for the security and protections of our staff and premises".
"Accordingly the UK has temporarily withdrawn a number of staff and families to ensure their safety and security," he added.

- Published
Christa Pike is "up and walking" while in hospital after last week's botched attempt to execute her in the US state of Tennessee, a member of her legal team says.
Pike, 50, who was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995, survived two lethal injections on 30 September. Experts described it as unprecedented.
Speaking late on Wednesday to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, lawyer Stephen Ferrell said he had not spoken to Pike directly but that he had learned she was moving around her hospital room for the first time while still being mentally "foggy".
Earlier, a court ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution.
That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.
The Pike case is now in uncharted territory, as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
The failed execution was branded a "mess" by the mother of Slemmer, who was among those pushing for Pike to be put to death.
Pike's boyfriend at the time of Slemmer's gruesome murder, Tadaryl Shipp, was spared the death penalty because he was not legally an adult when the crime was committed. He remains in prison.
Pike was 18 and Shipp was 17 when they beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
In their updates on Pike's condition after the attempted execution, her team had previously said she was awake and speaking, and experiencing anger and confusion. She was said at that stage to be handcuffed to her bed.
In the latest updates, given to the BBC, Ferrell said Pike was continuing to experience the after-effects of the drug pentobarbital, which was injected into her body in two doses by prison staff during the scheduled execution on 30 September.
Once it became clear that Pike was not going to die, she was taken to hospital, where she was initially unconscious and declared to have be in a critical condition.
As of late on Tuesday, though, she was "fairly well", Ferrell told the BBC.
"What's been described to me is that physically there's quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she's not able to use them very much."
Of her physical movements, he added: "She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far."
Turning to her mental state, he said: "I think it's kind of good and bad. Good that she is fairly with it, but she's also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she's going."
Ferrell said much remained unknown about what happens next. "I assume [the situation for Pike] will keep improving, but there could be some permanent damage. We don't know that yet."
He added that the team wanted Pike to receive psychological support, since that "clearly is necessary now".
Ferrell and his colleagues - who highlighted ahead of the attempted execution that Pike had a condition that would make the injection method difficult - oppose any new attempt by state prison authorities to follow the same approach.
They are also calling on the state governor, Bill Lee, to downgrade Pike's punishment to the lesser sentence of life in prison without parole.
Meanwhile, Tennessee's proponents of capital punishment have suggested that a different method be used. Senator Marsha Blackburn, the Republican candidate for state governor in next month's election, said: "Bring back the electric chair."
Asked during a court hearing on Wednesday whether the state intended to reschedule Pike's execution, the state's attorney general said he did not know.
For now, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has ordered a pause on all executions in the state for the rest of the year, and has said he wants answers about what went wrong. The state's prisons chief is resigning after the failed execution.
Wednesday's court hearing related to the preservation of evidence following the first attempt.
The judge, I'Ashea Myles, ordered that "anything that was in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," including IV lines and syringes, as well as waste, like packaging, inserts, and labels.
The judge also demanded documentation on Pike's psychological condition prior to, during and after the 30 September execution attempt.
She advised the state to take "special care" not to misplace or accidentally delete any information that may be pertinent to the case.

3927178bef3f.text: Data: Gallup; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios Americans' confidence in the safety of food on grocery store shelves — and in the federal government's ability to regulate it — has plummeted to new lows according to a new Gallup poll. The big picture: Simultaneous illness outbreaks put federal regulators under a microscope earlier this year, as layoffs across the nation's health apparatus were already causing food safety angst. By the numbers: Less than half of U.S. adults have a great deal (11%) or a fair amount (36%) of confidence in the federal government to ensure food safety, according to the poll, which was conducted last month. On the flip side, a majority have not much or no confidence in the government's ability to police their food — a first in Gallup's trend, which has been intermittent for two decades. Zoom out: Meanwhile, Americans' confidence in the food sold at grocery stores has mirrored that drop, falling to a record low of 65% saying they are somewhat or very confident. That share has plunged from the 81% recorded in 2019. Zoom in: That growing food safety suspicion is driven by Democrats and independents, while Republicans have actually become more confident in grocery store food. The partisan chasm over the federal government's ability to ensure food safety has flipped — and widened — under the second Trump administration. In 2024, half of Republicans had a great deal or fair amount of confidence in the government to ensure food safety, while nearly three-quarters of Democrats agreed. By 2025, Democrats' confidence fell to 48%, and to 30% in 2026. Republicans, meanwhile, found new faith, with their confidence climbing from 62% in 2025 to 70% to 2026. Catch up quick: This year's polling occurred during and after the federal government declared the end of an outbreak of Cyclospora, a parasite that caused stomach illnesses, two deaths and saw more than 500 hospitalizations across 21 states. Federal health officials eventually traced the rapidly spreading surge to iceberg lettuce from supplier Taylor Farms . But the food woes didn't stop there: This summer saw a flurry of overlapping recalls and FDA investigations, while health experts warned administration cuts had weakened the public health infrastructure responsible for detecting outbreaks. Meanwhile, significant shares of Americans report concerns or strain about affording those groceries. The food-at-home CPI, for grocery store or supermarket food purchases, was up 2.2% between August 2025 and 2026. Friction point: That collides with an administration that's pushed whole foods as part of its "Make America Healthy Again" campaign under Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. But Gallup's polling indicates Republicans have digested that food safety message far better than Democrats and independents. Go deeper: America's next grocery shock is brewing

Eritrean soldiers have crossed into northern Ethiopia heading towards an area where clashes have been taking place between national army troops and regional forces, residents in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat have told the BBC.
Fighting in the region broke out two weeks ago after months of tension between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF). Both blame one another for violating a 2022 deal that ended a two-year civil war.
Ethiopia has also accused Eritrea of backing the TPLF - something Asmara has previously denied.
The latest unrest follows the launch in September of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia, which includes the TPLF.
Over the weekend, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control.
Eritrea was a key ally of landlocked Ethiopia during the 2020-2022 war, fighting against the TPLF in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century and which drove the Tigray region to the precipice of famine.
But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports.
Last week the two countries severed diplomatic relations as the renewed fighting raised fears of a wider regional conflict.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas, though mobile phone connections and internet access have been restored to most areas since the military took over Mekelle.
According to multiple accounts, Eritrean troops have moved from the border town of Zalambessa towards central Tigray, with convoys reportedly passing through Adigrat and heading toward Edaga Hamus, a town between Adigrat and Mekelle.
"I saw about 40 trucks carrying soldiers. The convoy was moving south," one resident of Adigrat, who requested anonymity for security reasons, told BBC Tigrinya.
A second resident reported seeing troop movements, initially at night: "We have been seeing trucks with Eritrean registration plates passing through the city.
"Now this morning we witnessed around 20 to 30 large trucks heading toward Edaga Hamus."
He added that acquaintances travelling along the route had seen additional vehicles carrying heavy weapons, including anti-aircraft guns, and noted some troops were also moving on foot.
A source in Mekelle told the BBC that relatives in Adigrat described even larger troop movements, and estimated they saw up to 60 trucks carrying soldiers who were later deployed in mountainous terrain near Edaga Hamus.
Images circulating on social media appear to show heavily loaded military trucks carrying uniformed personnel towards Adigrat, Edaga Hamus and possibly Wukro, another key town along the corridor between Adigrat and Mekelle. The BBC has not independently verified the images.
Sources in Wukro told the BBC that national army soldiers and allied fighters had entered the town on Wednesday after an exchange of heavy weapons about 15km south of the town.
The BBC has not yet been able to independently verify any of the reported troop movements.
The reported return of Eritrean forces has sparked anxiety among many of Tigray's residents, with some recalling the atrocities allegedly committed by soldiers from Eritrea during the recent civil war, when they fought against the TPLF.
One Adigrat resident said that seeing Eritrean soldiers again was emotionally distressing: "The memories are still fresh. I was emotional myself. People are saddened to see them back again."
A resident of Edaga Hamus also reported Eritrean troops passing through the town and said drone strikes had occurred nearby, with soldiers targeted.
In a recent interview with private station Fana Television, senior Ethiopian government official Abraham Belay accused Eritrea of direct participation in the conflict.
"The Eritrean army has participated with its full capacity and logistics," he said.
"Many Eritrean soldiers have been killed and captured. There is no doubt that the retaliation will be double. They will see what it means to enter the border of another country and fight alongside bandits."

6e2bab150331.text: Bryan Johnson , the face of the longevity movement, wants to make staying alive more important than making money. The famous/infamous biohacker spends over $2 million a year on his health, talks about living forever and publicly tracks everything from his erections to his sperm strength. Why it matters: As Johnson fights to "live forever," he's doing so with a wink to his 8 million social media followers, a link to his business in his bio and a knack for drawing attention to himself. What they're saying: In his interview with The Axios Show, he offered some advice for Elon Musk, said he'd love to help President Trump with his health and revealed his ultimate goal. "Will the 25th century ... be like, 'thank you' in 500 years? Will they give me a head nod? That's the goal," he said. Zoom out: His big picture focus: change the focus of society to health, not wealth. "Society says making money... is the greatest trophy one can get...we are at this inflection moment as a species where we are transitioning to 'Don't Die,'" Johnson said, referring to the title of his longevity movement. "What creates status and power and prestige is going to be different. And as crazy as it sounds, it may be your nighttime erections...It may be your ability to dunk a basketball at age 49," he said. Johnson, 49, is currently trying to dunk . Zoom out: That focus is what drives some of his more extreme experiments and interventions. In 2023, Johnson injected his teenage son's plasma , which he found to be a helpful regimen for his dad but not for himself, saying his own biomarkers are already "pretty similar to my 18-year-old." Through the help of wearables, tests and a concierge team, Johnson has gathered over 4.2 billion data points about his own body and health, and he relies on AI tools to help parse takeaways from that data. He has an in-home medical lab of sorts where he can do continuous testing, monitoring and procedures. Zoom in: Perhaps his most extreme act is his online presence , which Johnson called "performance art" in our conversation. When talking about humans dramatically increasing lifespans through scientific methods, "no one cares," he said. But "if you talk about it in performance art where it has a vibe and an energy to it, people will engage." The intrigue: Still, even Johnson recommends many of the basics for health: sleep, healthy diet and exercise. For those who want to go further, he recommends a blood draw or MRI, sitting in a sauna several times a week and testing out psychedelics. When asked which longevity treatments feel like snake oil, Johnson said "Basically everything on social media." When I pointed out that includes Bryan, he said, "you're right. I've done this for years. Most things don't work." Reality check: Johnson has multiple longevity businesses that he calls successful, though the financials of the companies are not public. Blueprint , his consumer products business, sells "the most tested healthy longevity protocols," per the company: protein powders, supplements and even extra virgin olive oil. Immortals , another one of his companies, offers concierge longevity care for a limited group of members. Prices range from $75,000 a year to $1 million per year. Johnson has "very complicated emotions about this business because I started the company to try to help other people and not to make money. ...I'd rather just be clean and be like, "I'm going to help you out." But to help people out, I have to have infrastructure to actually deliver these things." The intrigue: Johnson said he gets calls from world leaders asking for his advice, and he's in group chats with top tech leaders and influencers. When asked for his health advice for Elon Musk, Johnson said "I hope Elon would clean up his health. I mean, he's worked so hard. He has a lot of potential to enjoy what he's built." The bottom line: Johnson believes wealth is out, health and longevity are in as the new status symbols.

2fd8e7d6a811.text: Republicans have spent months griping privately to Fox News about coverage they argue is helping Abdul El-Sayed , Michigan's Democratic nominee for Senate, moderate his image. The frustration boiled into public view Tuesday when President Trump lashed out at his favorite network. Why it matters: Republicans worry that Fox is undercutting their efforts to brand the charismatic El-Sayed as a liberal who's far outside the mainstream. Polls show El-Sayed, a critic of Israel's government who'd be the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, in a tight race against former Rep. Mike Rogers (R). Behind the scenes: White House officials reached out to Fox on Tuesday to complain about anchor Martha MacCallum's interview with El-Sayed, according to people familiar with the conversations. On Truth Social, Trump blasted the interview as "softball." "Fox is promoting the Dumocrats, not the Republicans and MAGA. They have totally lost their way!" he wrote. The White House's frustration over Fox's coverage of El-Sayed had been bubbling for weeks before Trump's post. Senior GOP operatives repeatedly contacted Fox producers and executives in early August, warning that El-Sayed could use favorable commentary from host Jesse Watters to cast himself as moderate. After El-Sayed's upset primary win over an establishment-backed candidate, Watters said: "You gotta respect Abdul because he beat the [Democratic] machine." Later that month, El-Sayed released a TV ad featuring Watters' remark. His campaign called Watters an "unlikely validator." Republicans were reassured when Watters pressed El-Sayed on his criticism of ICE, support for Medicare for All and opinion on Sharia law during an Aug. 24 interview — only to be frustrated again when Watters said the next day: "I actually like Abdul. I probably shouldn't like him, but I do." State of play: Fox News has become a significant part of El-Sayed's effort to reach voters beyond the Democratic base. From Oct. 1 to 6, El-Sayed campaign ads aired 129 times on Fox News — roughly twice as often as they did on ESPN, according to ad-tracking data. Michigan-based GOP strategist Dennis Lennox told Axios: "It's not just that he is doing interviews with Fox. It's that he is on Fox every commercial break." Between the lines: Republicans acknowledge El-Sayed has shown he can hold his own under tough questioning — even when pressed on issues the GOP is using against him. El-Sayed said during Monday's interview with MacCallum: "I am going to have conversations with all kinds of folks." According to Fox, Watters' interview with El-Sayed in August drew nearly 3.4 million viewers, making it the highest-rated cable news primetime telecast of the month. Michigan-based GOP strategist Jason Roe told Axios: "They are doing him a favor. It's only helping him reach center-right voters. But they are in business to make money, and he attracts eyeballs." The other side: A Fox News spokesperson said Rogers also was invited to be interviewed on Watters' show but didn't respond. The White House didn't respond to a request for comment Wednesday. Jay Wallace , Fox News Media president and executive editor, told Axios on Tuesday that MacCallum's interview of El-Sayed reflected the network's willingness to air programming its core audience may not want to hear. "Someone didn't necessarily like that," Wallace said, apparently referring to Trump. "But that's what we do."

efed8cf514e4.text: AI's conquest of computer programming offered an early demonstration of what happens when models become good enough at a specialized field that experts can no longer treat them as a novelty. Mathematics appears to be next. Why it matters : OpenAI's latest mathematical results — which involved releasing hundreds of new proofs generated by a powerful, unreleased model — demonstrate that the startling advances of AI are likely to continue moving across entirely new fields. Catch up quick : OpenAI on Tuesday released 722 manuscripts organized into 372 groups of findings (" families ") on longstanding mathematical problems, inviting academics and researchers to examine and build on the material. The reception has mixed scientific excitement with genuine unease. One Rutgers University mathematician said on X that a result connected to the Riemann hypothesis would warrant an automatic Fields Medal if a human had done the work. Some mathematicians have questioned these results, as well as another solution OpenAI released last month, asking whether they represent original breakthroughs or draw heavily from previous human input. Others downplayed the utility of AI-generated math. "You can discover new math easily," Stephen Wolfram, a renowned computer scientist and physicist who has followed AI closely for years, said at a Tuesday event for the National Museum of Mathematics. "You can make a trillion theorems easily. The problem is most of those theorems are not ones that anybody will care about." Zoom in : Like computer programming, mathematics gives AI something unusually valuable: a way to tell when it is right. A proof can be scrutinized by mathematicians and, increasingly, translated into formal languages that computers can verify line by line. Similarly, it is immediately possible to know whether autonomously written AI code actually works. The big picture: Software engineers have already lived through this transition. AI coding tools progressed from autocomplete and debugging to agents capable of writing substantial amounts of software and carrying out complex engineering tasks. The shift has changed not only how code gets written, but what it means to be a programmer, bringing a fair dose of awe, amazement and dread to many lifelong software engineers. Much as software engineers did before them, mathematicians have begun to question the implications of some of the OpenAI discoveries on graduate work, and on training a new generation of theorists. Yes, but : Some software engineers have successfully mapped out the roles humans still play in generating quality products. While new AI coding tools have dramatically increased the code one engineer can ship, humans still play a crucial role in building quality software. Mathematicians have begun to echo that point, noting that the most meaningful advances in their field often involve building a framework or bringing structure to a complex idea. Many are skeptical about whether any AI system will be able to replicate human originality. Between the lines : Beyond mathematics, the results do point to the likelihood that AI disruption will continue moving into new areas, partially answering a longstanding question from AI skeptics. While researchers at rival startups questioned the utility of OpenAI's mathematical findings because of limited practical applications, some acknowledged that they provide evidence of AI's rapid advances.

e86eb0b8b880.text: Lawmakers are considering forcing data centers to shoulder new costs and restrictions while speeding up the energy infrastructure needed to power the AI boom. Why it matters: The bipartisan legislation, unveiled last week, represents the most aggressive response yet from Washington to data centers amid growing backlash over their energy and environmental impacts. Driving the news: The provisions are part of broader Senate legislation aimed at speeding up permitting for energy — but make no mistake: The data-center measures are significant and would go far beyond Washington's largely voluntary efforts to date. The bill's sponsors say it would accelerate energy development while ensuring data centers pay their share of grid upgrades. "I don't think we've seen it before," said Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School, about the proposed additional costs and restrictions. "But I don't think we've seen growth that's comparable to data centers today, and I certainly don't know any industry whose electricity usage has captured so much political attention." Between the lines: For tech companies, the bill cuts both ways. Congress would make it easier to build the energy infrastructure they need while erecting a sweeping framework aimed at keeping other electricity customers from footing the bill. "Just to be candid, having some teeth on data center accountability and ratepayer protection is just table stakes to getting a deal done," said Jane Flegal, a former White House official under President Biden and now a senior fellow at the nonprofit Searchlight Institute. The big picture: Congress has been talking about overhauling permitting for years. The AI boom has given lawmakers an urgent reason to finally act: America suddenly needs enormous amounts of new power infrastructure, fast. Faster approvals for power plants and transmission lines could directly benefit data centers struggling to secure enough electricity for their expansion. How it works: The bill reaches into virtually every part of the relationship between large data centers and the electric grid. Data centers would be required to pay both their share of the existing transmission network and the incremental transmission costs needed to serve them, reversing a decades-old federal pricing policy that generally prevents charging both. This is the biggie, but it doesn't stop there. New data centers of at least 20 megawatts would have to bear the incremental costs they impose across the power system, including generation, storage, transmission and distribution. Regulators at both the federal and state levels could charge large data centers even more than those incremental costs — and use the excess to reduce other customers' bills. Data centers would remain on the hook for infrastructure costs even if they stop buying electricity before those costs have been recovered. Utilities would also have to secure financial guarantees before building infrastructure to serve them, protecting ratepayers if projects don't materialize. Zoom in: States are already moving aggressively to protect ratepayers, with dozens of policies pending or in place across more than half the states aimed at making data centers shoulder more of the costs of serving them. The bill would explicitly give states wide latitude to go further, including treating data centers less favorably than other large industrial customers, competitively allocating access to electricity and requiring them to secure new power supplies or accept limits on electricity use. What they're saying: Not much publicly, yet. The Data Center Coalition, which represents companies across the industry, said it is still reviewing the legislation. Microsoft, Google and Nvidia declined to comment, while Meta didn't respond to a request for comment. Amazon energy policy director Craig Sundstrom said the aging grid and slow permitting are putting pressure on electricity costs, adding that the bill "could unlock the investment needed to build new generation and transmission faster." The intrigue: One tech industry official called some provisions an "unprecedented level of discriminatory treatment" for a single industry. The official, who spoke anonymously to discuss industry deliberations, said tougher grid-connected requirements could encourage some developers to build more power systems completely off-grid instead — potentially undermining the overarching purpose of the bill. The other side: Travis Fisher, a former Trump White House energy official now at the libertarian Cato Institute, said he has "mild support" for the approach despite concerns about setting a discriminatory precedent. He said the provisions "break new ground" at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission but are consistent with the White House's ratepayer-protection pledge many of the largest data center companies have already signed . What we're watching: Flegal said she would be "incredibly surprised" if tech companies ultimately oppose the broader package. What's next: With the Senate out of town ahead of the midterm elections, lawmakers and stakeholders have plenty of time to push for changes before a possible lame-duck debate.

77abbe608e2c.text:
Fewer Americans are keen on businesses taking public stances on issues than they were a year ago, a decline largely driven by Democrats.
Forty-seven percent support businesses taking stances on current events, per Gallup â down from a high of 51% last year, as the Trump administration engaged in high-profile fights with law firms, private universities, and other organizations.
While 62% of Democrats now say that businesses should be taking public stances, that has declined nine points since 2025. Just over a quarter of Republicans say the same, down five points.
Majorities back businesses taking stances on free speech, climate change, DEI, mental health, and healthcare, while far fewer support positions on abortion and religion.
Corporations that have cozied up to the Trump administration are likely to be on Democratsâ target list if they win a House majority next year and take over investigative powers.

The News
Nigeriaâs president is locked in a fierce reelection battle â one that is not just playing out among voters ahead of January polls, but pitting teams of lawyers and lobbyists against a lone litigant half a world away in California. Remarkably, this latter-day David just won a significant victory over Goliath.
For three years, Bola Tinubu has fought to keep old FBI records tied to a 1990s Chicago drug probe about him sealed, hiring US lawyers to support the Justice Department in the fight. His main adversary is not a political rival or a diaspora activist, however. Itâs a Freedom of Information Act litigant in California with no apparent connection to Nigeria who says he just wants to get to the truth.
Tinubuâs efforts to prevent disclosure have partly failed. In August, the FBI acknowledged for the first time that it holds an investigative file on him and alongside the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) has released hundreds of pages of partially redacted records.
The fight now underway is over whether that is enough. On one side is Tinubuâs team of US attorneys, led by Chicago firm Henderson Parks. On the other is Aaron Greenspan, founder of legal document website PlainSite, who argues more documents should be released, with fewer redactions.
The FBI declined to comment on this story. The DEA did not respond to requests for comment.
Know More
The case centers around an alleged heroin trafficking network run from Nigeria: A 1993 affidavit drafted by an Internal Revenue Service agent describes the scheme, and cites an associate of the narcotics-selling group as saying the networkâs ringleader â allegedly Mueez Adegboyega Akande, a businessman who had returned to Nigeria in 1990Â â directed its finances by phone and periodic US trips â and that Tinubu helped move money for him. In the 1990s, Nigerian rings often trafficked drugs from Southeast Asia to Chicago via couriers, according to the Justice Department.
The Nigerian president has repeatedly denied wrongdoing. And his links to the case have been known and partially reported within Nigeria, often in the run-up to elections where opponents have used it to raise questions about his past. But the latest release â though unlikely to materially affect the results of the upcoming election â once again concentrates attention on Tinubuâs time in the US.
A young Tinubu first arrived in Chicago in the 1970s to study accounting, graduating in 1979. By the time of the alleged scheme at the center of this case, he split time between Lagos and the US, having risen to treasurer at Mobil Oil Nigeria, and eventually winning a seat in Nigeriaâs Senate â all while still opening bank accounts, and moving âlargeâ amounts of money in the Chicago metro area, according to the IRS affidavit. Bank records cited show Tinubu went on to deposit nearly $1.9 million in Chicago-area accounts in 1990 and 1991. Tinubuâs then-employers at Mobil Oil told investigators his treasurer role did not involve moving large sums and that the company never authorized him to hold its funds personally.
US authorities said that several of the transactions were linked to the alleged drug-trafficking ringleader Akande and seized roughly $460,000 from accounts tied to Tinubu in a 1993 civil forfeiture, alleging that the money was likely the laundered proceeds of drug dealing. Tinubu was not criminally charged, and the case was dismissed with prejudice after the money was forfeited.
Tinubuâs US lawyers have argued that the latest files that Greenspan wants released are shielded by FOIA exemptions that protect against âan unwarranted invasion of personal privacy.â In a filing, the lawyers said that curiosity about a foreign leaderâs background was not a FOIA-protected interest, and described Greenspanâs requests as driven by Nigerian politics rather than by an effort to expose US agency misconduct.
They also said the records concern Tinubuâs life as a private âstudentâ who âshould retain his full privacy interests because he was not a public official in 1993.â However, Tinubu was not a student in 1993 â he had graduated over a decade earlier â and he was, in fact, a public official for most of that year, serving in Nigeriaâs Senate until November. Greenspan protested the inaccuracies in subsequent filings, and Tinubuâs team later recanted the claims.
In a statement to Semafor, Henderson Parks attorney Christopher Carmichael argued that commentary on the case had outpaced the facts: âInterested persons and parties are attempting to infer what they believe may be in undisclosed records, but that is speculation.â He said Tinubuâs team would not speculate on non-public records while the FOIA case was pending.
Tinubuâs aides have long presented the 1993 case as a closed civil matter. In a July statement, presidential spokesman Bayo Onanuga called it âa civil forfeiture case from 1993 â a matter long settled, with no criminal conviction or finding of guilt,â and added that the issue had been âthoroughly litigated, explained, and rendered mootâ by Tinubuâs electoral victories.
Representing himself, Greenspan said in an interview with Semafor that he had no personal or national stake in Nigerian politics and had kept his distance from partisans on both sides. He is not new to protracted fights with well-resourced opponents: A Los Angeles-area tech entrepreneur, Greenspan has spent years trading lawsuits with Elon Musk and Tesla, often alone and against larger legal teams. When a lobbyist for former Nigerian Vice President Atiku Abubakar â an electoral opponent of Tinubu â filed an amicus brief, Greenspan sought to make clear that the two were not working together.
The case has been a political flashpoint in Nigeria for years, flaring up ahead of the 2023 election that brought Tinubu to office and again now with the 2027 vote fast approaching. Along with the Washington lobbying firm working for Atiku, a different organization retained by the Nigerian government has targeted Greenspan o

b7ac2fab5d23.text: Republican super PACs are flooding the airwaves in once-safe states, and pulling down ads for races that look like lost causes. President Trump, his approval ratings near record lows, is popping up in some of America's reddest states. Why it matters: The polls showing Democrats headed toward a blue wave on Nov. 3 may not be quite right. But money — and how campaigns and PACs spend it — rarely lies. Nor do the contrails of Air Force One. While Republicans are scrambling, Democrats are cutting some spending in contests they think are in the bag, such as North Carolina's Senate race. No one wants to pay too much for a landslide, just as no one wants to throw good money after bad. Republicans have been forced to pour well over $100 million into Ken Paxton's Senate race in Texas against Democrat James Talarico, and to plead for millions more to defend Senate seats in Alaska, Iowa and Ohio. Call it political triage. Republican operatives are making the kind of hard decisions that would be familiar to any battlefield medic: Save the wounded, and say a prayer for the lost. Driving the news: Trump was in San Antonio on Wednesday to try to boost Paxton — his second trip in less than a week to Texas, a state he won by 14 points in 2024. During the past week the president also has campaigned in Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio and Nebraska. He's planning another trip to Alabama this weekend for the Georgia-Alabama football game. Vice President Vance showed up in Alaska this week, and will be in Ohio this weekend. What they're saying: Republicans' efforts now appear more focused on calling for party loyalists to show up at the polls than on persuading new voters. "Every time they up a buy [ads] on their end, it's always in the red states," said J.B. Poersch, president of Senate Majority PAC, the Democrats' main outside group working to win the Senate. "Some of these outside [GOP] groups such as the Senate Leadership Fund and others are going to have to figure out where their money is best spent," said Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who lost the GOP primary to Paxton. "It looks like the money has already started to shift." Zoom in: After pulling out of North Carolina (which Trump won by 3 points) last Friday, the SLF — Republicans' main Senate super PAC — put a fresh $14 million in normally deep-red Kansas. This week, it sent a $5 million "insurance policy" to South Carolina (which Trump won by 18 points) to boost Republican Sen. Darline Graham. The other side: Democrats are pulling down some advertising, but in states where polling has solidified in their favor. Their spending moves reflect confidence, not concern. After the Senate Republicans' PAC cried uncle and pulled out of North Carolina, the Senate Democrats' group decided to go dark there as well. One of Democratic group's ad reservations for North Carolina — which was actually in the Greenville market in South Carolina — was gobbled up by an allied group, Fresh Start SC PAC, which will use the time to attack Graham. Between the lines: There's triage campaigning in House races as well, but it's not as pronounced — yet. The GOP's Congressional Leadership Fund pulled down $1.1 million in advertising in Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District, one of three GOP-held seats where former Vice President Harris won in 2024. Democrats followed suit, with House Majority PAC canceling the $1.1 million it had reserved for the race. Both sides appear to agree that there's no obvious path for Republican Brinker Harding to win the seat left open by retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon. In a San Diego-area House district, the Democratic group pulled down $200,000 in ads in a redistricted seat Harris would have won. Zoom out: Republicans insist that their reallocation of funds doesn't mean they're admitting that the House or the Senate are lost. One thing neither side disputes: The Senate Leadership Fund, which is closely associated with Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), is well capitalized. That allows it to shore up candidates in red states, which wouldn't be necessary in a better political environment. In Texas, one of its subsidiaries spent $131 million in 17 days — more than $7.7 million a day. The group has announced another $4 million for the Alaska race, bringing its total there to $21 million for Sen. Dan Sullivan, who's being challenged by former Rep. Mary Peltola. In Maine, it has reserved another $8 million, for a total of $50 million for Sen. Susan Collins, who's in a battle with Democrat Troy Jackson. In Michigan, it's putting in another $2 million, for a total of $53 million for former Rep. Mike Rogers in his race against Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. And in Ohio, it's spending another $14 million, bringing the total to $93 million for Sen. John Husted, who faces former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D). What we're watching: All eyes are on Georgia. SLF announced an initial investment of $44 million there to back Republican Mike Collins, but Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has a healthy lead . The bottom line: Republicans can dismiss bad polls as noise, or the result of liberal bias. But their concern is evident in their thundering attack ads in red states such as Kansas, South Carolina and Texas.

a34a872631ed.text: House Speaker Mike Johnson raised $30 million in the third quarter, bringing his total haul this cycle to $156 million as Republicans fight to hold on to their increasingly endangered majority, Axios has learned. Why it matters: Johnson's team says that's the most raised by a Republican speaker or leader at this point in an election cycle. Johnson has distributed more than $91 million to Republican members, candidates, committees and state parties this cycle, according to figures first shared with Axios. That includes $46 million transferred to the National Republican Congressional Committee, putting him on pace to make the largest cycle transfer to the group by a Republican speaker or leader. He's also sent $21.5 million directly to GOP incumbents and $7 million to challengers. Zoom out: Johnson's fundraising operation has brought in more than $220 million for House Republicans since he became speaker in October 2023. That's a notable turnaround from when Johnson first took the gavel, when Republicans worried whether the relatively unknown Louisiana Republican could replace former Speaker Kevin McCarthy's formidable fundraising operation . Johnson is also crisscrossing the country to help House Republicans, traveling to more than 40 districts across 22 states in the final stretch before Election Day, Axios previously reported. What they're saying: "We are focused on getting unprecedented resources to the Districts that will decide the majority," Johnson said in a statement to Axios. "With this continued momentum, we are in place to defy history and defend the House to save America from the far-left!" State of play: House Republicans have a cash advantage over Democrats. The NRCC ended August with $13 million more in cash on hand than the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, its largest-ever advantage at this point in an election cycle. But the House battlefield has continued to move toward Democrats. Cook Political Report shifted 15 House races toward Democrats last month, while Sabato's Crystal Ball moved 11 races toward Democrats days later. Many of the most competitive races are now in districts President Trump carried in 2024.

a0db7eb39500.text:
‘Medicare for All’ Is Back. Now Comes the Hard Part.
Turning an inspirational slogan into law gets gnarly.
As Americans grow increasingly frustrated with their healthcare system, a proposal that has long been kicked around on the Democratic periphery is showing up in debates and on political platforms: “Medicare for All.”
According to a 2025 Economist-YouGov poll, nearly 60% of Americans favor a system of Medicare for All, while 85% of Democrats support it. For years, Democrats in Congress have proposed symbolic Medicare for All bills that have had no chance of passage but have been supported by dozens of members.
Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland added his support in December. “I was listening to my constituents,” he said. “It’s just reached the complete breaking point. Our system is unaffordable and unsustainable with premiums going up, copays going up and up.”
At a time when more than 100 million Americans carry medical debt, it’s easy to get behind a promise of free, or free-ish, no-hassle health care. But turning an inspirational slogan into law gets gnarly. Those three words, Medicare for All — a pledge to bring universal healthcare to every American — mean not one thing to supporters but many. And all versions of such a system face considerable obstacles to enactment.
“Medicare for All is a slogan, not a concrete proposal, so it’s hard to have an opinion on,” said Amy Finkelstein, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology economist who, with Stanford’s Liran Einav, wrote We’ve Got You Covered, which laid out what the pair considered a realistic and fiscally responsible plan for providing basic insurance to every American.
“What we can afford is a basic plan — what we call a shack, not a chateau,” Finkelstein said. Its bedrock would be a government-funded skinny plan less generous than Medicare, with potential constraints such as a limited number of physical therapy visits or stricter criteria for getting a knee replacement, but guaranteed robust basic coverage for catastrophic medical conditions. She estimated that most Americans would opt for supplemental coverage.
The most high-profile political proponent of Medicare for All this election season is Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic senatorial candidate in Michigan, who has made a more sweeping proposal central to his platform — far more chateau than shack. It would create one plan that covers a suite of medical needs with no cost to patients, including dental and vision care, which traditional Medicare doesn’t cover.
(Traditional Medicare has increasingly come to resemble private insurance with premiums and coinsurance, and, unlike standard commercial plans, it has no annual out-of-pocket maximum. To fill such gaps, patients buy separate Medigap and drug plans.)
“The most important thing is just to make Medicare whole — meaning no charge for medical care — rolling back the complexity and costs of the last 10 years,” El-Sayed told KFF Health News.
His program would start off covering children and adults five years younger than the current eligibility age for Medicare and close the gap over a period, he has estimated, of eight years. To ease the transition for the healthcare system, he would initially set the Medicare payment rates to mirror the totals doctors and hospitals receive now to avoid a “price shock” to their operations. Future increases would be limited to the rate of inflation.
One big question is how to make the financing work in a highly profitable industry. National health spending was projected to hit $5.7 trillion in 2025, or nearly 20% of the U.S. gross domestic product.
The United States spends twice as much on healthcare per person than many peer countries. And health insurance is often a company’s second-largest expense after payroll.
But how will the government divert financial outlays of employers and households into a new Medicare for All system without new taxes or massive government spending?
When polls ask voters whether they would support Medicare for All if it meant losing their insurance or paying new taxes, support often drops.
“You could decide to raise taxes and cover more,” Finkelstein said. “If you don’t want to cut current Medicare benefits, you could decide to bust the budget, which seems to be a common practice.”
Joe Biden said that, as president, he would veto any Medicare for All bill, given the cost, which was estimated at up to $40 trillion over 10 years. The bills in Congress don’t include very detailed financing plans.
Economists who have mapped out the possibilities are divided on a realistic path.
A group of Yale researchers estimated that converting to a Medicare for All program could save $450 billion annually. That’s in part because a government plan could negotiate — or simply set — far better prices for hospitals, doctors, drugs, and devices than private insurers. It would reduce the overhead created by private insurance with its army of negotiators, coders, and claim deniers — and reduce profits.
Strong forces are pushing back against such “rightsizing” of exorbitant prices, most notably: insurers, hospitals, and drug and device manufacturers. In 2022, they spent over $700 million on lobbying and have been a powerful force for job creation. But a grand Medicare for All proposal may simply be a strategy to open the debate to lesser possibilities. President Barack Obama’s initial Affordable Care Act proposal contained ambitious ideas — such as drug price negotiation — that fell by the wayside to get the votes for passage.
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico supports what he calls “Medicare for Y’all” — allowing people under 65 to buy into Medicare.
“There are versions of Medicare for All that could potentially include our proposal, and versions that could look extremely different,” Finkelstein said.
Support in some parts of the industry is growing.
According to one survey, more than half of all physicians have said they’d prefer some sort of single-payer system.

Medical Debt Is Crushing Hospital Patients in Los Angeles. Health Officials May Have a Fix.
LOS ANGELES — Every Tuesday, Naman Shah sees tuberculosis patients at a small public clinic in Los Angeles’ San Fernando Valley. Shah, a physician and epidemiologist at the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, pores over images of battered lungs, listens to labored breathing, and checks medications.
It’s part of an initiative dating to the early 20th century to control infections so tuberculosis doesn’t spread. “We like doing things upstream,” Shah said, “meaning before they happen, not after the damage is done.”
Today, Shah and his colleagues are applying the same principle to medical debt. A key part of that effort is a new system to allow every hospital in Los Angeles County to easily screen patients for financial aid. The goal: to stop low-income families from getting a bill that buries them in debt.
Shah estimates this system could prevent several hundred million dollars of medical debt every year.
Vicious Cycle
Nationwide, an estimated 100 million adults have some form of healthcare debt. In Los Angeles County, the nation’s most populous, public health officials calculate that about 800,000 residents have medical bills they can’t pay.
“The impacts of medical debt were staggering,” said Shah, who used to staff a rural health clinic in India and, since 2023, has led a county initiative in Los Angeles to tackle the debt problem.
“People end up with credit card debt and then a vicious cycle of high interest rates and poverty,” he said. “People forgo their prescriptions. People forgo appointments. And then you get into worse health.”
Hospitals typically offer financial aid to patients with low incomes. But information about assistance is often hard for patients to get. Applying can be cumbersome. And many eligible patients never seek aid, research shows.
“Most people walk into the hospital and walk out without any knowledge of financial assistance,” said Jared Walker, founder of Dollar For, a nonprofit that helps patients nationwide apply for aid, often called charity care.
That’s fueling debt. It’s also driving costly collection efforts that even hospital officials acknowledge pointlessly target low-income patients who are unlikely to be able to pay.
“They’re turning their wheels trying to collect on debt that isn’t collectable,” said Adena Tessler, regional vice president for the Hospital Association of Southern California.
Presumptive Eligibility
One potential solution is a system that automatically screens and qualifies low-income patients for financial aid without requiring an application. This is called presumptive eligibility.
Some hospitals already use such systems, which rely on software that checks patient eligibility based on publicly available information such as credit history.
The strategy can be very effective. Shah said hospitals that have deployed presumptive eligibility systems have reported as much as a 50% increase in the amount of financial aid they give patients.
Under a state law passed last year, all California hospitals will have to start doing presumptive eligibility screening by next July.
But the systems can be expensive and difficult for smaller hospitals to implement. Only about 1 in 5 hospitals in Los Angeles County currently use them, Shah said.
Public health officials wondered if they could help more hospitals set them up.
The county, which, like many local governments, faces major fiscal challenges, couldn’t pay for this, Shah said. But the public health department could bring together healthcare and hospital officials in the county to figure out another solution.
“The beauty of government is not when it always has to do the work,” Shah said. “We have the ability to make sure that people cooperate.”
The Hospital Association of Southern California, initially wary of the county initiative, came to see improving hospital financial aid programs as beneficial to hospitals, many of which were wasting money on collections. “The billing process is cumbersome and costly,” said Paul Young, a senior vice president with the association.
The association agreed to procure a presumptive eligibility system and make it available to its members. This bulk-purchasing approach, which Young compared to “a Costco model,” would lower the cost for individual hospitals, he said.
At the same time, L.A. Care, a nonprofit health plan that administers Medicaid coverage for more than 2.5 million low-income county residents, committed $2 million to set up the system.
The investment reflected the safety net insurer’s mission to make medical care accessible to more people, said Melanie Fontes Rainer, who leads strategic planning for L.A. Care. “It’s going to make Los Angeles County better,” she said.
Making It Work
Getting the new system up and running by January, as the partners hope, faces challenges.
Hospital officials are figuring out how the system will be funded in the long term. And it’s unclear how many of the county’s 88 acute care hospitals will ultimately use it, even if it’s cheaper and easier to access.
The partners are also working to improve data that the system relies on to screen patients. One goal is to link the system to tax records maintained by the state of California. This would provide hospitals with more accurate information on patients’ income than current systems, which often rely on estimated income.
Walker, the patient advocate at Dollar For, said he’s heartened by the county’s effort. “I’m optimistic that we can make a better charity care system,” he said. “And the fact that hospitals in Los Angeles County are willing to be innovative and creative about ways we can do that is super encouraging.”

Maryland environmental regulators say jet fuel continues to seep into Piscataway Creek from Joint Base Andrews more than six months after the spill was reported, despite the base’s assurances that it has isolated the damaged fuel system and stopped the leak.
“MDE remains deeply concerned about the ongoing environmental impacts and continues to observe signs of jet fuel coming from the site,” the Maryland Department of the Environment said in a written response. “Jet fuel continues to flush into the creek, particularly after heavy rain.”
In its response to Inside Climate News, the installation acknowledged that they continue to “actively contain and recover” spilled fuel trapped in soil that flushes into the creek during storms.
Piscataway Creek connects Joint Base Andrews, located in Prince George’s County, to the Potomac River near Fort Washington Park. The adjacent Piscataway Park provides public access points to the creek and the river for fishing and boating.
The initial incident drew criticism from lawmakers and environmental advocates over the base’s delay in reporting the spill. The fuel system failed a tightness test on Dec. 11, according to the MDE, which said the base’s leak detection system failed multiple times between January and March, spilling roughly 32,000 gallons of jet fuel into the creek.
The agency said it was not notified until fuel odors and a sheen were seen near the creek’s headwaters on March 23, and the base did not report the full extent of the discharge until April 8. The MDE, which has enforcement authority under state environmental regulations, then ordered the military facility to carry out an emergency soil investigation, install monitoring wells and remediate contaminated soils.
Differing estimates of how much fuel has spilled has complicated the mitigation work. A May letter nine members of Maryland’s Congressional delegation sent to U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink described approximately 32,000 gallons leaking across multiple dates and locations. Approximately 10,000 gallons from January and February incidents were reportedly contained within the fuel infrastructure and approximately 22,000 gallons were discharged into the environment.
The lawmakers asked for an accounting of how much fuel had entered the creek and how much remained underground, along with plans to prevent further contamination during rain events.
In its June 22 reply, the Air Force said the pressure-test failure on Dec. 11 was caused by a faulty valve that did not release fuel into the environment but distorted pressure readings. It said the anomaly delayed leak detection until the fuel was detected in the waters on March 23.
“JBA did not notify MDE of the failed pressure tests,” the Air Force said, adding that the matter is part of an ongoing internal investigation.
The Air Force did not provide the exact volume of the spill, saying it was “not yet possible” to determine how much fuel remained in soil, groundwater and the creek, and said it had recovered more than 35,000 gallons of a fuel-water mixture from the creek, a value the MDE has yet to verify.
“Over six months since the jet fuel leak was reported, JBA has yet to identify the exact location of the leak, diagnose the cause of the failure, or take appropriate action to fix the problem,” MDE representatives told Inside Climate News in the latest response.
In background interviews, agency officials vented their frustration that despite repeated requests over months, the base continues to stonewall requests for site-specific information, such as a basic site model displaying a map of fuel lines, creeks and environmental assets nearby, or the precise location of the crack in the underground fuel line. It has also not carried out standard subsurface probing to map the contamination plume under the tarmac. Under state oil control rules, agency officials noted, handlers of jet fuel are expected to account for every drop and quantify spills and the installation has not met that basic requirement.
The base did not respond to allegations that the MDE’s requests for information have been rebuffed. It offered a different assessment of the situation on the ground.
“The compromised section of the hydrant system was identified, isolated, and completely drained to eliminate any residual risk of fuel contaminating a water source,” a JBA spokesperson said in emailed comments. They did not say when this correction took place.
Asked whether its assertion that “the active leak has been stopped” meant the spilled fuel was no longer entering the creek, the spokesperson clarified that the assessment applied specifically to “fuel escaping from the infrastructure.”
The base further stated that its June testing could not conclusively determine the location and cause of the leak, and a pressure test is planned within the next few weeks. “The exact timeline for repairs will be dependent on the test results and subsequent engineering assessments,” it said, and that the affected sections would remain drained and isolated until repairs and retesting were completed.

Tight polls for Republicans are throwing future GOP leadership of the Senate health panel into question.
With Sens. Roger Marshall, R-Kansas, and Susan Collins, R-Maine, fighting difficult reelection battles, itâs unclear who will replace Louisiana Sen. Bill Cassidy as the top Republican on the Senate HELP Committee.
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., is the next most senior person, but he would have to give up leading the Homeland Security Committee to helm the health panel. And Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, another member, could be in line to be the top GOP appropriator if Collins loses her reelection bid.
Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., would be next up after Paul and Murkowski, but he already leads the Senate Banking Committee.
Itâs not impossible that Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley, a staunch abortion opponent, lands the role opposite Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., on the committee.

The News
Democrats are hoping to persuade Latino voters to get out and vote for their candidates in droves in the midterms. A Latino organization says theyâll have the best chance of doing that by presenting solutions to the economy, housing, and abuses by ICE.
Polling by Voto Latino shared first with Semafor shows 40% of Latinos backing Democrats on the generic ballot, while just 21% support Republicans.
The group argues that bringing more Latinos into the Democratic fold will require running on solutions to pocketbook issues: Latino voters rank the cost of necessities as their top frustration, and view food and housing costs as most unreasonable.
âThis is where Democrats really have an opportunity to really bring back Latinos back to their corner,â said Beatriz Lopez, Voto Latinoâs executive director. âI think this is a pure opportunity, and itâs not to be wasted because if they waste it right now, itâs going to be even harder in â28.â
Know More
Voters are looking for âsome long-term solutions, some short-term solutions,â said Lopez. Among those surveyed, Latinos who didnât vote in 2024 were more likely than those who had voted to have economic frustrations, like struggling to earn enough money or find a good job.
âWhat we see in this poll is the people that are struggling the most are the ones who want the most,â said Voto Latino deputy director Ameer Patel.
Republicans have been hoping that the shift of Latino voters towards Trump and Republicans in 2024 would be part of a more durable trend, and drew new congressional districts in Florida and Texas to favor Republicans that relied in part on the Latino voting trends. Democrats, on the other hand, have hoped Latino voters would return to the left, motivated by economic concerns and the Trump administrationâs immigration enforcement.
Immigration still remains a major issue for Latino voters. Asked about immigration solutions for Congress to tackle, Latino voters polled picked investigating ICE as a top priority, alongside immigration changes like a pathway to citizenship and ending the immigration detention of children and families.

The News
A bipartisan pair of senators wants to do something bold before a new Congress takes over: Fix the Senateâs frequently maligned rules.
No, Sens. Jeff Merkley, D-Ore., and Steve Daines, R-Mont., donât want to end the filibuster. But they have a proposal that would allow more bipartisan bills to get votes, end time-wasting procedures, and actually allow popular bills to come to the Senate floor and pass, according to details reviewed by Semafor.
âMore bills passed, more votes taken, less time wasted. That sums up,â Daines told Semafor in a joint interview with Merkley.
Itâs a big undertaking for the odd couple, but the effort has more momentum behind it than one would expect. Merkley is the Senateâs resident rules expert and has literally written the book on Senate gridlock. Daines, who is retiring, is close to two of the people theyâll need on board to pass the proposal: President Donald Trump and Senate Majority Leader John Thune. When Daines started exploring how to fix the Senate, all roads led to Merkley, who wrote Democratsâ last rules change proposal and spearheaded the push to end the 60-vote threshold for nominees.
The senators told Semafor they hear plenty of complaints from their colleagues about the Senateâs sluggish progress as an institution. One senator can force a week of debate on a popular bill, the government often runs on zombie continuing resolutions, and securing an amendment vote often requires consent from all 100 senators. Whatâs more, plenty of time is wasted for antiquated time rules like the âintervening dayâ on legislation or âpost-cloture timeâ â things Senate hopefuls arenât exactly briefed on when they launch their campaigns.
ââWe had productive professional lives in functional institutions, and what the hell happened to the Senate?ââ Merkley said, summing up complaints heâs heard from colleagues. âThe American people are saying the same thing.â
âOne thing you see here is people thinking about going home and being a governor. Why? Because states are not paralyzed the way the US Senate and House are,â the Oregon Democrat added. Daines agreed: âWe have morale challenges now in the United States Senate.â
Know More
The two senators have four major asks: They want to get rid of procedural (known as cloture) votes to begin debate on nominees, bills, and amendments while retaining the ability for the lawmakers in the minority to oppose efforts to close debate on controversial bills via the filibuster. Under their proposal, the intervening day before a vote to break a filibuster would be eliminated and debate time condensed, removing dead time from the Senate floor.
They also want to establish a fast-track suspension calendar, not unlike the House, that would allow the Senate to more quickly take up bills at a supermajority requirement of two-thirds of the Senate. Debate time for those bills would be limited and require coordination from committee leaders in both parties to get on the fast-track.
Daines and Merkley also want committee leaders to have a one-day fast-track for considering popular bills with strong committee support from both parties that would allow those bills to pass the Senate with a simple majority. Finally, their proposal would give Appropriations Committee leaders a quick route to the Senate floor for popular spending bills with plentiful spending amendment opportunities.
Itâs a tradeoff that would still allow the Senate minority to stop party-line bills or those without broad support and require real work by committee chairs and ranking members to get their products on the Senate floor.
But it would ensure that, like the House, a bill with two-thirds support can come to the floor quickly. It would minimize the ability of a single senator to block bills with huge support, like last week when Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., blocked the popular Kids Online Safety Act.
âThe goal here is to not make this a political fight. I think what we have proposed here is durable, regardless of which party is in power. We realize the benefits, no matter if Ds or Rs have a gavel,â Daines said. âAcross the last four Congresses, there have been 665 bipartisan bills passing through committees that go to the elephant graveyard.â
The pair is already talking to their respective party leaders about modernizing the Senate rules and theyâre optimistic about getting it passed at the required 67-vote threshold for a rules change. Daines is keeping Thune apprised.
Thune spokesman Ryan Wrasse said âThune is always open to discussing ways to make the Senate function in a more effective and efficient way, and he applauds Sen. Daines for thinking outside the box. Since no rules change can be implemented unilaterally, building a bipartisan consensus will be key to any modification of the existing process.â
Merkley said he talked to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and the Democratic leader âdidnât say, âstop the discussion.ââ
Schumer and Thune ârecognize that there is frustration and dysfunction that merits a conversation,â Merkley said.
Trump, of course, wants to just kill the filibuster entirely. But Daines said the presidentâs team is engaged in their talks too.
âWe also ran the traps with key players in the White House. And got a thumbs up on it,â Daines said.
In an ideal world, they said theyâd also move the Senate more toward a talking filibuster and restrict the use of party-line budget reconciliation bills in order to reduce deficit spending. But they are starting with what they believe are broadly popular proposals that could get the chamber to devote a time to debate the rules â preferably before Daines leaves office.
That hasnât happened for awhile. Recent changes to Senate precedent have been made using the unilateral ânuclear optionâ which can be done in a party-line fashion by the majority. The next time a party uses the nuclear option to change Senate rules, they might nuke the supermajority requirement altogether, Merkley warned.
