a050e963d359.text: By — Adriana Morga, Associated Press Adriana Morga, Associated Press By — Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press Wyatte Grantham-Philips, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/your-child-may-be-automatically-enrolled-in-a-trump-account-heres-what-to-know Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Your child may be automatically enrolled in a Trump Account. Here's what to know Nation Oct 9, 2026 9:44 AM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — Whether you realize it or not, your child may be enrolled in a "Trump Account." Rolled out earlier this year, the Trump Accounts program allows parents to claim special investment accounts for children who are 18 years old or younger. And some babies are eligible to receive a one-time $1,000 contribution from the government. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Now, because of automatic enrollment highlighted Wednesday by President Donald Trump, the Treasury Department says every eligible child with a valid Social Security number has a Trump Account. But parents and legal guardians would still need to formally activate the accounts if they haven't already. WATCH: Trump announces eligible U.S. children automatically enrolled in Trump accounts Here's what we know. How Trump Accounts work The accounts are a savings tool that invests money in the stock market on a child's behalf. The child can't access the money until they turn 18 and can use it only for specific purposes, such as paying tuition, starting a business or making a down payment on a home. Families can activate an account through the program's trumpaccounts.gov website or its mobile phone app. WATCH: How 'Trump accounts' for children work, and who will benefit most The government will make a $1,000 contribution for some babies after the account is claimed. To qualify for the $1,000 seed money, a baby must be a U.S. citizen, have a Social Security number and be born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028 — covering Trump's current term. Any parent — regardless of their immigration status — can open an account for a qualifying child. Parents of older children also are encouraged to open accounts. Even though they aren't eligible for the government's $1,000 contribution, some older children are eligible for seed money of $250 drawn from separate investments from wealthy donors. Watch the PBS News Hour segment in the player above. Otherwise, family contributions will need to come out of pocket. Parents can contribute up to $2,500 annually in pretax income, much like retirement accounts. Employers, relatives, friends, local governments and philanthropic groups can also pitch in. Yearly contributions are capped at $5,000, although contributions from governments and charities don't count toward that total. Private banks and brokerages will manage the money. When the accounts were originally conceived, investments were restricted to broader index funds. But with updated rules from the Treasury Department late last month, eligible wealthy investors can now also donate stock from individual companies. Automatic enrollments — but not activation of accounts With automatic enrollment, Trump said 70 million children will now have the accounts, up from 8 million created since their launch in July. Researchers from the Brown School's Center for Social Development at Washington University in St. Louis advocated for the automatic enrollment. And Jin Huang, co-director of the center, called the administration's move "a big step." READ MORE: What experts want you to know about the Trump accounts and a new massive donation "Automatic enrollment is the most important policy design feature for early wealth building programs, in order to ensure full inclusion of all eligible children," said Huang, citing research from his team. Still, he says, more work needs to be done. Parents and legal guardians need to formally claim the accounts to activate them — as well as elect the $1,000 seed money if they're eligible — and Huang says "each of these steps will lower the participation," with particular barriers facing low-income families who may not already have access to similar investments. Wealthy investors can now donate individual stocks When Trump Accounts were first rolled out, investments were initially restricted to broad index funds — in theory to decrease risk while still yielding incremental growth. But among additional updates to the program, eligible wealthy investors can now also donate stock from individual companies. WATCH: Trump officially launches Trump Accounts for kids, ringing Wall Street opening bell "It's a way to encourage participation in the program," explained Nathan C. Goldman, a professor of accounting at North Carolina State University. He said many of the world's wealthiest people don't have "a whole lot of liquid cash sitting around" and might instead turn to shares. Still, he notes, individual stocks are more volatile than indexes. And families wouldn't get a say about which companies might donate to their children's portfolios. Once a child turns 18, they can access the money It's important to note that the child won't be able to access the money until they turn 18, except in rare circumstances. So the money can't help with immediate expenses. But once a beneficiary of a Trump Account turns 18, they can choose to use the money from it however they want. Trump account beneficiaries can also choose to roll the investment over to a Roth IRA account. "You're extending the life of this thing beyond the 18 years; you're going all the way out into the child's potential retirement," said Myranda Fabian, a certified financial planner with Plante Moran Financial Advisors. Moving the earnings from a Trump Account to a Roth IRA will be subject to taxation. Roth

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of an "all-out invasion" of its northern Tigray region and warned it will defend itself, days after residents told the BBC Eritrean troops had crossed into the country.
In a letter to the UN Security Council, Ethiopia's foreign minister called it a "blatant act of aggression that engages Ethiopia's inherent right to self-defence", following reported strikes on Eritrean troops in Tigray.
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel responded by saying it was facing "an unprovoked war of aggression" from its neighbour.
Fighting broke out between the government and the party that controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), two weeks ago.
Both blame each other for violating a 2022 deal that ended its civil war. Ethiopia says Eritrea backs the TPLF, which it denies.
During the two-year civil war, Eritrea was a key ally of the Ethiopian government, having fought alongside them against the TPLF.
But relations between the two neighbours have since deteriorated - largely over the Ethiopian prime minister's ambition to take ownership of one of Eritrea's Red Sea ports - leading to the severing of diplomatic ties last week.
Accusing Eritrea of violating its sovereignty, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said Eritrean forces had advanced up to 60km (37 miles) into Tigray.
Ethiopian drone strikes reportedly targeted Eritrean forces in the Tigrayan town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday, amid fears of a wider regional war.
US-based conflict monitor Acled said "Eritrean troops and ammunition" in Adigrat were hit by "multiple drone strikes" overnight.
One resident told AFP news agency "there were many, many drone strikes", and that some Eritrean lorries had been destroyed.
Another witness said Eritrean forces appeared to be retreating north after the strikes, AFP reported.
Dated 8 October, Ethiopia's letter to UN Security Council members read: "In this time of difficulty, when Ethiopia is left with no other option but to defend itself, we count on your understanding, support, and solidarity."
But while Ethiopia accuses its neighbour of supporting the TPLF, Eritrea has blamed the conflict on Ethiopia's leaders, and accused them looking for a reason to seize Eritrean territory.
On Friday, Eritrea's information minister called the accusations levelled against Asmara as "duplicity in their most extreme forms".
In a post on X, he said Ethiopia was "openly working to bring about regime change in Eritrea by providing shelter and support to certain mercenaries who claim to be opposition".
Eritrea gained independence from Ethiopia in 1993, but ties were only normalised in 2018, when Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power.
This latest unrest follows months of tension and the launch of new alliance of armed groups in Ethiopia - including the TPLF - in September.
Last week, TPLF forces withdrew from Tigray's main city of Mekelle, which is 115km (71 miles) south of Adigrat and is now under army control.
Additional reporting by Kaleb Moges

d9bef991e55b.text: Congress has its best chance in years to pass sweeping permitting legislation, but a series of political and policy obstacles could derail the bipartisan Senate plan. Why it matters: Cutting hurdles for energy projects is a top priority for fossil fuels and renewables sectors, and major business groups more broadly. Here are five risks to a lame-duck deal: 👱‍♂️ President Trump himself. The White House says it supports the bill, but Trump is mercurial, so nothing is final until it's final. His administration's willingness — or not — to loosen the screws on wind and solar projects it's restricting could also sway the lame-duck politics and complicate efforts to win Democratic support. Flashback: Co-author Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) last month cited "unresolved" questions about Trump officials returning to "regular order" for renewables, but credited their "very reasonable" proposal. 🗳️ A big blue wave. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), a senior House Democrat, has been arguing that Democrats will have more leverage next year. For now, there's little evidence that view is gaining traction among Democrats. The few definitive statements on the bill from lawmakers in both parties are supportive. But a strong Democratic showing in November could change that calculation. The big arguments against waiting: Dems won't have 60 votes even if they take the Senate, and Trump still needs to sign anything, limiting the prospects for a better deal next year. 🟩 Environmentalists. Groups with close ties to Dems — such as the Natural Resources Defense Council, League of Conservation Voters and Evergreen Action — are still weighing their positions on the bill. A coordinated push against it could make it harder for Democratic lawmakers to back the legislation. ⚡ Utilities. Regulated utilities would see new competition in transmission development and greater oversight of their planning and business. American Electric Power and Berkshire Hathaway Energy support the bill , but the sector's trade group — the Edison Electric Institute — has not taken a position. ⏰ The lame-duck squeeze. A busy legislative calendar, potential changes to the bill and uncertainty about lawmakers' appetite for legislating after the election could leave too little time to secure passage through both chambers. Already, House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) told Punchbowl News that he wants to modify the electricity provisions. If Republicans lose the House majority, their willingness to push a major bipartisan deal across the finish line could diminish. "It's hard to convince people to hang around and wait for something to happen when they're being constantly reminded that they lost," Jeff Navin , a former Democratic Hill staffer and co-founder of clean tech lobbying firm Boundary Stone Partners, said via email. The bottom line: This is a partial list! To riff on Mickey Rourke's advice to William Hurt in the great 1981 noir flick "Body Heat," there are 50 ways to mess up any bill, and if you can think of 25, you're a genius. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

- Published
The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified following concerns raised by other scientists that it was fake.
Nikon said the use of generative AI in the composition of the video broke the rules of its Small World In Motion contest, which accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes.
The firm said the video "did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI", but added it was not a judgement of the entrant's professional reputation or scientific contributions.
It said it would now look at the rules and procedures of the annual contest, which has been running for 15 years and is specifically for microscopic images.
Nikon said it came to the decision "after thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel".
The winning entry came from Dr Ning Xu, from Tsinghua University in China, who submitted a short video showing tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving in the airway of a child with the respiratory condition PCD.
The BBC has approached him for comment.
A number of scientists, including former competition judges, complained to Nikon on its LinkedIn page that the video did not appear to be real.
Xu had acknowledged using AI, but said he believed he had acted within the rules, and had cooperated with Nikon's investigation.
University of Leicester scientist Dr Robert Hirst, who was among the first experts to voice concerns, said he was "not surprised" and he "knew immediately that the video was fabricated".
"I have been diagnosing PCD for 20 years by examining their cilia waveform, length, cell size and shape," he said.
Hirst, who is lead scientist for the NHS centre for PCD diagnosis at the university, said the cells and cilia "look nothing like those from PCD patients".
"This controversy has impacted a lot of patients, scientists, doctors and PCD support networks around the world," he said.

In the Grand Canyon, rock layers preserve a relatively continuous record of Earth’s geologic history going back about 2 billion years. But between 520 million and 1.8 billion years, the record is noticeably empty. It’s as if someone broke into a museum and made off with almost an entire wing’s worth of rocks, and sorting out “whodunnit” is one of the coldest cases in all geology.
Now, scientists studying the Grand Canyon’s rocks say that a gigantic Earth-spanning cliff —with a global glaciation as its accomplice — could be to blame for the heist.
The giant cliff started forming about 800 million years ago as an ancient supercontinent called Rodinia split apart, Thomas Gernon, an earth scientist at the University of Southampton in England, and colleagues report August 17 in Geology. Forces like rain and ice weathered and eroded the rock and, like waves at the beach steadily erasing one layer of sand after another, deleted a billion years of Earth’s history.
The group used computer models to simulate how ancient Earth evolved over hundreds of millions of years. They watched as the cliff — known as an escarpment — formed around the time in Earth’s history when rocks in the region vanished.
The escarpment most likely extended across much of a continent called Laurentia, the ancient precursor to North America. It stretched from what was to become Alaska all the way to Arizona and would have been about one to two kilometers high.
Spanning a continent
Some 65 million years ago, the Great Escarpment of Laurentia would have stretched across much of North America, including the spot that would one day become the Grand Canyon and the site of an enduring geologic mystery. The escarpment itself is thought to have formed around 800 million years ago.
“No study has previously suggested the existence of a continental-scale escarpment in the Grand Canyon region. Our study shows it’s a plausible, straightforward explanation for the immense erosion that took place in the Grand Canyon,” Gernon says. Such an immense cliff created steep slopes that were ideal places for the elements to loosen and make off with exposed rock.
And the escarpment had a lot of help when it came to its disappearing act: ice, lots and lots of ice. The theft of the rocks coincided with an extreme period of glaciation called Snowball Earth. Massive ice sheets formed and may have extended all the way from the poles to equatorial latitudes. As the ice expanded, it would have eroded great quantities of rock, helping create the gap in the record.
And the escarpment, due to its high elevation, would have created ideal conditions for Snowball Earth glaciers and ice sheets to form. In a separate study published in Science, Gernon and a team explained how an escarpment created by tectonic activity was responsible for the formation of the East Antarctic Ice Sheet starting some 34 million years ago. “The exposed rocky peaks of the escarpment would have acted as glacier factories,” Gernon says.
It remains unclear, however, whether the erosion that erased the rocks occurred before, during or after the Snowball Earth glaciations. “That’s the real hole that needs filling: pinning down the erosion history in space and time, continent by continent, precisely enough,” Gernon says.
Linking the disappearance of the rocks to verified events in Earth’s history such as the breakup of Rodinia bolsters the case, says Alan Collins, a geologist at Adelaide University in Australia who was not involved in the new study. Not only that, but Gernon’s team points to modern-day examples where similar erosive processes are at work, including a similar escarpment in Antarctica as well as one in South Africa.
Maybe not quite case closed yet, but “I find this very convincing,” Collins says.

Former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge Navi Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize.
The South African judge was recognised "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.
Pillay, 85, has taken part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations during a decades-long career, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.
Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.
Pillay's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee JÃ¸rgen Watne Frydnes.
"Navi Pillay's commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career," he said.
"At a time of existential challenges - including more wars and conflicts than the world has seen in a long time - international law is no longer just a supplement to peace and security. It is an absolute necessity."
Frydnes said the committee had not been able to notify Pillay that she had won in advance, "so my message to her would be 'if you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up'".
Shortly afterwards, Pillay reacted to the news by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her.
"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked. Last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition leader MarÃa Corina Machado, gave her medal to the US president in January as "recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom".
Navanethem "Navi" Pillay grew up in South Africa during apartheid as a bus driver's daughter in a poor Indian section of Durban.
She went on to become the first woman to establish a law practice in Natal Province in 1967, and later the first non-white woman to be appointed to the country's high court.
Pillay served as a judge on the UN-backed International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda - focused on the 1994 genocide in which 800,000 people were killed - including four years as its president.
From 2021-25, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory - a fact-finding body established by the UN Human Rights Council to investigate alleged violations of international law.
The commission concluded that Israel had committed genocidal acts in Gaza and that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, had "incited the commission of genocide" in their speeches and statements.
The three-member expert panel did not speak officially for the UN and had no legal authority. Israel rejected its findings and accused the three members of the commission of serving as "Hamas proxies".
The panel had previously concluded that Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups committed war crimes and other grave violations of international law on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and another 251 taken hostage. The same report also accused Israel of war crimes.
Reacting to Pillay's award on Friday, Israel's Foreign Ministry said it represented a "grotesque weaponisation of an award to legitimise anti-Israel hatred and prejudice".
It said in a statement: "Her role in the relentless, politically motivated demonisation of Israel and promotion of the genoLIE speaks volumes."
Frydnes said the Nobel organisation was not taking a position on whether the Israeli offensive in Gaza amounted to genocide.
Pillay is currently a judge on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in the case where Myanmar stands accused by The Gambia of genocide against the Rohingya people.
Myanmar has denied deliberately trying to destroy the minority Muslim population, with a government representative telling the court in January that the allegation was "unsubstantiated".
UN human rights chief Volker Turk said Pillay's recognition was "a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice, and accountability are fundamental to everything, to peace, to security, and prosperity".
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa said she had been a "pioneering defence attorney for anti-apartheid activists" who had worked to "uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally".
Amnesty International Secretary-General AgnÃ¨s Callamard said she was with Pillay when she learned she had won - and called her an "inspired choice" for the award.
"At a time when both international law and justice are under attack, when too many states attempt to hollow them out, her Nobel Peace Prize could not come at a better time," she said.

Convicted murderer Christa Pike is walking and talking in limited ways in her hospital room about a week after authorities in the US state of Tennessee botched her execution, her lawyers say.
Pike, 50, was sent to hospital after surviving two attempts to execute her via lethal injection for the 1995 murder of a 19-year-old she met at a summer camp for troubled teens.
An independent review of what went wrong in the Nashville execution chamber on 30 September has been ordered by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee.
He has also halted executions in the state for the rest of the year.
Warning: This article contains details that readers may find distressing
How did Pike survive?
The Tennessee Department of Correction is yet to say why the execution did not go as planned, though it has defended the method it used.
Dr Joel Zivot, an anaesthesiologist advising Pike's defence team, says it was not the case that Pike had some "special immunity" but suggested it was simply that not enough of the drug pentobarbital reached her bloodstream to kill her.
Pike was injected with a second dose of the drug, according to the prison authorities' protocol, after the first did not kill her.
In interviews with the BBC, Zivot has suggested the pentobarbital was more likely to have spread across the tissue under Pike's skin than to have entered her bloodstream.
"Most of the pentobarbital, instead of circulating in her body, ended up in her arms, and that's how she lived," Zivot said.
Pike's medical condition of thrombocytosis, a blood-clotting condition, was highlighted in advance by Pike's legal team as an additional issue that could scupper the process. Before the attempted execution, they had filed a legal case challenging the injection protocol.
If clots of blood formed at the injection site as a result of thrombocytosis, they would potentially have blocked the chemical from entering her veins, the lawyers warned.
As the attempted execution took place, prison officials used at least seven needles on Pike during their efforts to establish intravenous (IV) lines, Pike's lawyers said afterwards. The woman could simultaneously be heard "crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly".
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who was murdered by Pike and her then-boyfriend, told NBC the failed execution had been "a mess".
The Tennessee Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out".
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.
After it became clear that Pike was not going to die from the two doses, she was taken to hospital for life-saving treatment. States have a legal obligation not to deny medical treatment to prisoners.
What is pentobarbital?
Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions, but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.
Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use in federal executions, but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.
The Tennessee correction department has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded".
But the department said the lethal injection chemical had "consistently been effective".
What happens next?
The full picture of Pike's current physical condition is unknown.
Although she was said to be awake and speaking in hospital as of 6 October, and walking short distances around her room as of the next day, it remains unclear whether she has any long-term health defects.
At one stage she was reported by her lawyers to still be handcuffed to her bed.
There is then the question of what happens to Pike next.
Executions in the state have been paused for the rest of the year. During a court hearing on 7 October, a lawyer for Tennessee said the decision on scheduling a new execution date was up to the state's supreme court.
Meanwhile, an investigation is taking place into what happened. During the hearing, a judge ordered state authorities to preserve all evidence related to the failed execution.
The state's Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada is stepping down.
Pike's lawyers have made repeated calls for Lee to use his powers as state governor to commute her sentence to the lesser punishment of life in prison without parole.
Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
In 2024, it allowed Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, using an experimental oxygen deprivation method, after their plan to kill him by lethal injection failed two years earlier.
The Supreme Court has already been involved in Pike's case: it allowed the lethal injections to go ahead after a legal battle.
Has this happened before?
While there is a lengthy history of botched executions across the US, Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived after receiving a lethal injection.
Deborah Denno, a criminologist and professor at Fordham Law School, said she was "absolutely astonished" that Pike is conscious and speaking.
There had been seven previous cases in which prisoners survived executions, but in those cases, executioners were not able to inject anything into the inmates' veins, Denno told the BBC.

The Trump administration has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), saying it wants to restrict the tribunal's resources and ability to operate.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.
The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.
The announcement comes just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law.
US President Donald Trump has reacted sourly to the Norwegian prize's choice of winner this year and last, after having expressed a desire to receive it himself. He criticised Pillay for being part of a panel that accused Israel, as well as Hamas, of war crimes during the 7 October conflict.
The US says the ICC has no jurisdiction over it as it never ratified the statute founding it - but the international court has investigated US actions elsewhere.
Rubio said Trump would not allow the ICC to prosecute Americans, adding: "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC."
The US sanctions will stop US companies from providing goods or services to the ICC, such as banking or software.
Rubio said Washington had delayed imposing the sanctions in the hope that the ICC and its member countries would address US concerns. He said the measures had been structured to allow other countries to negotiate a possible solution.
He also called on US allies that were ICC signatories to "rein in" the institution.
The ICC responded by saying that the sanctions were aimed at disrupting its work and intimidating those who co-operate with it - but that it "will not be deterred".
The Trump administration has repeatedly criticised the court, including over its investigation into the actions of US forces in Afghanistan, a probe it has since deprioritised.
It has also been critical of the ICC issuing arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

fe5a664df615.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/the-plague-never-went-away-cases-are-reported-in-parts-of-africa-and-the-u-s-nearly-every-year Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter The plague never went away. Cases are reported in parts of Africa and the U.S. nearly every year Health Oct 9, 2026 11:54 AM EDT The plague, the rare bacterial infection infamously known for killing tens of millions in 14th-century Europe, never went away. It is now easily treated with antibiotics. Since the 1990s, most human cases have been reported in Africa, especially Congo and Madagascar, according to the World Health Organization. READ MORE: What we know so far about a Russian lab worker's death and pneumonic plague There are an average of about seven human cases per year in the U.S., according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, mostly in rural areas of the American West. A worker at a plague research institute in Siberia recently died of pneumonia. The case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague. Russian authorities say testing showed no evidence of plague, but the research institute has been quarantined. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "People think the plague is gone, it was something that occurred 500 years ago. It's not. It's here amongst us," said Simon Clarke of the University of Reading in the U.K. "Unless you get rid of those wild animals, which of course is not possible, then you're not going to get rid of the bacteria." Surprised to hear the plague is still around? Here's what to know. Plague can attack lymph nodes, lungs and blood People in Siberia have been dying of plague for at least 5,500 years. The earliest evidence of a form of the disease was found in teeth from ancient hunter-gatherers north of the region's Lake Baikal. Pneumonic plague and the more well-known bubonic plague — also called the Black Death — are caused by the same bacteria, called Yersinia pestis. The bacteria spread naturally among rodents like prairie dogs and rats. Fleas that jump from infected animals and bite people can spread the disease. WATCH: Understanding pneumonic plague after Russian lab worker's death The bubonic plague is the most common form of the infection. It causes painfully swollen lymph nodes that are most commonly found in the groin, armpit and neck, called buboes. Other symptoms include sudden high fever and chills, headaches, and pain in the abdomen, legs and arms, according to the Cleveland Clinic. There are two other forms of the plague: pneumonic plague, which can be caused by inhaling the bacteria, infects the lungs, while septicemic plague is an infection in the bloodstream. Both are fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization. Bubonic plague will often develop into the other two forms of plague if untreated. Plague can spread through fleas or bodily fluids Other than bites from infected fleas, people can also get plague by touching infected bodily fluids, so health experts recommend taking extra care when handling dead or sick animals. The plague can also spread through the respiratory droplets of someone who has pneumonic plague. READ MORE: The U.S. sees 7 plague cases a year. Here's why "If you cough, you can spread it to another person, but that doesn't travel very far," said Dr. Glenn Wortmann, MedStar Washington Hospital Center. "So you really need to be in face-to-face contact with that person to get pneumonic plague." That's why "the chance of this spreading widely in Russia and then extending here to the U.S. will not happen," he said. Antibiotics can treat plague The plague was never eradicated, but we've gotten better at preventing its spread and treating it in humans. When treated early with antibiotics, the plague can be cured. The key is to get to a doctor fast — otherwise the plague can be deadly. There is a vaccine, but the WHO only recommends it for people who are at high risk of infection, like laboratory and healthcare workers. There isn't strong evidence that vaccines can work against the pneumonic form. There's no plague vaccine available in the U.S. AP video journalist Javier Arciga contributed to this story from San Diego. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. "Our officers, using their training and believing that their life and the life of the partners and the general public were in danger, used their training and fired weapons," Charles said. Belgal had a 5-year-old boy in the car with him when the shooting happened, officials said. READ MORE: New ICE guidance bans high-speed car chases and sets tighter rules for traffic stops, memo shows Mullin said ICE agents didn't know the child was in the car, but that Belgal "was aware" and chose to knowingly put the boy at risk by trying to evade officers. ICE had issued a detainer on Belgal, who runs with a gang known for thefts using weapons and mopeds, Charles said. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, both Democrats, said late Thursday that they had pressed Mullin and Republican President Donald Trump to release Belgal, to no avail. They also urged the administration to immediately release body camera footage of the shooting and to halt immigration enforcement operations in the city. Mullin said Belgal is being held in a facility outside New York City but declined to provide the location. He confirmed ICE officers were wearing body cameras that were activated, but didn't say when any footage would be released. READ MORE: Shock gloves purchased by ICE cause pain, compliance and fear, Army study found Protesters and local officials had decried the shooting as an example of the dangers of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown. "There is no justification for what we have seen today," Mamdani said late Thursday at the scene of the shooting. Federal officers who surrounded the vehicle wore construction vests and masks, making it difficult to identify them as immigration officers, he said. New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Belgal was pulling into a parking space when a federal officer in plainclothes approached with gun drawn, followed by another federal officer who also wasn't in uniform. Belgal started to pull the car forward, and at least one of the officers fired seven rounds, hitting the man below his left ear. Much of Mullin's remarks Friday were reserved for excoriating Mamdani and his immigration policy. "Sanctuary politicians, they create an environment for criminal activity to thrive, not for the American citizens to be safe," he said. Mullin said ICE has asked local officials in New York to hold onto more than 14,000 people for federal officers to collect and place in immigration detention. "Silence. Absolute silence is what we have gotten back," he said. "Why would they release these individuals back onto the streets?" "We're enforcing our nation's laws. We're not picking and choosing," Mullin continued. "Why is that controversial? We should all want law and order on our streets." Mullin also criticized the attention surrounding the case. "This was a thug. The absolute worst of the worst," he complained. "We're giving so much attention to this thug." Marcelo reported from New York. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 0d64f2538f74.text: By — Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Seth Borenstein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/el-ninos-storm-killer-winds-and-climates-warming-waters-in-fight-over-future-of-hurricane-isaias Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter El Niño's storm-killer winds and climate's warming waters in fight over future of Hurricane Isaias Nation Oct 9, 2026 11:35 AM EDT A supersized El Niño's decapitating winds and the Gulf of Mexico's toasty, storm-fueling waters are battling over the future strength of Hurricane Isaias. And the storm's tilt and eye show who's winning. For now, it's the waters charged by climate change. LIVE MAP: Track the path of Hurricane Isaias All Atlantic hurricane season there has been "this battle between shear and just the overall conducive conditions," said Colorado State University hurricane researcher Phil Klotzbach. El Niño — the natural temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps weather worldwide — dominated. Its wind patterns smothered almost any wisp of a storm from strengthening in the Atlantic, while boosting what will soon be record high levels in the Pacific, Klotzbach said. Wind shear versus warm waters It's called wind shear and it pushes the tops and middle of storms around, making them lopsided and keeping them from making a complete circular eyewall, which is when storms can really power up, Klotzbach and University at Albany's Kristen Corbosiero said. Grow your mind Subscribe to our Science Newsletter to explore the wide worlds of science, health and technology. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The other ingredients for a storm to turbocharge a storm are pushing back. There is plenty of fuel in warm water and moisture. The Gulf of Mexico is about 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (1.5 degrees Celsius) warmer than normal. The 86 degree waters (30 degrees Celsius) are 100 to 500 times more likely to be that extra hot because of climate change from the burning of coal, oil and gas, said climate scientist Kristina Dahl, vice president of the nonprofit Climate Central, which calculates the boost global warming causes to extreme weather. WATCH: Gulf Coast prepares for landfall as Hurricane Isaias gains power "But there's a certain point where it's like, I don't care how hot the waters are and how much moisture you have, if shear gets to a certain point, the shear is gonna win," Klotzbach said. The thunderstorm seeds of something bigger earlier in the week grew from circular winds over Central America but often were lopsided and couldn't quite form a crucial eyewall, all because of El Niño's high-level strong winds that pushed a would-be storm's top sideways, experts said. Then a window of moderation opened for just a couple of days, but it was enough, Corbosiero said. It makes sense it was in the Gulf of Mexico and in October, because El Niño has less of an effect in the Gulf than it does in the main Atlantic, she said. And storms often pop up in that region in October because of more northerly storm systems that help foster the right conditions. READ MORE: How El Niño is playing a role in Hurricane Isaias Wind shear wasn't exactly low, but it was a moderate level, when other factors like unusually warm waters and heavy moisture can kick in. Isaias rapidly intensified from 40 mph to 80 mph (64 kph to 129 kph) in a day and by late Wednesday, Isaias became the latest-in-the-season first Atlantic hurricane to form since 1914, Klotzbach said. "The warm waters and high moisture won," Klotzbach said. Isaias Friday was not tilting and had a strong eye, the hurricane center said. By Friday morning, Isaias blew past the threshold for becoming a major hurricane with winds of 111 mph (178 kph), strengthening to 120 mph winds (195 kph). The National Hurricane Center forecasts it to weaken to a strong Category 2 storm before landfall. What to expect before landfall Before Isaias comes ashore — forecast for probably somewhere from the Mississippi and Alabama coast to the Florida Panhandle late Friday night or early Saturday — the wind shear will strengthen from moderate levels of around 20 mph (32 kph) to 52 mph (84 kph) and then Isaias will start to struggle, which is good news for coastal residents, Klotzbach said. But as of Friday morning, hurricane center forecasters said the coast is in "a tenuous spot" because it would only take a six-hour delay in the onset of that more intense wind shear for Isaias to bring a stronger-than-expected landfall. Regardless of what will happen with wind shear, it will still be a dangerous hurricane when it hits land, forecasters said. WATCH: How a super El Niño is fueling extreme weather patterns "Once it gets to the coast, we know that the storm surge is going to be deeper and farther reaching because of sea level rise caused by climate change," Dahl said. "So in this part of the world, there's been about six and a half inches of sea level rise over the past 100 years or so that's attributable directly to climate change." The National Hurricane Center is calling the surge "life-threatening." A warmer atmosphere means storms hold and then dump more rain, worsening flooding, Dahl said. The hurricane center is warning about urban, river and flash flooding in the Southeast this weekend. "There's a little bit of a battle here going on, but I think the really important thing to remember is that climate change is like this long-term big kahuna warming everywhere, and El Niño's like a little icing on the cake," Dahl said. Anthropic has raised eyebrows by announcing it will ban users from "sustained and needless" abusive behaviour towards its AI.
The Claude-maker said on Thursday it was updating its usage policy to let its tools end interactions where people are "cruel" - something it said it had done in "rare" cases prior.
It will now be included on a list of forbidden conduct which also contains bullying others, promoting self-harm and creating non-consensual intimate imagery.
While Anthropic said the policy would only apply in "extreme cases" of repeated abuse, it has reignited debate over how we should communicate with AI tools.
The company said it would not apply to "common versions of user frustration, pushback, dark creative themes, or model testing and research" - suggesting it would only apply in clearly deliberate instances.
But what Anthropic would consider "abusive or cruel behaviour" towards its models remains unclear.
Screenshots of the new policy have been widely shared and commented on across social media - with some praising it as advancing good manners or "model welfare".
But others criticised the plan, with one person calling it "deeply wrong, external" and another suggesting it might undermine abuse directed at humans and animals.
"You can't be cruel to numbers and maths," wrote Dr Barry Scannell, technology partner at Irish law firm William Fry, on LinkedIn, external.
"This level of anthropomorphisation of AI is harmful. It leads people to believe that it's something it's not."
Microsoft AI director Mustafa Suleyman, who in September criticised rival firm Anthropic for treating AI like it is human, reacted to Anthropic's update with a melting face emoji.
The changes, first reported by tech outlet The Verge, came following an annual review of the usage policy at the firm.
It was also updated to address new or emerging risks in other areas, including by forbidding use of Claude for "deceptive campaigns" or clarifying that, as US midterm elections loom, it cannot be used to "deceive voters or disrupt elections".
Anthropic also said on Thursday its usage policy previously prevented its tools being used to develop weapons.
But none of the updates have attracted as much attention or scrutiny as its move to forbid users abusing its chatbots.
It has also tapped into the much-debated question of whether we should be curt or polite when using generative AI tools.
Some experts say writing or saying "please" or "thank you" to tools like ChatGPT is unnecessary and wastes tokens - used by the large language models powering generative AI tools to process and reply to you.
Others argue politeness can lead to higher quality answers or responses.
When a X user last year asked about electricity costs incurred by ChatGPT replying to users' "please" and "thank you" messages, OpenAI boss Sam Altman said it was, external "tens of millions of dollars well spent - you never know".
The Collins Dictionary meanwhile last November highlighted the re-emergence of the term "clanker" for disparagingly referring to AI tools.
Used to describe robots in Star Wars games and movies since the mid 2000s, the term made its shortlist of words reflecting the mood of 2025 after last July saw many take to TikTok to share their frustrations with AI-powered machines.
Some experts have also posited that being rude to AI chatbots could adversely impact human communication, by seeping into how we talk to and treat others.

Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days.
Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres.
Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex.
Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended".
Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service".
Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.
It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task".
The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure.
The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems.
Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households.
Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack.
Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity".
Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion".
Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages.
Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.
Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence.
But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022.

408f0293a797.text: The Department of Homeland Security is coming under fire for publicly attacking Democratic congressional candidate Janelle Stelson less than a month before the midterm election . Why it matters: The Stelson campaign is threatening a lawsuit over the allegations, while a watchdog group is seeking an investigation into whether an ICE official violated restrictions on partisan political activity by federal employees. "We are likely to take legal action to combat the blatant lies and coordinated misinformation campaign," Stelson campaign manager Alma Baker said in a statement to Axios. The campaign said Friday it has sent out cease and desist letters, viewed by Axios, to several news outlets that reported DHS's claims as fact. The race between Stelson and Republican Rep. Scott Perry in Pennsylvania's 10th district is one of the most competitive and expensive House elections in the country, attracting more than $26 million in spending, according to AdImpact. Driving the news: DHS published a press release on Wednesday announcing the arrest of what it said was an "illegal alien from Nigeria who exposed himself in public while working for congressional campaign in Pennsylvania." The migrant, Chimaobim Adedayo Igbojekwe, was arrested by ICE on Oct. 1 after pleading guilty to disorderly conduct last month, according to the press release. The release included a statement from ICE Deputy Director Charles Wall saying: "It's unbelievable that Janelle Stelson would employ an illegal alien to work on a Congressional campaign, let alone a pervert who exposed himself in public." Stelson herself quickly batted down the claim: "He's not an employee. He's not a volunteer," she said at an event on Wednesday. Nobody named Igbojekwe was paid by the Stelson campaign as of Sept. 30, according to disbursements tracked by the Federal Election Commission. The campaign also showed Axios a search of its volunteer database that turned up no results for the name. In its cease-and-desist letter, the campaign said Igbojekwe has also "never been employed by any vendors of the campaign." Asked Thursday for comment on this story, DHS sent Axios its initial press release. The agency did not respond to multiple follow-up emails requesting comment on the Stelson campaign's threat of legal action. Between the lines: DHS cited a New Jersey-based news outlet called "Shore News Network" as its source for the claim that Igbojekwe was a Stelson canvasser. That outlet cited a social media post from conservative activist Scott Presler. "A canvasser for democrat Janelle Stelson ... was reportedly charged for indecent exposure," Presler wrote in a post on X , which included a photo of a court document that did not make reference to the Stelson campaign. Presler did not respond to a request for comment from Axios. Axios obtained an affidavit in which Trevor Jeffers, the East Pennsboro, Pa., police officer who made the initial arrest, testified that Igbojekwe was sitting in a parked car in a residential neighborhood "wearing nothing but a shirt" with his "genitals ... exposed." "Igbojekwe advised that he was in the neighborhood for work and that he was waiting to hand out flyers for Janelle Stelson's political campaign," Jeffers said in the affidavit, adding that Igbojekwe "was able to provide a stack of flyers showing he was there for work." The East Pennsboro Police did not provide a comment and denied Axios' public records request for documents related to the case. Several news outlets that covered the initial arrest or the DHS press release have since deleted their stories and posts. None responded to Axios' requests for comment. The Stelson campaign, asked about the affidavit, referred Axios to Baker's statement on Wednesday saying Igbojekwe had "never been employed" by them and that they had "never heard of him prior to the news of his arrest." Zoom in: Igbojekwe was charged with indecent exposure and disorderly conduct, later pleading guilty to a single count of disorderly conduct, according to court records. The attorney listed as his representative in court documents, Cumberland County first assistant public defender Arla Waller, did not return multiple phone calls seeking comment. Igbojekwe did not respond to a request for comment sent to an email address listed under his name. The latest: The Office of Special Counsel "will open a file" in response to questions about whether Wall violated the Hatch Act, which prohibits mixing federal government work with political campaigning, according to emails shared with Axios. Donald Sherman, the executive director of ethics watchdog Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, wrote in an email to OSC that Wall's statement was "gratuitous partisanship that constitutes prohibited political activity." An OSC staffer replied to Sherman: "We received your complaint and will open a file to address this matter." An OSC spokesperson confirmed the authenticity of the emails but declined to comment further. Wall did not respond to a request for comment. What they're saying: Deborah Fleischaker, a former acting ICE chief of staff under the Biden administration, told Axios that legal counsel at the agency during her tenure "almost certainly would have recommended not to say something like" what Wall did in his statement. Directly referencing an election in an official statement "really is seen as a no no," she told Axios. Fleischaker acknowledged that federal ethics rules aren't the deterrent they used to be . The bottom line: Cook Political Report rates the race between Stelson and Perry for the Harrisburg-based House seat as a toss-up. The Freedom Caucus Fund, a hybrid PAC dedicated to electing and supporting House Freedom Caucus members, released a digital ad on Thursday calling Igbojekwe a "Nigerian illegal alien campaigning for Democrat Janelle Stelson."

619a6f6697eb.text: By — Steve Peoples, Associated Press Steve Peoples, Associated Press By — Jill Colvin, Associated Press Jill Colvin, Associated Press By — Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Joey Cappelletti, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/the-midterms-stakes-are-high-for-these-2028-presidential-prospects Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter The midterms stakes are high for these 2028 presidential prospects Politics Oct 9, 2026 1:04 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — As most of the political world focuses on next month's midterm elections, the shadow primary for the 2028 presidential contest is quietly playing out in public view. Democratic and Republican presidential prospects have been crisscrossing the country, raising money and tapping their political connections to help boost their parties' candidates — and their own White House ambitions. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Here's a closer look at some of the leading prospects and how their political futures may be influenced by what happens Nov. 3. California Governor Gavin Newsom speaks at the Center for American Progress (CAP) IDEAS Conference at The Mayflower Hotel in Washington, D.C., May 19, 2026. Photo by Annabelle Gordon/Reuters Newsom has a Southern strategy Gavin Newsom leaves the California governor's office at the end of the year, and he's been among the most active Democrats throughout the midterms. He's paid particular attention to the South, where he's campaigned with candidates up and down the ballot in states like Alabama, Mississippi, North Carolina and, not surprisingly, South Carolina, which hosts the party's first presidential primary contest in 2028. The Southern focus aligns with the mission of Newsom's Campaign for Democracy political action committee, which was established in 2023 to help his party compete in red states. But it could also help endear him to African American voters, who make up the heart of the Democratic base. Newsom's star power — and his extensive email list — has strengthened his relationships with key Democratic officials in states like Nevada and New Hampshire, where he's sent out fundraising emails that have generated a surge of donations in recent months. WATCH: Gavin Newsom on how to beat the GOP: 'Democrats need to grow a backbone' Perhaps Newsom's biggest midterm contribution was backing Proposition 50, California's response to the Texas Republican mid-decade gerrymander. The proposition, approved by California voters last year, created a new congressional map that may allow Democrats to pick up as many as five additional U.S. House seats in California this fall. As a presidential candidate, the California governor could argue that he was on the front lines of the redistricting battle. But if Democrats do not win all five seats in his state, Newsom's message could be muffled. Vice President JD Vance casts his ballot during early voting at the Hamilton County Board of Elections on Oct. 09, 2026 in Norwood, Ohio. Pool photo by Samuel Corum/Reuters Vance's fate is tied to Trump No potential candidate's fate is as closely tied to President Donald Trump and Republicans' performance as Vice President JD Vance. The 42-year-old has embarked on an aggressive midterm campaign schedule — from the Midwest, to the South, to Alaska — and focused on the administration's efforts to root out fraud. READ MORE: Erika Kirk backs JD Vance's potential 2028 presidential bid at Turning Point USA conference A key state will be Ohio, which Vance briefly represented in the Senate. Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill Vance's seat in 2025, is facing an aggressive challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown. And in the governor's race, Democrat Amy Acton is in a close contest with Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. The effectiveness of the conservative group Turning Point Action will also be scrutinized. Erika Kirk, the widow of Turning Point co-founder Charlie Kirk and the organization's new leader, has already endorsed Vance's potential presidential bid and leaders have said they intend to use the group to support his campaign. Vance has said he is not focused on running for president, but "trying to help elect Republicans." Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro speaks during an event to mark 100 days until the midterm elections with U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY), and Congressional Candidate Bob Brooks (Pennsylvania's District 7) in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, July 26, 2026. Photo by Hannah Beier/Reuters Shapiro is all about Pennsylvania Among the Democrats leading the 2028 conversation, none have done less beyond their home state than Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. He hasn't visited any early primary states or campaigned with any midterm candidates beyond his state. That's by design for a 53-year-old Democrat whose selling point as a presidential candidate might be his clout in Pennsylvania, which has emerged as perhaps the most important swing state in the nation. READ MORE: Pennsylvania's Democratic Gov. Shapiro wins his primary, as do his endorsed candidates Shapiro is expected to cruise to reelection over his Republican challenger, state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, which has allowed him to spend his political capital elsewhere. Shapiro has gone all in to ensure Democrats win both chambers of the state legislature in November, and he's devoted significant time and resources to flipping four congressional seats. If Shapiro can demonstrate strength in swing counties like Beaver, Luzerne or Erie, it could help him make a credible claim to winning back some of the working-class voters that Democrats have lost in the Trump era. 5ff625cb38b6.text: By — Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Anthony Izaguirre, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/watch-live-trump-rallies-with-new-yorks-gop-gubernatorial-candidate-bruce-blakeman Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH LIVE: Trump rallies with New York's GOP gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman Politics Oct 9, 2026 12:50 PM EDT NEW YORK (AP) — In his campaign to become the next governor of New York, Republican Bruce Blakeman has suggested Democrats might steal the election, played up fears about immigrant criminals and posted AI-generated videos depicting the state as dangerous and unaffordable. President Donald Trump is expected to speak at 7:30 p.m. EDT. Watch live in our video player above And on Friday night, he'll rally with President Donald Trump in Syracuse. It is not exactly a message that seems geared toward winning over moderate voters. WATCH: Republican and Democratic strategists on closing messages and where they expect to win At a political moment where Republicans are hoping to capture centrists wary of an ascendent progressive left, Blakeman has instead embraced the president and his aggressive conservative tactics. The approach has puzzled some in a state where Democrats outnumber Republicans by more than 2-to-1. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "If his advertising to get the job is to champion Trump, it's going to create a whole lot of problems," said former Gov. David Paterson, a Democrat. He said Blakeman's alliance with the president "could drive a lot of people who are in the middle over the edge." Blakeman, who serves as the Nassau County executive on Long Island, has framed himself as a bulwark against urban progressives, pushing policies related to transgender athletes and Trump's immigration crackdown. After the election of Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Blakeman pledged to erect a wall of surveillance gear to protect his suburban county. READ MORE: In combative first Michigan Senate debate, Rogers and El-Sayed trade attacks But Trump hasn't exactly helped that message. While visiting New York City last month, the president was chummy with Mamdani, one of the country's leading democratic socialists, and even expressed optimism about his work as mayor. "Hopefully you're going to be a great one," said Trump, who grew up in Queens, where Mamdani first entered politics. It's unclear what Trump will get out of his trip to Syracuse with the clock ticking toward midterm elections where his party's control of Congress is on the line. The most closely watched U.S. House race in the state is hours away, where Republican Rep. Mike Lawler is trying to fend off a challenge from Democratic candidate Cait Conley. However, Trump has steered clear of political battlegrounds in his travels so far, focusing on red states and friendly crowds at a moment when Republicans worry that his unpopularity could drag down the party. Blakeman says he doesn't always agree with Trump On the campaign trail, Blakeman argues he's winning over Democrats and independents, painting himself as the moderate candidate in his race against incumbent Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul. He dismisses the idea that his closeness with the president could hurt his chances in blue New York. "I don't think it has an effect," he said when asked about his relationship with Trump. "I've proved my independence over and over and over again. I make my own decisions. I call my own shots." Hochul has emphasized Blakeman's ties to Trump — mirroring much of the Democrats' national strategy for the midterm elections — hoping the president's dismal approval ratings help to sink her Republican foe at the ballot box. In an interview, Blakeman denied that he was aligned with the president on everything. "I am somebody who takes every issue and makes a decision based on good advice from smart people and common sense," he said. For example, Blakeman said of Trump, "he's pro-life. I'm pro-choice." He added: "I believe in a comprehensive guest worker immigration program. He hasn't embraced that yet." Despite a long history of Republican leadership, the party has not fared well in recent statewide elections. No Republican has taken up residence in the governor's mansion since former Gov. George Pataki lived there between 1995 and 2006. All levels of state government are firmly controlled by Democrats, and Democrats hold a wide majority of the state's House seats as well as both Senate seats. Blakeman emerged as the leading Republican candidate The Republican field for the governor's race this year was shaping up much differently before Trump waded in. U.S. Rep. Elise Stefanik, a Trump ally who represents a conservative district in northern New York, was expected to mount a strong candidacy but unexpectedly dropped out in December after Trump waffled on an endorsement. U.S. Rep. Mike Lawler, who represents a swing congressional seat in New York's Hudson Valley, had been teasing a statewide run but abandoned the plan not long after Trump endorsed him for reelection to the House, a move seen as a way to nudge Lawler back toward Congress. With Stefanik and Lawler out of the picture, Trump swiftly backed Blakeman. In the last governor's race, Lee Zeldin, a former Long Island congressman and current Trump administration Environmental Protection Agency head, was able to come within about 6 points of upsetting Hochul by focusing on concerns about crime. Blakeman is recreating elements of Zeldin's campaign on public safety even though crime rates have dropped significantly since then. "I think over the years, the Republican Party in New York has spent more time mirroring what the national Republican Party is saying," Paterson said. Protests were held across the US on 8 October, calling for an end to sexual violence, following allegations of sexual assault involving members of a fraternity at Cornell University.
Survivors, students and advocates rallied and protested in communities and on college campuses across more than 40 states.
This comes after a lawsuit was filed against by âJane Doeâ, who alleges she was given drugs and alcohol before being sexually assaulted by several members of Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity while incapacitated in October 2024. She has accused Cornell University of failing to adequately investigate and discipline those involved.

US Vice President JD Vance has cast doubt on the Pentagon's plans to livestream a firing squad execution of the Fort Hood shooter.
Talking with reporters, Vance expressed doubt that it would happen as planned, saying: "I don't know that that's actually going to happen".
He added, that "if it's through live stream, I'm not going to be watching it". Vance described the actions by former US Army major Nidal Hasan as "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11".
Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32. His execution by firing squad would be the first military execution in more than 60 years.

Dems in majority could have familiar faces in key roles Politics Oct 9, 2026 2:05 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrats hope to bring a new agenda to the House next year if they take the majority, but they will most likely do so with many of the same faces that have steered their party's legislative work for a decade or more. Potential committee chairs in the next Congress include Rep. Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, who has served as top Democrat on the House Homeland Security panel since 2005. Then, there's Adam Smith of Washington, who began serving as top Democrat on Armed Services in 2011, and Rep. Maxine Waters of California, who became the lead Democrat on Financial Services in 2013. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Other longtime committee leaders include Reps. Frank Pallone at Energy and Commerce and Bobby Scott at Education and Workforce, who assumed their leadership posts in 2015. Rep. Richie Neal became the top Democrat on the Ways and Means Committee in 2017. None would be able to continue in that position under the rules used by House Republicans, which generally limit lawmakers to three terms as chairman or ranking member. For Democrats, the question is whether to stick with their current system, which emphasizes seniority, or move closer to the one that Republicans have established. It's a discussion that some Democrats say they are having behind the scenes. WATCH: Republican and Democratic strategists on closing messages and where they expect to win "I think that the idea of term limits could be appealing to the American people, to the Democratic base. It sounds Democratic," said Rep. Eugene Vindman, D-Va. "I'm open to the idea. I've spoken to a number of folks who are open to the idea." "I personally think it makes for a more vibrant Congress, but I know I'm in the minority in the minority," said Rep. Chrissy Houlahan, D-Pa. Party leaders are playing down the issue for now. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said seniority has always been a factor when it comes to committee leadership, but not the only one. "The caucus is going to work its will as we move forward," Jeffries told reporters. "At the end of the day, we can't put the cart before the horse. We've got to still go out and win this thing in November." Democrats have been here before Term limits are not a new discussion for Democrats. When they were weighing whether to return Nancy Pelosi as speaker in 2018, those opposing her bid wanted her to commit to limiting how long lawmakers could serve as House party leaders or committee chairs. She eventually agreed to serve in the post for no more than four more years. No such restrictions were added for committee chairs. In 2022, Democrats voted overwhelmingly against a six-year term limit for committee leaders. Rep. Jim McGovern, D-Mass., who has served as top Democrat on the House Rules Committee since 2018, called term limits an "artificial, random mechanism that doesn't always serve the best interest of the institution." "I want people in chairs who are going to fight to get things over the finish line and make a real difference," McGovern said. "Some of those people may have been around for a long time and some of them may be relatively new." WATCH: Karl Rove and David Axelrod give their midterm predictions Pallone said he intends to be the next Energy and Commerce chairman or ranking member. He called term limits for chairs "very undemocratic." "If people want to vote for somebody they should be allowed to," Pallone said. He also said that term limits can lead to short-term thinking from chairs looking at their next opportunity in the private sector. "People serve for a couple years, then they go work for some lobbying firm," he said. "What they do when they're here is very much influenced by what lobbying firm they're going to work for." Thompson also said he would like to serve again as top Democrat on Homeland Security if he wins reelection. He dismissed the way Republicans limit committee leaders to three terms. "I don't want to be like Republicans. I'm a Democrat," Thompson said. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., says term limits have served Republicans well. "It's been really good to show younger members that you're always going to have a path to leadership if you keep working hard, if you do your job really well," Scalise said. "We definitely lose some good chairmen along the way, but we also get new leaders who otherwise would not have been able to rise up." Democrats have broken with seniority on occasion Democrats don't always stick with seniority. One recent exception is Rep. Jamie Raskin, the lead Democrat on the Judiciary Committee. He challenged Rep. Jerry Nadler for the job in late 2024, prompting Nadler, then 77, to step aside. Similarly, Democrats selected Rep. Angie Craig to become the top Democrat on the Agriculture Committee after she challenged the late Rep. David Scott for the post. Scott had been the panel's top Democrat for the previous two sessions, but was in poor health. Democrats also elected Rep. Robert Garcia last year to succeed Rep. Gerry Connolly on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. Connolly died after a battle with esophageal cancer. Garcia defeated veteran Rep. Stephen Lynch of Massachusetts for the job. "He has done, by everybody's measure here, an incredible job," said Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas. "We would not have all of the Epstein files that we've gotten so far without his leadership on that committee." Casar
