The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission issued an unusual warning this week to the country’s largest asset managers and a climate-focused investor group over their roles in a 2021 campaign that replaced board directors at ExxonMobil.
The commission published a letter saying it had concluded a probe into the entities, and while it found no evidence of violations, it expressed “serious concerns” about their actions.
Investor advocates and some former SEC staff say the letter clearly aims to suppress shareholder advocacy on climate change and pressure large asset managers like BlackRock, State Street and Vanguard, each of which were named in the letter, to steer clear of the topic entirely.
It is only the latest move by the SEC this year to limit investors’ ability to address climate risks and engage with corporate boards more broadly. The Trump administration and Republican officials across the country have spent years clamping down on efforts to press corporations for climate action.
In 2022, Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives opened an antitrust investigation into some of the same groups, accusing them of acting like a “cartel.” More than a dozen Republican state attorneys general also launched probes. Oil industry campaign contributions have gone overwhelmingly to Republican candidates.
Mika Morse, who was a policy counsel on climate risk to former SEC Chair Gary Gensler, said many investors and asset managers view climate change as a significant risk to their portfolios and feel a fiduciary duty to engage with companies on the topic, but may now hesitate to continue that work.
“Investors are feeling really inhibited because of this fear that they will become the target of investigations,” Morse said. “And this type of harassment is really effective, unfortunately.”
SEC Enforcement Director David Woodcock, who began that position in May, was an attorney at Exxon during the investors’ campaign, according to his LinkedIn profile. An SEC spokesperson said the investigation began last year and that Woodcock recused himself.
The investigation probed the communications of some of the country’s largest asset managers and pension funds—including BlackRock, State Street, Vanguard, the California Public Employees’ Retirement System and the New York State Common Retirement Fund—with a group called Climate Action 100+, an investor initiative that pushes for climate action by large corporate emitters.
“This type of harassment is really effective, unfortunately.”
— Mika Morse, former SEC policy counsel on climate risk
The report traced what it called a campaign by Climate Action 100+ beginning in 2019 to change Exxon’s board because of the company’s inaction on global warming. The California and New York pension funds were active in the climate group, and BlackRock and State Street joined the initiative in 2020.
By 2021, a small activist investor firm called Engine No. 1 had launched a campaign to replace some of Exxon’s directors. That campaign focused on what the firm said was the company’s poor financial performance—Exxon had been removed from the Dow Jones Industrial Average the previous year as its stock price lagged—rather than inaction on climate change. But the SEC letter said Engine No. 1 had communicated with some Climate Action 100+ members and with Ceres, a sustainable business advocacy group that helps coordinate the climate investor organization.
That year, the campaign succeeded in appointing three new members to Exxon’s board, in large part by convincing large asset managers like BlackRock to vote yes.
It was a huge blow to Exxon and came at a low point for the oil industry. Profits had plummeted during the COVID-19 pandemic. Some analysts were predicting peak oil consumption had passed. Major investors lined up behind the notion that climate risks were systemic, and President Joe Biden had won election the prior year after pledging to shift away from fossil fuels.
In the following years, the oil industry and its allies in public office and think tanks pushed back forcefully, filing lawsuits, investigations and legislation that targeted opponents in the financial sector, academia and elsewhere.
The Trump administration has incorporated this effort as public policy through the Department of Justice, SEC and other agencies, siding with the oil industry in numerous lawsuits, for example.
The SEC investigation examined whether the asset managers and other members of the climate organization coordinated their votes, which could have triggered onerous reporting requirements under SEC rules meant to give public insight into campaigns by activist investors to influence companies.
Firms like BlackRock are exempt from these reporting requirements even though they hold large stakes in many companies because they are considered passive investors. The SEC letter raised the question of whether the firms should have been required to report more extensively in the case of the Exxon campaign.
Experts in securities law say the difference is significant and that a finding of violation could have had serious implications. Ultimately, the commission did not find evidence to support any of these claims but still issued a public report.

Shareholder advocates have criticized the SEC report, arguing that it sought to intimidate investors.

US immigration officials have defended the actions of officers who shot and wounded a man in his car in New York on Thursday while his five-year-old son was in the back seat.
Markwayne Mullin, the head of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which runs the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), said officers fired their weapons while trying to arrest a man with a criminal history.
"We weren't aware the child was in the car," Mullin added at a news conference on Friday, arguing that it was the man, Oscar Belgal, who had put his child in danger. Belgal is now being held at a detention facility.
The legal organisation representing Belgal told the BBC that lawyers had not yet been able to speak to him.
The shooting happened in the residential neighbourhood of Marble Hill.
Marcos Charles, a top ICE official who was also at Friday's news conference, said agents used their vehicles to try and stop Belgal in his car but that he resisted orders to get out and instead accelerated, smashing into two ICE vehicles.
Charles said Belgal then "weaponised his vehicle and proceeded to accelerate going towards other officers", adding: "Our officers, using their training, and believing that their life and the life of their partners in the general public were in danger, used their training and fired weapons."
The number of officers who fired their weapons is being investigated.
Charles said Belgal "was struck by one of the bullets or fragments superficially in the neck".
New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who called what happened "unconscionable and incredibly serious", said ICE agents surrounded Belgal's car before opening fire.
"They wore construction vests and masks that concealed their faces. There is no reasonable way to identify them as ICE agents," Mamdani said. He confirmed that the child was unharmed.
Mullin said the officers identified themselves and were wearing body-worn cameras that were turned on during the incident.
Video of the shooting, including body camera footage, has not been made public but unverified videos on social media appear to align with Mamdani's comments.
Body-worn camera footage released by the New York Police Department (NYPD) on Friday shows its officers arriving on scene and attempting to help Belgal after he has been shot. One ICE officer appears to be wearing a neon construction vest and carrying a large gun.
The NYPD officers then call for an ambulance and putting him in a police car to take him to hospital. They are later seen pulling Belgal from the vehicle and carrying him into the hospital.
Mamdani said on Thursday that he had spoken to US President Donald Trump and Mullin for two hours but failed to negotiate Belgal's release.
Mamdani said he would ask Trump, who has not yet commented publicly on the shooting, to end ICE enforcement actions in New York. Mullin has said he will not pause enforcement.
The DHS said Belgal, 28, was from the Dominican Republic and had "a prior criminal conviction for grand larceny and multiple prior arrests for assault, robbery, possession of drugs and weapons possession".
Belgal was arrested by police officers in New York in December 2023 and released "a few days later", according to the DHS.
New York City Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said there was also still a pending case against Belgal for criminal sale of a controlled substance in 2025.
DHS has also alleged Belgal was associated with the Trinitarios, described by the US justice department as a transnational criminal group.
Mullin said the DHS believed Belgal "has either indirect or direct knowledge" of a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer shooting, "and that's why he became a target".
Mamdani is not the only New York official to have criticised the incident. Governor Kathy Hochul said federal officials needed to provide answers quickly about what happened.
"New Yorkers have witnessed far too many acts of violence by a rogue federal agency and untrained agents that operate with impunity," Hochul said, adding that she had spoken to Mullin and Trump as well.
There have been several high-profile shootings involving ICE officers this year, including one that caused the death of Renee Good in Minneapolis in January.

Talarico couldn't be happier Politics Oct 9, 2026 1:33 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — When Democratic nominee James Talarico stopped holding campaign events in the Texas Senate race, his Republican opponent Ken Paxton saw an opening to pounce. "Where is James Talarico?" he called out Wednesday during a rally with President Donald Trump in San Antonio. WATCH: Trump speaks at rally for Senate candidate Ken Paxton in San Antonio But that night, while flying back to Washington on Air Force One, Trump seemed to inadvertently throw Talarico a lifeline. The president said on social media that Talarico — who has the flu, according to his campaign — "should immediately report to a Debate Stage" to face off with Paxton. I agree," Talarico posted on Thursday morning. "Ball's in your court @KenPaxtonTX." No debate has been scheduled so far. Paxton has not publicly responded to Trump's debate demand. So far, the campaign has played out almost entirely on the airwaves. The candidates' campaigns and more than a dozen outside groups have spent more than $247 million on advertising, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. The candidates have yet to appear jointly before voters. Later that month, it suggested an agreement with a news outlet was imminent, though none was announced. Without a debate, Paxton has focused on Talarico's absence, even demanding video proof that he was alive. "Low-T Jimmy appears to be having a full-blown mental Tala-freak-out on the national stage. We have a simple request: proof of life," said Madison Cercy, campaign spokeswoman. Talarico is expected to resume campaigning this weekend through the Nov. 3 election, aides said. 28e9416835fb.text: Data: Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios Middle- and lower-earners' inflation-adjusted incomes rose during the Biden years — but high earners saw their incomes fall. That's a surprising finding from one of the most thorough datasets on American household finances , released Friday morning by the Federal Reserve. Why it matters: The data sheds granular new information on a much-contested question: What happened to Americans' real incomes during the post-pandemic period? It featured an exceptionally tight job market and the highest inflation in decades, followed by aggressive Fed rate hikes. The median American family's income rose 7% in inflation-adjusted terms between 2021 and 2024. But that masked significant differences among income brackets. The average real income of families in the top 10% of earners fell 14%, to $652,000 from $757,000 (both figures are 2025 dollars). That implies, contrary to a common narrative about the K-shaped economy, that income inequality fell during the post-pandemic period. Yes, but: The story for wealth is very different. Families that were already wealthy — and tend to own stocks, houses and other assets — became much richer from 2022 to 2025. Among families in the top 10% of income, median net worth rose a whopping 31% from 2022 to 2025, compared with a 2% rise in net worth for the median family. Families in the bottom 40% of income actually saw their net worth decline slightly in that span. The intrigue: The data, from the Survey of Consumer Finances, is collected and released every three years. Friday morning's release is the 2025 survey — but questions about income cover the preceding calendar year. As such, the income numbers compare 2024 with 2021 — conveniently capturing the change from the early part of the Biden administration to near its end. Between the lines: While the compression in income inequality seen in this data may seem surprising, it aligns with other evidence that blue-collar workers saw bigger raises during the super-tight job market and inflationary episode of 2021 and 2022 than did higher-earning white-collar professionals. Moreover, in a footnote, the Fed researchers note that top earners tend to have income from volatile sources, mainly capital gains and business income. Big swings in those income sources among the highest earners can create outsized movement in the averages. Of note: The survey also sheds light on how the Fed's aggressive interest rate hikes in 2022 and 2023, meant to bring inflation under control, hammered borrowers. The median debt payment-to-income ratio rose 2 percentage points from 2022 to 2025, reaching 15.4%. The share of families with debt payment-to-income ratios above 40%, a threshold for high debt obligations, increased to 8.6% from 6.5%, reaching a level last seen in the 2013 survey. The bottom line: Low earners saw bigger percentage gains in their incomes' purchasing power amid the post-pandemic inflation than did high earners — but the rich got a lot richer at the same time.

US President Donald Trump says he has reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Moscow to "immediately release" diesel into the global market.
He said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.
"Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Trump wrote on Truth social.
Diesel prices in the US have doubled since the war with Iran began in February, putting pressure on Republicans ahead of the midterm elections over the rising cost of living.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the the end of September.
Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary license allowing Russian diesel into the market.
An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."

- Published
Conservative commentator Katie Zacharia has been offered the job of White House press secretary, a White House official confirmed to the BBC.
Zacharia, who currently works as a communications adviser for Trump Media & Technology Group would become the president's sixth chief spokesperson across his two administrations. She previously had a brief stint as a spokesperson at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).
Former White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, who left the White House in August, has reportedly taken a job with Fox News.
The BBC has contacted Zacharia for comment.
The 42-year-old political strategist is a frequent fixture on conservative Newsmax and Fox News, and has been active in Republican politics for most of her adult life, having worked as an intern for the Republican National Committee and for the White House Office of Political Affairs during the Bush administration in 2006.
Since June, she has been a senior communications adviser for Trump's media company and Truth Social platform, according to her LinkedIn profile. She worked in Homeland Security briefly from February to March this year.
While she was only briefly in government at DHS - which she later said she left because of the strain of travel between California and Washington on her family - she has long been a ferocious defender of President Trump and his administration's policies.
In a June interview with the BBC, for example, she dismissed criticism of Trump's controversial use of the White House to host a televised UFC fight, saying the principles of the UFC "are the kind of principles that founded our Constitutional Republic".
"It's about not giving up the fight until the bitter end," she said. "I think there's no better summation of the American ethos than a good UFC fight."
A lawyer educated at Pepperdine University in California, Zacharia also served as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative non-profit started by Trump ally - and current Special Presidential Envoy for Special Missions - Ric Grenell.
In 2011, she spent nearly two years clerking at a law firm in Beijing, China.
The complex job of press secretary goes beyond the briefing room podium to include managing contentious relationships with the press, coordinating with other parts of the White House, and providing media advice to the president. The secretary also oversees an office that receives a significant amount of inquiries and requests on a daily basis.
Trump called Leavitt one of his "most trusted aides" when she left the role, saying she wanted to spend more time with her family, which set a high bar for her replacement.
A lawyer educated at Pepperdine University in California, Zacharia, 42, has four children. She has also worked as general counsel for Fix California, a conservative advocacy group headed by Trump ally Ric Grenell.

There was still "lots of room for improvement" when it comes to how much we recycle at work compared with our habits at home, according to an expert.
Figures suggest only 61% of people in Wales recycle often at their workplace, with one in five saying they do not recall seeing the appropriate facilities to do so.
Providing more bins or clearer labelling are some of the ways in which businesses could make a difference, said waste reduction charity Wrap.
But one business had already seen a "significant improvement" at their offices after removing staff's personal bins, a move that was initially met with resistance.
When recruitment firm Acorn by Synergie first moved into their offices on the outskirts of Newport in 2003, they were producing six large wheelie bins' worth of rubbish a week.
It now has just one weekly collection thanks to increased recycling, including food waste, which was their biggest adaptation, following the introduction of the Welsh government's Workplace Recycling Law in 2024.
"The main thing that we changed was removing desk bins and individual bins," said director Mark Rudge.
"We had quite a bit of resistance to that. Individuals liked having their own little waster station.
"But we put central recycling areas within each zone of the business, and eventually, people get the hang of that.
"A lot of home recycling is extremely similar, so people brought those good habits to the workplace."
Office worker Ann-Marie Derrick admitted fellow staff members had found it a pain to begin with, but it had now become "second nature".
"Anybody new coming to the office is just straight away onboard and I think we're probably quite proud as a team about how much recycling we do."
The company's environmental manager Anthony Lee said it had taken a few months for staff to fully mirror their home recycling habits at the workplace, and that there had been a "significant improvement in compliance".
Not all workers and business have adapted to the same degree.
WRAP's annual tracker survey indicated that although 94% of people in Wales say they recycle at home, only 61% do so "very often at work" with that figure dropping to below half for students at college or university.
Only 30% of respondents said they had seen lots of recycling facilities at their workplace, despite the new requirements, while 20% said they could not recall seeing any.
"It's still a relatively new thing to have recycling bins when we're away from home," said Angela Spiteri, senior marketing manager at WRAP.
"It's a very positive step in the right direction for Wales, but it's not perfect and there's a lot of things we can do to improve."
She said there was a responsibility on businesses to ensure that was possible, "providing the right bins and facilities for people to make that easier".
"I don't recycle as much when I am out and about, I just bin it," admits Gerwyn Pugh, 56, from Barry.
"It's routine [at home], but out and about every bin takes a bit more time to work out."
James Jenkins, 30, said he often took rubbish home with him given the limited options where he works.
"We only recycle cardboard because that's our only waste.
"The more industrialised businesses need to do more, because they'll have more of an impact than smaller businesses."
Natalie James, 47, said she recycled "probably about the same" at work and at home.
"Because I work at a hospital we've got the recycling categories everywhere, so we have to."
Although businesses in Wales are now required to sort their waste into six categories, collection arrangements can vary from area to area.
In the Vale of Glamorgan, businesses use a mix of council and private services, and the local authority said the change has resulted in a "higher quality of recycling".
Carys Stephens, the council's waste project officer, said there had been a "fantastic response from businesses."
"There's obviously going to be some that are critical of the idea, and they're worried about extra costs and effort that goes into segregated recycling.
"But we've been doing segregated recycling for a couple of years now, and most people just take it in their stride."
Although Wales' workplace recycling rates are "reasonably high", said consultant Rebecca Colley-Jones, "there's lots of room for improvement".
"It is a new system, so there's always a period of settling down."
She said that she was sure "we would see that 61% rise".
"Often they can be tourism or hospitality businesses, so they're having to educate their customers what to do."
Colley-Jones said individuals also needed to personally take more care.
"Our home is our castle, we're responsible for the waste and people are under a little bit of pressure, perhaps from their neighbours to look like they're recycling.
"Whereas you don't have that in the workplace.
"When people come to work, they come to work, they don't necessarily thing recycling is part of their job description.
She added: "It's trying to get people to understand that they also need to be buying into the culture of an organisation, and also the culture of Wales as a country. We are the second-best recycler in the world."
She added that the changes had inevitably led to some costs for businesses, and varying collection arrangements can sometimes be "confusing".
Natural Resources Wales, which monitors compliance on behalf of the Welsh government, said so far no workplace had been prosecuted for failing to follow the new regulations.
A spokesperson added that 56% of businesses were found to be compliant in the first two years of the new rules, but it had provided "advice and support" and the majority of non-compliant companies "had taken steps" to address their issues.

a0db27ca5841.text: Former Department of Homeland Security spokesperson Katie Zacharia has been offered the White House press secretary post, multiple sources familiar with the offer tell Axios. The big picture: If she accepts, Zacharia will take over the podium from Karoline Leavitt, a tenacious Trump loyalist who announced her departure from the administration in August. Zoom in: Zacharia is a conservative lawyer and commentator who works as a senior communications advisor at Trump Media & Technology Group, which oversees Truth Social. She also served for about two months as the Department of Homeland Security's deputy assistant secretary for Public Affairs and spokesperson. Zacharia has worked as a commentator on Fox News, CNN, Newsmax, One America News, and other outlets. She holds both a law degree and a bachelor's degree from Pepperdine University, where she currently serves on the school's Dean's Council. The intrigue: Zacharia is less well known than some of her predecessors, but she is a vocal defender of the administration on TV and online. She previously worked for Trump ally Richard Grenell at Fix California, an advocacy group that works to advance conservative values in the state. Zacharia has previously described herself as a "native Californian and lifelong conservative." She told CNN in April that she's a "huge fan of ICE and a big fan of the Border Patrol" and praised Border Czar Tom Homan's work on immigration. Axios' Avery Lotz contributed to this reporting. f898417baade.text: By — Ali Rogin Ali Rogin Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-relaxes-rules-around-political-events-for-blanche-other-senate-approved-appointees Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration relaxes rules around political events for Blanche, other Senate-approved DOJ appointees Politics Updated on Oct 9, 2026 2:59 PM EDT — Published on Oct 9, 2026 2:53 PM EDT The Department of Justice is making it easier for Attorney General Todd Blanche and other Senate-confirmed DOJ appointees to participate in political activities, according to a new internal memo obtained by PBS News. The memo, penned by the agency's top ethics official, includes new language noting that Senate-approved presidential appointees are exempt from strict restrictions that govern the political conduct of most senior officials. It specifically allows those employees, including the attorney general, to address political gatherings and endorse or oppose candidates – a swerve away from long-standing precedent within the DOJ that experts say may further erode trust in the U.S. justice system. WATCH: How Blanche is shattering DOJ's standard of political independence The document is the latest version of a memo the department's ethics office circulates from time to time, reminding employees of the restrictions on their political activities under a law known as the Hatch Act. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The existence of exceptions for presidential Senate-confirmed appointees themselves is not new, and is codified in the language of the Hatch Act, which governs the political activity of all federal employees. But presidential appointees at the Department of Justice have a history of holding themselves to a more restrictive code of conduct, noted Joseph Tirrell, who led the DOJ's Departmental Ethics Office before his dismissal last year. "This policy, and its recent update, have lowered the bar so that DOJ employees are now only held to the standard set by [the Hatch Act], as opposed to the higher and more restrictive standard set by attorneys general for the last 20-plus years that help ensure, to the greatest extent possible, that DOJ was above politicking," Tirrell wrote in an email to PBS News. "DOJ's lowering of its standards regarding political activism by senior officials means that Americans can no longer trust that Department decisions and actions are made fairly and without regard to political affiliation." The updated guidance comes as Blanche has made a number of appearances at political rallies and official events where political candidates spoke. Recent events have included an election rally for a Senate candidate in North Carolina, where Blanche introduced President Donald Trump, the Republican Party's midterm election convention, as well as a roundtable on violent crime in South Carolina, where Blanche sat next to Sen. Darline Graham, who is on the ballot in November. READ MORE: Attorney General Blanche blurs Justice Department boundaries by appearing at political events Tirrell said he believes these appearances still violate a separate Hatch Act prohibition on the use of official authority to influence the outcome of elections. Previous iterations of the same DOJ document said some individuals serving in "further restricted" positions, like those in the Senior Executive Service (SES), were barred from an even wider array of election activities – including addressing a political rally or endorsing a political candidate – than most other career executive branch employees. The latest revision lists most of the same "further restricted" roles, but adds a new line specifically exempting "employees appointed by the President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate (PAS)." And in a section listing the prohibited activities for "further restricted employees," the memo explicitly states that it does not apply to "PAS." That acronym for presidential appointees is common in other contexts, but recent previous versions of the same DOJ ethics guidance make no such distinctions between those appointees and other "further restricted" employees. In a statement to PBS, a Department of Justice spokesperson said that the updated version of the memo clarifies, rather than changes, Hatch Act rules. "The updated guidance clarifies an existing exception under the Hatch Act for Presidentially-appointed, Senate-confirmed officials, and clarifies that appearances with partisan candidates should be reviewed by ethics officials to ensure proper designations," the spokesperson said. U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche waves as he arrives on stage at the Republican National Midterm Convention in Dallas on Sept. 9, 2026. Photo by Brian Snyder/ Reuters The new language clarifying rules for employees' official appearances with partisan candidates no longer recommends employees avoid appearing alongside political candidates at official events taking place shortly before a political election. The previous guidance, released when Blanche's predecessor Pam Bondi was serving in the top role, said: "Previous Attorneys General have made an effort, and also encouraged Presidentially appointed officials, or those acting in such positions, to avoid making public appearances in any state shortly before a primary or general election in that state, to the greatest extent practicable. The Attorney General has determined that this precedent should be followed." The new October memo says such appearances "warrant heightened scrutiny — especially when close to an election" and that the Office of Special Counsel has identified several factors to consider when determining whether an event is "official vs. political for purposes of the Hatch Act." A no-holds-barred televised debate between Michigan Senate rivals Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers has highlighted how ugly personal attacks are ramping up in the US midterms elections race.
In Thursday evening's duel, Rogers questioned whether someone in his Muslim opponent's family might be on a "watchlist". El-Sayed, a Democrat, called the Republican "a sock puppet for the Trump administration".
Moderator Rick Albin said the barbs continued off camera, spilling into the commercial break - something Albin said he has never seen in 30 years of doing debates.
On the morning after the debate, US President Donald Trump posted on social media attacking the Democrat and bringing up his Muslim identity.
The Michigan race could affect which party controls the Senate after November's midterm elections as Democrats campaign to wrest control of both chambers of Congress from the Republicans.
Little was considered off limits in the verbal jousting between Rogers and El-Sayed, which saw the Republican repeatedly suggest the Democrat and his family had ties to terrorist organisations.
El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate, denied this.
A fact-check from a state news outlet, Bridge Michigan, has said there is no evidence, external that El-Sayed is personally connected to the Muslim Brotherhood, branches of which have been designated as terrorist organisations by the US.
The Democrat questioned whether Rogers was even from Michigan and labelled his opponent a "Florida man", with yachts and a mansion in the Sunshine State. Rogers denied the Florida ties and boat ownership.
"Weak, cowardly, won't stand up until his poll numbers drop," El-Sayed said during one heated exchange.
The economy, immigration and support for Israel were topics that came up as expected during the debate.
But tensions flared as Rogers appeared to attack El-Sayed's family.
The rivals were discussing Flock cameras, the controversial AI-powered surveillance system, which El-Sayed said should be federally regulated.
"And why would that bother you?" Rogers shot back. "Well, if you have someone in your family that might be on the watchlist."
El-Sayed challenged Rogers to "go ahead and say it", adding: "Are you going after my mom?"
The Democrat's mother, Fatten Elkomy, previously worked as a nurse practitioner for the Islamic American Relief Agency (IARA), according to the Midwesterner, external, a conservative regional news outlet.
The US treasury department designated IARA, external in 2004 for supporting terrorism.
The US justice department charged figures within IARA, external in 2007 with illegal wire transfers to Iraq, but El-Sayed's mother was not among those indicted and she left the agency in 2004.
The BBC has contacted El-Sayed's campaign and Elkomy for comment.
One academic told the BBC that Thursday's debate underscores how anti-Muslim sentiment is becoming increasingly normalised at the highest level of US politics.
Quardricos Driskell, a George Washington University political science professor, pointed to the period after the 9/11 attacks as a time when there was similar rhetoric, but he noted the distinction in presidential leadership.
In the wake of the attacks, then-President George W Bush stood in front of a mosque and defended the Muslim faith, saying: "Islam is peace."
Driskell said: "Islamophobia has long existed, I think across American political society from both parties.
"What distinguishes the current moment is that the explicit use of Muslim identity as a political attack is by prominent Republican leaders."
On Friday morning, President Trump issued the latest in a series of attacks on the Democrat.
"Mohammad is a Jihadist lunatic who hates our Country," Trump wrote on social media.
Some questioned why Trump chose to refer to El-Sayed as Mohammad - his full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed ElâSayed, but he has been known as Abdul since kindergarten, according to the Detroit News, external.
Trump's comment follows several other similar anti-Muslim remarks from elected officials, including Tennessee Republican congressman Andy Ogles posting on X earlier this year: "Muslim's don't belong in American society."
After Zohran Mamdani was elected as the first ever Muslim mayor of New York City, he faced similar attacks.
"After 9/11 we said 'Never Forget.' I think we sadly have forgotten," Republican congresswoman Nancy Mace wrote on X, after Mamdani's election.
Gregg Nunziata, a Republican policy adviser, told the BBC these types of comments were "extremely destructive and deeply alarming".
He also noted the absence of condemnation for these remarks, saying it's "the responsibility of leaders to tamp down that type of rhetoric and police their own side and that's not happening today".
There has been a rise in anti-Muslim sentiment across the US, according to the Pew Research Center.
In 2002, 25% of adults said Islam "is more likely" to encourage violence than other religions. That number jumped to 51% in 2026.
It comes amid a rise in hatred more broadly in the US, including antisemitism.
Haris Tarin, vice-president of the Muslim Public Affairs Council (MPAC), said Trump's comments like his social media post on Friday morning make him feel "sick".
He said his organisation had tracked an eight-fold increase in anti-Muslim speech over the last year.
"This rise has coincided with elections, and it has allowed for candidates who oppose American Muslims licence to openly attack their faith," Tarin said.
Driskell said such attacks often exploit voters' fears.
"We have to keep in mind the motivating factor often in politics, and particularly during campaigning, which is fear," he said.
"That's what ultimately Islamophobia is - the fear," he continued, "instilling fear that people get out and vote".

A massive magnitude 7.7 earthquake has hit Panama, damaging buildings and prompting a wide-ranging tsunami warning for neighbouring countries.
About 4.6 million people felt moderate to severe shaking as a result of the quake, according to the US Geological Survey, which has said that the effects of the disaster were "likely to be widespread".
The quake, which hit just before 15:00 local time (18:00 GMT), could trigger tsunamis in Colombia, Costa Rica, Chile and Mexico, according to the US Tsunami Warning System.
The epicentre of the earthquake was about 6.2 miles (10km) from the small town of Pitaloza Arriba in south-central Panama, with a series of shallow aftershocks following it.
Footage shared online, which has not been verified by the BBC, appears to show collapsed buildings in the towns of PenonomÃ© and SonÃ¡.
The quake was registered as occurring at a depth of just 12km. The shallower the earthquake, the more likely it is to have more severe effects on the surface.
However, the full extent of the damage it has caused is not yet clear, nor whether there have been any casualties as a result.
Many people were evacuated from buildings in Panama City, about 200km (124 miles) away, according to new agency AFP.
The earthquake comes just three days before Panama was scheduled to hold a national evacuation drill for dealing with a major earthquake.
It also follows devastating earthquakes in Colombia and Venezuela earlier this year.

Three men have been found guilty of murdering Australian brothers, Jake and Callum Robinson, and their American friend Carter Rhoad during a surfing trip in Mexico in 2024.
During the trial, the court heard the tourists were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck in a secluded beach area. Their bodies were later found with gunshot wounds to their heads, dumped down a well.
The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the coastal area is usually safe from the violence in other parts of Mexico.
The verdict was handed down on Friday in the Mexican state of Baja California.
The parents of the two Australian brothers, Martin and Debra Robinson, have been at the court in the coastal town of Ensenada throughout the trial and they delivered emotional testimony during closing arguments heard earlier on Thursday.
"It's hard for a parent to lose a son, and we lost two sons," said their father, Martin.
Family members of Rhoad joined the trial by video link.
Speaking to media outside court a week ago, Debra Robinson said the couple were "deeply grateful" to Australians for the outpouring of support they had received and that they "feel the love and their arms around us".
During the month-long trial, the prosecution had sought 150 years in prison for each of the three defendants.
In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, JesÃºs "El Kekas" Gerardo, was sentenced in a separate trial to twenty years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.
At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.
The beach town has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers and the chilling murders revealed much about how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.
The only explanation the authorities appeared able to give was that the surfers â all in their early thirties â had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.
Their killings took place barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week when their families were able to identify them.
At the time, the surfer community in Ensenada turned out in force to commemorate the men by paddling out at one of the area's best known surfing spots and throwing flowers into the sea.
Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.
Amid the demands for action, the governor of Baja California, Marina del Pilar Ãvila, tried to ease public fears about the widespread violence in her state.
"Baja California is and will continue to be a state with safe tourism for the thousands of people who visit us from the rest of the country and the world", she said.
"I send my condolences and solidarity to the families at this difficult time."

(AP) — Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on Friday whether the Pentagon will livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan in December but told reporters that if it is livestreamed, "I'm not going to be watching it." Watch the clip in the video player above. The Republican vice president said, "I don't know that that's actually going to happen," when asked about the plans that the Pentagon confirmed on Thursday. But Vance then tried to set aside the controversy over the shocking plans for a public execution and said Hasan's crimes should not be forgotten. "So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said. "Now, that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it," he added. Vance is a convert to the Catholic Church, which has long opposed capital punishment. Watch Vance's full remarks in the video below. Earlier Friday morning, the head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the U.S. government's decision to livestream Hasan's execution. "It is with shock and great sorrow that I have learned of the Department of War's decision to publicly livestream the execution of Nidal Hassan. Our God is the God of life. In no way can Hassan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," said Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the Conference, in a statement. Earlier, President Donald Trump told a White House event that Hasan will be getting "the death penalty through firing squad. And he deserves it." Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the military hasn't executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging. b1c4f142c2db.text: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer is going to have his hands full next Congress, even without a threat to his leadership or a primary challenge from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.). Why it matters: Schumer (D-N.Y.) will have to grapple with the presidential ambitions of up to eight of his senators who may care more about winning the White House than following their leader. Roughly one in six Democratic senators eyeing the campaign trail would add a degree of difficulty to a job that rarely lacks challenges, as former President Obama acknowledged this week. "Being the head of the Democratic Party is a pain in the butt, because you've got people from every walk of life," Obama said of Schumer at a fundraiser Wednesday. Flashback: This year's ICE funding fights gave Schumer a taste of how presidential ambitions can complicate governing. Potential 2028 contenders competed to take the toughest stance against ICE funding, even at the risk of a government shutdown. Zoom in: The tension between individual ambition and party unity could surface early in Schumer's tenure if he becomes majority leader. Democrats are promising to lower costs and govern responsibly, while insisting they'll challenge and investigate the Trump administration at every turn. Schumer and President Trump have a long, complicated relationship — and each other's cell numbers. Between the lines: Democrats could control majorities in both chambers, giving them immense power against Trump. But majority power is dependent on members being present and unified. Presidential contenders have incentives to spend time outside Washington and show how they differ from their fellow 2028 hopefuls in the Senate. They also may want to pick high-profile fights with the party establishment to prove their progressive bona fides. But Schumer faced a similar challenge during the 2020 presidential cycle, when he was minority leader and seven sitting senators sought the Democratic nomination. Attendance was the biggest headache as candidates crisscrossed the country, complicating Senate scheduling. But Democrats didn't lose any major votes despite their presidential hopefuls being on the campaign trail. Who we're watching: Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) has visited South Carolina, New Hampshire and Nevada (twice). Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Ariz.): South Carolina, Nevada, New Hampshire and Iowa. Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.): South Carolina (twice), Nevada and Michigan. Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.): South Carolina. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.): Iowa and Nevada. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.): Iowa and New Hampshire (twice). Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.): Nevada (twice) and New Hampshire. Honorable mention: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) is focused on winning reelection, so he has no documented early-primary-state visits yet. That hasn't stopped presidential rumors from swirling. Zoom out: First, Schumer needs to get to at least 51 seats in November, navigate a high-stakes lame-duck session, and then win a secret-ballot election to reclaim his title as majority leader. Some of his potential new members — especially if Democrats have a good night on Nov. 3 — aren't overly enthusiastic about supporting him. Candidates like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and James Talarico in Texas have not committed to voting for him. The bottom line: Presidential candidates want to stand out. Senate majority leaders need their members to blend in — and fall in line.

fce783ce77c1.text: By — Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Christopher Rugaber, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-establishes-committee-to-investigate-federal-reserves-lisa-cook-in-latest-effort-to-fire-her Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump establishes committee to investigate Federal Reserve's Lisa Cook in latest effort to fire her Politics Oct 9, 2026 4:33 PM EDT WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump opened another chapter in his effort to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook Friday by establishing a "committee of inquiry" to investigate allegations that she made false statements in mortgage applications. The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House Nov. 5, Trump said in a written memo, that Cook "shall" attend to answer questions from the committee. The hearing wouldn't be public but a transcript would be published, the memo said. READ MORE: Trump administration proceeds with efforts to fire Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook Trump's extraordinary demand that Cook testify before the committee will likely renew concerns about threats to the Federal Reserve's independence. The president has repeatedly called for the central bank to cut its key interest rate, but just last month, the Fed raised it instead, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom Trump appointed earlier this year. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. Trump's attempts to fire Cook from the Fed's seven-member board of governors represent the first time in the central bank's 113-year history that a president has sought to remove a Fed governor. Cook was appointed by former President Joe Biden and is the first Black woman on the Fed's board. Trump's attacks on her followed other efforts to oust or indict Black officials, such as New York Attorney General Letitia James and Gen. Charles Q. Brown, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. "As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law," Trump wrote in the memorandum. Cook's attorneys, Abbe Lowell and Norman Eisen, said they were considering having Cook appear at the Nov. 5 hearing and respond to the charges. READ MORE: No criminal wrongdoing in Federal Reserve building renovation, watchdog says, but it was mismanaged "We have engaged with the White House to evaluate whether the process proposed has a possibility of being a genuine one and not simply a box checking exercise," Lowell and Eisen said in a statement. "Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her." The "committee of inquiry" will be composed of Kevin Hassett, the president's top economic adviser, who has frequently echoed Trump's criticisms of the Fed; Keith Sonderling, the acting director of the Office of Government Ethics, whom the president has also appointed to lead the Labor Department, and Andrea Lucas, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, whom Trump appointed in November 2025. Trump initially tried to fire Cook in August 2025 after alleging she had committed mortgage fraud by declaring two different properties to be her "primary" residence in mortgage applications in 2021. Mortgages on primary homes can often receive a lower interest rate or other beneficial terms. Cook has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime. Lowell and Eisen have previously said Cook committed an "inadvertent error" and did refer to one of the properties as a vacation home in other documents. "An inadvertent error is not fraud, as the President and a third of his cabinet should know because they reportedly did the same thing," Lowell and Eisen said in August. The Federal Reserve declined to comment on Trump's announcement. Trump and some of his economic advisers have blamed the Fed's broader rate-setting committee, which includes 12 voting members and 19 officials in total, for forcing last month's rate hike, even though it followed comments by Warsh in August that signaled higher rates were likely. As a member of the board of governors, Cook is also one of the 12 voting members of the committee. The vote to lift rates Sept. 16 was unanimous. The move also follows a Supreme Court ruling in June that Cook could keep her job after Trump sought to fire her last year. That ruling included a footnote that said nothing prevented Trump from "trying again" as long as she was given proper notice and an opportunity to respond to the charges. Trump said the committee of inquiry will seek to establish whether there is "cause" to fire Cook, as required under the law governing the Fed. The Supreme Court said in June that a for-cause firing required an alleged offense that was serious and related to an official's job. Scott Alvarez, formerly the chief counsel for the Fed, said that President William Howard Taft set up a similar commission in 1912 to remove two officials from an independent agency. The commission created by Trump goes beyond the type of process the Supreme Court said was needed to fire Cook. "It's an attempt to show that he's really giving Cook as much process as possible," Alvarez said. Still, the allegations against Cook don't appear to meet the "for cause" standard set out by the Supreme Court, Alvarez said. Other analysts said that Trump will likely use the process to ultimately fire Cook. "We do not see why the White House would start this process if it were not trying to create a way to justify removing Cook from her job," Jaret Seiberg, managing director of TD Cowen's Washington Research Group, said in a note to clients. Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.
Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.
Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.
The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.
As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public â stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation â has soured.
The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.
It is these states â places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio â that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.
For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.
He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.
He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms â an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.
His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.
Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return â besides much-needed hard currency â is unclear.
It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy".
"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.
It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.
The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.
Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes â attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.
The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.
Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.
With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked.
"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.
But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.
Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

Oil companies will no longer be required to conduct environmental reviews before exploring for fossil fuel reservoirs in the Western Arctic, the largest tract of federally managed public land in the United States.
The Bureau of Land Management announced a categorical exclusion under the National Environmental Policy Act for winter oil and gas exploration in the National Petroleum Reserve-Alaska, also known as the Western Arctic. Published Friday in the Federal Register, the exemption comes as the Trump administration moves to accelerate oil and gas drilling in Alaska.
The categorical exclusion will allow developers to “more nimbly locate energy resources in the Petroleum Reserve,” increasing domestic energy supply and lowering costs for the public, said Kevin Pendergast, Alaska State Director for the Bureau of Land Management. The agency said its decision reflects a “long history” of exploration in the region without “significant or lasting environmental impact.”
During Arctic exploration, oil and gas firms construct temporary roads, drill test wells and conduct seismic surveys, in which “thumper trucks” weighing up to 45 tons send shock waves through the ground to detect oil deposits. The activities are mostly limited to winter, when heavy machinery can travel over frozen ground without sinking into the delicate tundra and permafrost below.
Even then, exploration activities pose a significant risk to residents and an already threatened ecosystem.
The Western Arctic is the traditional land of the Iñupiat people and serves as a critical wildlife habitat for hundreds of thousands of caribou across three major herds. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s 2024 Arctic Report Card, caribou populations in the region have fallen by more than half since their historic highs in the 1990s.
Industrial development in the Arctic directly interferes with seasonal migration routes and the areas where herds return year after year to calve. United States Geological Survey research has documented changes in Arctic caribou behavior even at low vehicle traffic volumes.
The petroleum reserve is also home to millions of migratory birds, as well as polar bears and seals threatened by habitat loss due to rapidly melting sea ice.
The Arctic is warming at two to four times the global average rate. As snow and ice melt in the polar region, they expose a darker surface that absorbs more sunlight and drives further warming in a feedback loop scientists have dubbed “ice-albedo” feedback. Critics of the exemption say that signing off on oil exploration without any environmental review process further harms a fragile ecosystem.
“It is no secret that the Trump administration will ignore impacts to public lands and our nation’s laws if it benefits resource extraction corporations, but recent efforts to remove any and all public review of Arctic oil extraction are particularly egregious,” said Andy Moderow, senior director of policy for the Alaska Wilderness League in a statement by the organization. “This drill first and discover the impacts later approach puts Arctic lands, waters, and wildlife at risk.”
Opponents also question the legality of the categorical exclusion.
“The administration finalized this new approach with zero public input,” said Janet Bering, an Alaska-based attorney with the environmental law organization Earthjustice. “Combined with a similar proposal that rubber stamps new oil production, this is a one-two punch. It’s bad policy, and it is unlawful.”
Last month, the Bureau of Land Management proposed a rule to expedite all oil and gas drilling across the Western Arctic by cutting environmental review and public input for projects beyond the exploration phase.
The rule stemmed from a petition by the Alaska Oil and Gas Association, a trade group representing oil and gas firms exploring and producing offshore and in Alaska’s northernmost reaches, including the National Petroleum Reserve. The association did not respond immediately to requests for comment on Friday’s decision.

The Trump administration’s push to accelerate oil extraction in the Arctic has drawn mixed responses from Alaska Natives. Some Iñupiat communities in the region say they stand to benefit economically from drilling and corporate investments. Others see the development as a blow to already imperiled lands critical for subsistence hunting and, with it, their traditions and culture.
Rosemary Ahtuangaruak, a former mayor of the majority-Iñupiat community of Nuiqsut and founder of the organization Grandmothers Growing Goodness, said caribou have been pushed farther away from Nuiqsut as ConocoPhillips expands drilling operations in the area.
The community is located just four miles outside the petroleum reserve. For years, Nuiqsut residents have fought for stronger environmental mitigation measures in pending drilling permits. Ahtuangaruak has advocated for practices that would reduce air pollution from gas flares and protect caribou migration to their seasonal calving grounds.
By eliminating the environmental review process, Nuiqsut residents will have even fewer opportunities to weigh in through public comment, she said.
“We should not let the greed of profiteering lead our tables of decision-making over the cost of people and the life, health and safety of the generations to come,” Ahtuangaruak said.
First designated as a petroleum reserve for the U.S. Navy in 1923, the Department of the Interior assumed authority for oil and gas leasing in the region in 1976. Yet the 36,000-square-mile tract of wild Arctic tundra, wetlands and coastline was largely preserved as wilderness until the turn of the 21st century.

A crude oil pipeline spill last month in the Detroit suburbs has prompted federal authorities to open an investigation into the safety of all 20,000 miles of hazardous liquids pipelines operated by Energy Transfer.
The 600-gallon spill at a commercial intersection in Sterling Heights, Michigan, has received little media coverage. Local news reports at the time, based on a statement from the city, described a much smaller spill and stressed that no residents or homes were in danger. Neither the city nor news reports mentioned the name of the Dallas-based pipeline operator, one of the nation’s largest and most politically connected oil and gas companies.
But in a corrective-action order issued Sept. 21 without a press release, the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration revealed the failure on Energy Transfer’s 59-year-old, 130-mile crude oil pipeline between Marysville, Michigan, and Toledo, Ohio. The federal agency, part of the U.S. Department of Transportation, initially directed the company to shut down a 16-mile segment at the site of the spill. An agency spokesperson said the pipeline was restarted the following day at reduced pressure, slowing the flow of oil.
In an extraordinary move, due to “a system-wide risk of additional similar failures,” PHMSA gave Energy Transfer 90 days to submit a detailed inventory of past repairs made throughout its hazardous liquid pipeline network nationwide, as well as a plan to remediate vulnerabilities.
It was the only one of 23 corrective-action orders PHMSA has issued this year that seek to address safety issues on a company’s entire pipeline network. According to Energy Transfer’s website, that network includes about 20,000 miles of crude oil, refined product and natural gas liquids pipelines.
PHMSA said Energy Transfer’s initial investigation confirmed the spill occurred at the site of a past repair—a steel encasement sleeve that had been welded onto the Michigan pipeline in 2010 to fix a defect. The same kind of encasement sleeve failure caused a jet fuel leak discovered last year on another Energy Transfer pipeline that contaminated the drinking water source of a residential neighborhood north of Philadelphia, the PHMSA order said.
“Considering the characteristics of Energy Transfer’s larger pipeline network, the failures underneath at least two repair sleeves, each with indications of improper installation, point to a likelihood of future failures,” said the order, signed by the agency’s top official, Administrator Paul Roberti.
Last year, after Energy Transfer made a large political donation to a PAC supporting President Donald Trump, PHMSA backed off a proposal that would have forced the company to scrutinize all past repairs on its Twin Oaks pipeline in Pennsylvania and remediate any vulnerabilities. Now, the agency essentially is ordering Energy Transfer to develop such a remedial action plan for all of its hazardous liquids pipelines, including both the Twin Oaks and the Marysville-to-Toledo lines.
The agency issued the order three days after the Michigan spill was discovered, saying it was acting without giving Energy Transfer notice or an opportunity for a prior hearing because of the risk of “serious harm.” The company has since requested a hearing, which has not been scheduled yet, according to a PHMSA spokesperson.
Energy Transfer in an email declined to answer questions about the incident. “Please refer to PHMSA documents, which have all the available information,” said an unsigned email from the company’s media relations team.
A factor that figured into PHMSA’s decision on the nationwide order: Energy Transfer could not locate the original records for the steel repair sleeve at Sterling Heights, nor could it find records that would enable the agency to verify the integrity of 11 other such sleeves along the length of the Marysville-to-Toledo pipeline, the agency said.
In the Michigan order, PHMSA revealed for the first time that Energy Transfer also was not able to find records for four of the 45 repair sleeves along the length of its Twin Oaks pipeline that failed last year in Pennsylvania.
PHMSA had ordered Energy Transfer to submit records on the Twin Oaks repair sleeves to the agency last year, but the submission was not made public despite at least 11 Freedom of Information Act requests, including from Inside Climate News. PHMSA said it could not make the Twin Oaks documents public due to an ongoing enforcement investigation.
An agency spokesperson declined to answer further questions on the Michigan incident, saying by email that the investigation remains ongoing.
Energy Transfer inherited both the Michigan and Pennsylvania pipelines in 2012 when the company purchased Philadelphia-based Sunoco for $5.3 billion. The acquisition transformed Energy Transfer from mainly a natural gas pipeline firm into a diversified giant with crude oil and refined product pipelines in 10 states. Both spill sites, like much of the Sunoco network, are located in PHMSA-designated “high consequence areas,” locations where a pipeline rupture could have significant adverse impact on human health, safety, property or the environment.
Pipeline Politics
Energy Transfer has become a major player on the political scene, due largely to its founder and executive chairman Kelcy Warren’s support for President Donald Trump.
Last year, one week after PHMSA sent the company notice of a proposed safety order over the Pennsylvania spill, Warren and Energy Transfer donated a total $25 million to MAGA Inc., the political action committee established after Trump’s election. The president directly controls its $400 million war chest. It was the largest political donation Warren had ever given, and it made Energy Transfer the biggest oil and gas industry donor so far in the 2026 election cycle, according to data compiled by the nonprofit OpenSecrets for Inside Climate News. 5bb985bbde8e.text: By — Ed White, Associated Press Ed White, Associated Press By — Claudia Lauer, Associated Press Claudia Lauer, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/legal-path-seems-narrow-to-challenge-livestream-of-fort-hood-shooters-execution-experts-say Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Legal path seems narrow to challenge livestream of Fort Hood shooter's execution, experts say World Oct 9, 2026 5:55 PM EDT Any effort to challenge the Trump administration's plan to livestream the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan might rest solely with the man sentenced to death for killing 13 people at the Texas military base in 2009, experts say. Broadcasting the event worldwide isn't mentioned in the Army rules governing how rare military executions are carried out. But that doesn't mean there is a viable legal path to oppose it by anyone besides Hasan. And he hasn't signaled whether he will even try to stop anything related to his Dec. 3 death sentence. WATCH: Vance says he's 'not going to be watching' livestream of Fort Hood shooter's execution Officials at the Pentagon said Thursday that Hasan's execution by a firing squad would be livestreamed and that more details would follow. A day earlier, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said, "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public." Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "Other than Hasan, I'm not sure anyone could" have legal standing to stop a livestream, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova University's law school and an expert in military justice. Could U.S. parents try to halt livestream? Fissell, however, tossed up a novel possibility: parents who don't want their children to see a person blasted with bullets on the internet, either in real time or viewed later. Army regulations say, "No person under the age of 18 shall witness" a military execution. "That's explicit," Fissell said. "It's a question of whether a livestream counts as a presence. ... I think it violates the spirit of the regulation." READ MORE: Pentagon says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed The regulations, he added, weren't written to contemplate witnesses outside the actual site of an execution — and certainly not a livestream. "This actually has not been explored enough," Fissell said. Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law, said he doesn't see a lot of legal options to challenge most of the unfolding details of Hasan's execution, though he agrees that Hasan would have standing to object with a petition, known as habeas corpus, in U.S. District Court. "Arguing the Army can't livestream it because some parent wouldn't be able to stop their kid from watching it on the computer strikes me as a very unlikely piece of litigation," Fidell said. "Better legal minds than me maybe can come up with a way to make that argument, but I don't see it." Last firing squad was in WWII Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers at Fort Hood were waiting to receive medical clearance for deployment. He shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — and opened fire and also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot. Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. He is paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair. Clergy, including U.S. Catholic bishops, and some officials criticized the livestreaming announcement. Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, told reporters that he wouldn't watch it and expressed some doubt whether a livestream would happen. President Donald Trump signed off on Hasan's execution, which would be the first by a firing squad since World War II. The last military execution happened on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was killed by hanging. A 2023 update to the Army regulation on executions gave the Secretary of the Army discretion on choosing a method, in part to ease hurdles to conducting executions at Guantanamo Bay, Fidell said. A firing squad is "clearly a legal method of execution in the military," Fissell said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. MARTINEZ, Calif.—Scores of people tired of living near accident-prone refineries packed an elementary school auditorium to hear what their government officials were doing to protect them.
Two local refineries, Marathon Martinez Renewables and Martinez Refining Co., have racked up hundreds of air quality violations over the past five years. MRC agreed in February to pay $10 million in fines for 163 violations that included an accident that blanketed residents’ homes with 24 tons of metal-laden dust four years ago on Thanksgiving Day.
The settlement did not cover a similar episode in 2025, when a fireball sent thick clouds of smoke across town, leaving residents wondering, again, if it was safe to go outside or eat from their gardens.
Marathon’s Martinez Renewables, which recently locked out more than 100 workers in a labor dispute, has received more than 100 violations from the air district for flaring and other infractions since 2021.
Such incidents inspired U.S. Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, a Democrat, to meet with his constituents in this small city an hour northeast of San Francisco on Thursday night. DeSaulnier, a former air regulator whose district includes four refineries, stressed the need to balance the economic benefits refineries bring to the region with the risks they pose to workers and communities.
Refineries are among the county’s top property-tax contributors and provide thousands of good-paying jobs, DeSaulnier said. The region needs these refineries as it transitions toward renewable energy, but they need to be safe, he said. “It’s a constant battle.”
Flaring incidents have increased in recent years, spiking to nearly 70 in 2023. Flaring involves the controlled burning of flammable gases to manage a buildup of pressure in equipment and reduce the risk of explosions. It also releases a mixture of toxic chemicals, fine particles and climate pollutants.
Recognizing residents’ concerns about ongoing flaring, county officials at the meeting announced the release of a new public dashboard that allows people to track incidents, something residents like Heidi Taylor have been asking for.
Taylor, who co-founded Healthy Martinez after MRC showered her home with heavy metals, wants the refinery to undergo a new health risk assessment, which hasn’t been done in 36 years, she said.
“We need to know what health risks Martinez residents are facing, when that information will be made public and how quickly any unacceptable risks will be addressed,” Taylor said.
MRC did not respond to a request for comment from Inside Climate News.
These incidents require greater enforcement but the Trump administration is working to undermine federal oversight of refineries, DeSaulnier said.
The administration has repeatedly tried to eliminate the U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, an independent federal agency that investigates the root causes of industrial chemical accidents. So far, Congress has continued to fund the agency.
Keeping refinery workers and surrounding communities safe requires real-time accountability measures that trigger automatic investigations or corrective actions after incidents, DeSaulnier argued in a recent op-ed. He suggested following Chemical Safety Board recommendations such as tracking equipment failures, overdue inspections, leaks and failed safety systems.
DeSaulnier has a long history of trying to improve refinery safety, dating back to his days as a Contra Costa County supervisor. The congressman was briefly overcome with emotion during Thursday’s hearing as he recounted the deaths of five men at the Tosco Avon Refinery in the 1990s, when he said the county averaged one refinery-related death or serious injury every year.
“I went to a couple of funerals,” he said, regaining his composure, “and I will never forget hearing about the lives of five individuals who, in my opinion, never should have died.”
The Avon refinery is now operated by Marathon Petroleum as Martinez Renewables, where an explosion in 2023 left Jerome Serrano, an operator with four children, fighting for his life for months. Workers with the United Steelworkers Local 5 blamed understaffing and unsustainable overtime shifts for the accident.

More than 100 employees went on strike for safer conditions after Marathon refused to give them the same contract it had negotiated with the USW for more than 200 other bargaining units across the petroleum and renewables industry.
The strike turned into a lockout when the company rejected union members’ unconditional return to work offer. Workers have now been out of the plant for 165 days.
Nick Plurkowski, USW Local 5 president, was glad to see so many people show up to learn about refinery safety. The meeting covered current regulations and other important topics in a way “only the congressman can do,” Plurkowski said, referring to his personal connection to the workers who died. “He understands that the worst possible outcome isn’t the refineries paying fines, it’s when someone we know gets hurt or killed.”
“The amount of flaring is concerning to say the least,” said Plurkowski. He filed a complaint with state occupational health and safety regulators, alleging that the workers who replaced the USW Local 5 workers, who he said were illegally locked out, aren’t qualified to operate the plant safely. As a result, he said, the state is investigating Marathon’s training of the workers currently running the plant.
Marathon spokesperson Jamal Kheiry said the company continues to staff the Martinez Renewables facility with highly qualified personnel, including supervisors, engineers and technical experts with extensive experience and training in safe, reliable plant operations.
