e97c16fe6261.text: President Trump decided to make a diesel fuel deal with Russia after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ignored half a dozen U.S. requests to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, a U.S. official with direct knowledge told Axios. Why it matters: Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin sparked a new crisis with Ukraine and threatens to derail a new push by the Trump administration for a deal to end the war. "Zelensky is misreading the room. By continuing to hit refineries, he is eroding the good will that he has built with Trump over the last six months," the U.S. official said. Zelensky, in an interview with Axios after the announcement, said he was blindsided by the deal, which he called "not fair and not honest" and an unwarranted gift to Putin. Driving the news: Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries in recent months were highly effective and caused an energy crisis in Russia. Russia imposed a ban on diesel exports in response, which added more pressure to global diesel markets under strain from the war in Iran. Zelensky told Trump and his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner that he was prepared to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if the Russians halted attacks on Ukrainian power plants. The U.S. official said Trump wanted Ukraine to unilaterally stop attacking Russian refineries because the strikes were contributing to high gas prices in America. Trump didn't see the attacks on refineries as equivalent to Russian strikes on Ukraine's power grid, the U.S. official said. Inside the room: During eight hours of talks in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner told a Ukrainian negotiating team that the president was expected to speak to Putin and lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports. They were told that Trump decided to move forward after Ukraine ignored multiple requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries, which were directly affecting U.S. consumers. A Ukrainian official claimed that during the talks, Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could cut off Ukraine from U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests. The U.S. official denied such a threat was made and said Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, Witkoff and Kushner said. "The attacks on the refineries cause pain in Russia, but it causes pain for the U.S., too," the U.S. official said. Zoom in: The official said the new crisis over the diesel deal erupted after the U.S. mediators had constructive talks with Ukrainian and European diplomats in Miami on Friday. The main focus was on finalizing security guarantees that the U.S., Europe and NATO would provide to Ukraine as part of a deal to end the war. New proposals for territorial solutions were also raised. Witkoff and Kushner presented a postwar package for Ukraine that included ways to fund reconstruction and rebuild the Ukrainian military, as well as ideas on how to deal with budget deficits stemming from the war. The participants also discussed a roadmap for Ukraine's accession to the EU and the relationship Ukraine would have with NATO after the war ends. In addition, Witkoff and Kushner raised the possibility of a Europe-Russia postwar security framework that could appeal to both sides. What to watch: Witkoff and Kushner briefed the Ukrainians and Europeans on potential energy deals with Russia that the U.S. hopes would bring down energy prices and induce Russia to make concessions in peace talks, the U.S. official said. What's next: The U.S. official said Witkoff and Kushner are considering visiting Moscow and Kyiv next week to discuss peace proposals, but it's unclear how Friday's blowup will affect their plans. "Putin is hitting [Ukraine] hard but we think he is open to a discussion on ending the war. We want to work on a new proposal that will be good enough for him in order to get him to stop," the U.S. official said. Yes, but: During his 90-minute phone call with Trump, Putin declined to commit to resuming peace talks with Ukraine, his foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov told reporters. He said that Ukrainian strikes on Moscow and other cities during the Russian parliamentary elections "thwarted the possibility of an immediate resumption of the negotiation process." "The president said, we will think about when these negotiations can be resumed," Ushakov added.

A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.
The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.
That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo
The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-UÃ©lÃ©, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.
The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.
Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.
The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.
Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya
Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.
The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.

As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets.
"There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school.
"We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen."
He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycÃ©es, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.
Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down.
"They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population."
The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis.
The protests - ignited at the LycÃ©e Antoine-de-Saint-ExupÃ©ry in the deprived Paris suburb of CrÃ©teil - have struck a chord across the country.
Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycÃ©es soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter.
The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system.
The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them.
On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million.
But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them.
Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem.
It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages.
When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils).
"It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains.
On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.
Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget.
But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country.
"It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycÃ©e student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la RÃ©publique, a place synonymous with protest.
"It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future."
The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries.
So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry.
More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks.
But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers.
A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens.
Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade.
A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth.
"For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether."
Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests.
But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests.
"These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world."
Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard.
Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring.

Parts of the Indian capital, Delhi, have been turned into a fortress, with tens of thousands of security forces deployed, as the influential Gen Z-led "cockroach" movement has called for a major protest on Saturday.
The protesters are seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists.
The Election Commission has denied this and Kumar is yet to comment on the resignation demand.
Police say they have denied permission for the gathering and all roads leading to Jantar Mantar, the main protest venue, have been closed with huge metal barricades.
Several trains to Delhi have been cancelled and police have ordered dozens of metro stations shut to prevent protesters from gathering.
But Abhijeet Dipke, founder â of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) - the online satirical movement that is spearheading the protests - has said the CJP will march to Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning "come what may".
"If you want to jail us or even shoot us we are prepared," he added, addressing âPrime Minister Narendra Modi in a post on X.
The CJP's weeks-long protest in the summer seeking education reforms was its first major challenge to Modi's government. The CJP scored a major victory when it forced education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign in July.
The CJP protesters returned to streets last week with a rally in Mumbai city to press for CEC Kumar's resignation. On Thursday, they held a huge rally in the southern city of Bengaluru (formerly Bangalore).
Student groups and opposition parties have also protested in the capital over the past few days.
Saturday's protests are being billed as the biggest in recent times as they are also being supported by several opposition parties, farmer organisations and student groups.
CJP leaders allege the authorities have been preventing many of their supporters from reaching Delhi.
In the capital, more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed and authorities have appealed to citizens to stay away from protests.
Police official Nupur Prasad told a press conference, external that one of the reasons for denying permission to protest at Jantar Mantar was the "short notice" given by the CJP.
"Under current guidelines, an application to organise an event at Jantar Mantar must be submitted at least 10 days prior to the scheduled date," she said.
Also, she added that in the past, the CJP had not followed "lawful directions" given to them.
"In light of the non-compliance with prescribed procedures, the failure to adhere to past legal directions, and the current state of public safety, law and order, and traffic regulation, permission for the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar is hereby denied."
The CJP have questioned police denying them permission for the protest - they say that legally they only have to inform the police and do not need their approval to gather.
At the centre of the row is a controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year.
The Election Commission says it is to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.
But opposition parties and activists have alleged that many of those are eligible voters and that the process is being manipulated by CEC Kumar to favour Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.
The past few days have also seen a major escalation in the opposition's standoff with the Election Commission.
For three days in a row starting Tuesday, Delhi witnessed dramatic scenes with police breaking up protests by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other MPs over the issue.
Videos showing police forcing Gandhi on to a bus and preventing him from climbing out of the bus window subsequently went viral on social media.

4196f8786645.text: Hurricane Isaias has strengthened into a Category 3 hurricane as it heads toward the Gulf Coast. Residents are rushing to prepare for the storm, which is packing winds up to 120 mph and is expected to make landfall Friday night. Amna Nawaz speaks with Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, for more. Amna Nawaz: Hurricane Isaias has now strengthened into a Category 3 major hurricane as it heads towards the Gulf Coast. The storm is packing winds up to 120 miles an hour and is expected to make landfall later tonight. States of emergency have been declared in parts of Alabama, Florida, and Georgia, warning of storm surge up to nine feet and as many as 15 inches of rain in some coastal areas. All along the coast, residents are rushing to prepare, lining up for gas and boarding up their homes ahead of the storm. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis today urged people to get ready. Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL): You will face very hazardous conditions prior to the storm making landfall. So you really need to finish your preparations now. You have to execute your plans now. There's going to be a point in the not-too-distant future where it's not going to be safe to go outside, even though the storm may still be a distance away from reaching the shore. Do it now. Amna Nawaz: Joining us now is Michael Brennan. He's director of the National Hurricane Center. Michael, welcome back. So, give us the latest that we know about Hurricane Isaias' path. where and when is it expected to make landfall? Michael Brennan, Director, National Hurricane Center: Well, I can just tell you, Isaias is still a Category 3 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson scale, with maximum sustained winds of 115 miles per hour, down just a little bit from earlier in the day, but that's just a really minuscule change. You can see the center of circulation just offshore of the Florida Panhandle here, probably going to move inland on the coast and make landfall in the next couple of hours. And that's when the worst of the conditions will begin to materialize. But as you can see here behind me, all of this weather is pushing onshore now. So conditions are going downhill really, really rapidly. Amna Nawaz: Yesterday, you mentioned to us that it could weaken further as it approaches landfall. Is that still true? Michael Brennan: Yes, so it's experiencing what we call vertical shear, which hurricanes don't -- they don't strengthen usually in those types of environments. The storm so far has been able to cling to Category 3 status. A little bit more weakening is possible right before it makes landfall. But, for all practical purposes, it really won't matter because the hazards are already baked and set in place. Even if the storm comes down a little bit from a wind speed perspective, the rain and the storm surge and the wind impacts really won't change much. Amna Nawaz: And are your concerns still largely the same based on what's happened since the last day we spoke, flooding and storm surge mainly for coastal areas, or should folks inland be concerned as well? Michael Brennan: So we're a bit more concerned about inland impacts. The forward speed has increased today. It's now moving really, really rapidly at 17 miles per hour. And what that means is, it can carry the momentum a little bit farther inland. So I think what we're going to see is the winds and potential power loss extending deep into Alabama portions of Georgia and even Eastern portions of Mississippi, so absolutely not a coastal phenomenon. These winds are going to spread deep inland. Amna Nawaz: And at this point, would you say it is too late for people to try to evacuate? If they're not able to, what should they do to prepare? Michael Brennan: At this point, it is much too late to be moving around. Sun will be going down soon. Conditions are deteriorating rapidly. We're already seeing tornadoes form in some of these outer bands. You just need to be where you're going to be, hunker down, ride out the storm. Don't be out venturing around looking at it. Amna Nawaz: We're thinking about everybody in the storm's path and wishing them well. That is Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, joining us tonight once again. Thank you. Michael Brennan: Thank you.

a00c8973c245.text: An investigation is underway after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents shot a man in New York City Thursday. Federal authorities say 28-year-old Oscar Belgal attempted to ram officers with his vehicle when they tried to detain him. ICE agents then fired at his car, where a young child was in the back seat. William Brangham reports. Amna Nawaz: An investigation is under way after ICE agents shot a man in New York City yesterday. Federal authorities say 28-year-old Oscar Belgal, who is illegally in the U.S., attempted to ram officers with a vehicle when they tried to detain him. ICE agents then fired at his car where a young child was in the back seat. William Brangham has this report. William Brangham: Bodycam footage released today shows New York City police arriving at the scene of the ICE shooting finding plainclothes ICE officers, one seemingly dressed as a construction worker, carrying a long gun, another tending to Oscar Belgal, the man they'd shot in the neck minutes before, in the background, the car Belgal was driving with his 5-year-old son. The boy was unharmed and is now with family members. Man: It was really quick. It was boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. Zohran Mamdani (D), Mayor of New York City: Let me say this plainly. William Brangham: New York's mayor, Zohran Mamdani, called the shooting an outrage. Zohran Mamdani: Tonight, a 5-year-old child sits traumatized and terrified. Tonight, millions of our neighbors are wondering whether they will be safe on our streets, in our schools, at their worksites. William Brangham: That night, protesters gathered at the site. Protester: Whose streets? Protesters: Our streets! Protester: Whose streets? Protesters: Our streets! William Brangham: The growing crowd clashed with police. Federal authorities say ICE agents were attempting to arrest Belgal when he tried to flee, and agents shot at least seven rounds at his car believing their lives were in danger. They said agents were unaware a child was in the back seat. Marcos Charles, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement: Mr. Belgal was struck by one of the bullets or fragments superficially in the neck. He stopped his vehicle. We arrested him, rendered first aid information and then took him to the hospital. William Brangham: DHS said the 28-year-old suspect has now been transferred to an undisclosed detention facility outside New York. Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Homeland Security Secretary: It is shameful that we're giving this particular case so much attention when this was a thug. William Brangham: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Belgal had a criminal history and blamed this escalation on the actions of New York officials. Sen. Markwayne Mullin: Sanctuary politicians, they create an environment for criminal activity to thrive, not for the American citizens to be safe. Underneath President Trump, he made it very clear he was going to restore law and order in our cities and our towns and our states, despite what happens with career politicians that put criminals in front of law-abiding citizens. William Brangham: Mayor Mamdani and New York Governor Kathy Hochul both talked with President Trump trying to negotiate Mr. Belgal's release and pressed him to stop immigration enforcement operations in New York. In a statement posted to social media, Governor Hochul wrote -- quote -- "New Yorkers have witnessed far too many acts of violence by a rogue federal agency and untrained agents that operate with impunity." Federal immigration agents have now reportedly shot at least two dozen people since the start of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown in January 2025. For the "PBS News Hour," I'm William Brangham.

c9b1934a01d2.text: Candidates for U.S. Senate in three battleground states faced off in fiery debates Thursday night that frequently veered into personal attacks. David Brooks of The Atlantic and Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW join Amna Nawaz to discuss the week in politics, including the battle for control of Congress. Amna Nawaz: Candidates for U.S. Senate in three battleground states faced off in fiery debates last night that frequently veered into personal attacks. In Michigan, Republican Mike Rogers tried to tie Democrat Abdul El-Sayed's family to terrorism, despite there being no evidence. Abdul El-Sayed (D), Michigan Senatorial Candidate: You go after my mom? Mike Rogers (R), Michigan Senatorial Candidate: I'm not going after your mom. Abdul El-Sayed: That's exactly what you're doing. Mike Rogers: What your mom was working at, I was going after that organization that was indicted for funneling money to al-Qaida. Amna Nawaz: In Georgia, Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff accused Republican Congressman Mike Collins of bigotry and racism. Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA): It's not just that you have hired half the Third Reich to staff your congressional office and you have promoted neo-Nazi content online. It's that you're robbing your constituents to subsidize your donors. If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club. Rep. Mike Collins (R-GA), Senatorial Candidate: I have condemned racism, antisemitism, hate. I don't care where the source is. And I tell him that too. It's wrong. We have no place in this world for that. Amna Nawaz: And, in Maine, Republican Senator Susan Collins demanded that Democrat Troy Jackson apologize after he accused her of corruption. Troy Jackson (D), Maine Senatorial Candidate: She could use her leverage to stop this war, but instead they're making money. I mean, Senator Collins and her husband are making money more off of this war, and so is a whole bunch of other people, and that's why this doesn't stop. Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME): That is absolutely outrageous, and you owe me an apology. Troy Jackson: No, you owe me an apology. Amna Nawaz: For more on the battle for control of Congress, we turn now to the analysis of Brooks and Capehart. That is "The Atlantic"'s David Brooks and Jonathan Capehart of MS NOW. Good to see you both. Jonathan Capehart: Hey, Amna. Amna Nawaz: Speaking with those debates last night, some policy discussions, but very heavy on the personal attacks. And in the context of this, we should say The Cook Political Report just this week shifted eight house races and three Senate races in Kansas, North Carolina, and New Hampshire toward Democrats. Jonathan, Senate control is on the line here. Is that why these are getting so heated? Jonathan Capehart: Yes. I mean, I have said many times -- excuse me -- I have said many times here that this election cycle, midterm election cycle, reminds me of 2006, exactly 20 years ago. These same conversations were happening, particularly with the Senate. The Senate map then and now was supposed to be extremely difficult, if not impossible for Democrats to retake the majority. And here we are in just Georgia, Michigan, Maine. I mean, Maine would be the only pickup of the three. But the fact that these debates are so nasty and personal shows that Democrats feel they are within striking distance. Republicans feel perhaps that they are on their on their back foot -- on their back feet. And, I mean, given who the president is, same -- president of their party, they should feel that they're on their back feet. Amna Nawaz: David, you agree? David Brooks: Some -- I agree with Jonathan, but I think something has changed since 2006, which is we have had 10 years of political, moral decay, and sound a lot -- the candidates used to be inhibited a bit by the sense that, if I lie, if I'm a total sleazebag, it might hurt me. And now they realize it won't hurt me at all. And, in fact, my partisans may actually like it. And so you had -- I think, in those three cases, all three of those things were sleazy behavior, Troy Jackson. Susan Collins has some Boeing stock in her portfolio. And he calls her a war profiteer because of that? That's ridiculous. The insinuations that El-Sayed is involved in terrorism because he's Muslim, ridiculous. Jon Ossoff, my advice to him is, if you start calling your political opponents Nazis, maybe it's time to shut up. That's just not what we do here in this country. And the Bull Connor stuff -- and a lot of these candidates have real weaknesses. Like, Mike Collins, who's the Georgia Republican, I think what's accurate to say about him is, he has a disturbing number of young men on his -- around him who have ties to the alt-right and some of the vile antisemitic stuff online. El-Sayed can... Amna Nawaz: Who have shared, we should say, white nationalist content online, right. David Brooks: Right. Amna Nawaz: That's the accusation. David Brooks: El-Sayed, he can't tell the difference between Iran and Israel. When asked whether -- which was a greater threat, he couldn't tell the difference. Iran has killed thousands of Americans. Iran is the leading cause of -- or leading sponsor of terrorism around the world. If you can't tell the difference, then something's wrong here. And so they could have gone after legitimate weaknesses. But in each case, they took it to 11 and it was dishonest. Amna Nawaz: Meanwhile, we know the cost of living, price of gas, these are the things at the top of all voters' minds. And I want to ask you about what we heard from the president himself late today, which was a deal with Vladimir Putin to get diesel from Russia. That reverses years of pressure on Moscow for their war in Ukraine. It also flies in the face of new legislation that Congress just passed that would allow the president broad powers to punish countries that buy Russian oil. It also follows Trump pledging that there would be no more strikes on Iran, David, until after the midterm e

bbeaae5bcbb3.text: Actor Ke Huy Quan went from arriving in America as a refugee to starring in Indiana Jones and The Goonies. Decades later, he made an Oscar-winning comeback. In the latest episode of our PBS News podcast “Settle In,” Amna Nawaz spoke with him about his debut memoir “Never Say Die,” which starts with his family’s harrowing attempts to escape post-war Vietnam. Amna Nawaz: Actor Ke Huy Quan went from arriving in America as a refugee to starring in "Indiana Jones" and "The Goonies." Decades later, he made an Oscar-winning comeback. In the latest episode of our PBS News podcast "Settle In," I spoke with him about his debut memoir, "Never Say Die," which starts with his family's harrowing attempts to escape postwar Vietnam. Ke Huy Quan, Author, "Never Say Die": My parents have nine kids, so there's 11 of us. So their whole idea was that if we were to all escape at the same time, the chance of us making out, it's unlikely. So, very early on, they decided we're going to separate. So my mom took three of my siblings, including my best friend, David. They got on a boat and went to Malaysia. And they made it on the first attempt. And so my mom and three of my siblings were separated for more than a year-and-a-half. Amna Nawaz: I mean, for a parent to have to make that kind of decision, I can't even imagine. Have you talked to your parents about that, about that moment and having to make those kinds of decisions for your family? Ke Huy Quan: Interestingly, no. We never spoke about it. I think that's why I love that quote that I put in the very beginning of the boat. "No one ever puts their kids on a boat unless the unless the water is safer than land," from Warsan Shire. Amna Nawaz: Yes, the poet, yes. Ke Huy Quan: And that really speaks volumes to what my parents were going through, the incredibly difficult decision that they had to make. Amna Nawaz: I love you quoted Warsan Shire as well that line from the poem about no one leaves home unless home is the mouth of a shark. Is that what it felt like? Ke Huy Quan: Yes. It was really incredible, and I didn't really know -- it was -- believe it or not, it's been almost 50 years. None of our family members ever talked about it, and because... Amna Nawaz: Never? Ke Huy Quan: Never. And because they were so -- such distant memories, I wanted to make sure that what I remembered is accurate. Amna Nawaz: Yes. Ke Huy Quan: So, right before I sat down to write this book, I actually called some of my older siblings, which I know because of they were -- they were at a -- at that age where they remember much more than I did. Amna Nawaz: And did they? Ke Huy Quan: They were older. And they did. So, having that conversation with them was unbelievable. And it was just as traumatic for them, but I -- each of us dealt with that trauma in our own separate and individual ways. And what they told me was exactly how I remembered it. But they had it even more tough because they were older. I was 7. I was well protected, even though, being in that circumstances, they did everything they can to shield me from, honestly everything, that was going on. I just -- I didn't know much of it. So, having that conversation with them was really unbelievable, and I'm glad I did. Now I get to understand a little bit of what they went through. And, interestingly enough, they have -- they have to read the book to fully understand what I went through, because we never shared. Amna Nawaz: And you can watch that full conversation and more episodes of "Settle In" on our YouTube page or wherever you get your podcasts.

- Published
Hurricane Isaias has made landfall in the US state of Florida and is expected to bring life-threatening flooding and winds that have forced thousands to evacuate.
The storm weakened slightly to a category 2 hurricane, with 110 mph (175 kph) winds, before ramming into Florida's western panhandle on Friday evening.
Florida, Alabama, and Georgia have each issued states of emergency as meteorologists warned of life-threatening storm surge that could cause up to 9 feet (2.7m) of flooding in some areas.
Isaias is one of three storm systems affecting North America this weekend, with the two others hitting Mexico and Southern California in the El-NiÃ±o fuelled warm waters of the Pacific Ocean.
Both Florida and Alabama instituted mandatory evacuations due to the storm.
In Florida, those evacuations includes coastal communities in direct aim of the powerful storm. Florida Senator Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible, as he warned in a social media post: "DO NOT WAIT! Get out NOW!"
Governor of Alabama Kay Ivey issued a mandatory evacuation for all non-residents, tourists and visitors in key counties likely to be heavily affected by the storm.
Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El NiÃ±o conditions in the Pacific.
It marks the first time in more than 30 years that a hurricane did not form till October.
The storm is likely to bring "life-threatening storm surge" to the US Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center warned.
After hitting Florida, the centre of Isaias is forecast to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on Saturday and Sunday, the National Weather Service said late on Friday.
As of Friday evening, hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 35 miles (55 km) from Isaias' centre, and tropical storm-force winds extended as far as 205 miles (335 km).
The Florida Panhandle and the rest of the US Gulf Coast are facing fierce winds and heavy rain as the hurricane barrels down. There is also the potential for accompanying tornadoes, Melissa Watson, a Florida-based meteorologist at the National Weather Service told the BBC.
For those who have not evacuated, "the main thing will be having multiple ways to receive warnings" about tornadoes and storm surges, Watson said. "If you are near the coast, being able to move to higher ground," is also essential in the event of storm surges.
"We want people to be safe, so don't go out there trying to look for damage ... to post on social media," she added. "We want people to remain inside and safe while the hurricane is moving through."
Even before the storm made landfall, hundreds of thousands were without power in the country's southeast - and Alabama, Florida and Georgia have issued states of emergency as they brace for heavy rains and flooding.
More than 350,000 were in the dark in Florida and another 170,000 in Alabama saw outages, according to PowerOutage.us.
The hurricane's winds are expected to be felt further inland in Georgia, albeit at a lesser intensity, where already about 8,000 customers were without power.
People on the coast of the Florida panhandle have been told to seek immediate shelter under an "Extreme Wind Warning".
Some Florida officials have ordered residents to "Get out NOW!", urging people to follow evacuation orders.
John Guoth, a resident of Navarre, Florida, told the BBC that he and his wife will remain in their home despite the rest of his street having already left.
"It's a hurricane, we get them all the time... we kind of knew that when we moved here," he said.
"Pretty much everything that can fly and will fly is battened down, and everything that cannot fly is really, really secured," he said,
Guoth said he put his ducks and chickens in the bathroom and weighed down his boats and trailers so "nothing flips over".
A few households have remained in the area, describing them as "long-term locals" who are "going to protect our homes".
Pensacola resident Brandin Ruth told the BBC that they have been turning the gas off to the buildings, icing down product and trying to get team members home.
People in the Florida city have "seen bad storms before" but are "bunkering up", he said, adding: "You don't want to underestimate a storm like this".
One indicator of a storm's severity to communities in the southern US is whether the stalwart restaurant chain The Waffle House would close its doors to customers. On Friday, it did.
A Waffle House spokesperson confirmed to the BBC that the chain had already closed a number of locations in the hurricane's path and "will continue monitoring conditions".
US President Donald Trump said he will no longer attend a major American football college game in Tuscaloosa, Alabama because of the hurricane, shifting plans to attend a rally in Tennessee instead.
Two other storms are also forecast to batter North America this weekend.
Hurricane Simon is bearing down on the Pacific coast of Mexico as a category one hurricane. It is set to pick up speed and become category four by Saturday, eventually making landfall near Puerto Vallarta on Sunday, according to Reuters.
Further north, Tropical Storm Rachel, a downgraded hurricane, is heading toward landfall around the US-Mexico border, along the Pacific.
While, Rachel is expected to reach the coast late on Saturday, the impact of the storm is already being felt due to high tides in southern California.
Video footage and photos show several streets under water in Newport Beach, California, through a combination of the tropical storm swells at sea and high tide.
Posting on its account on X, the City of Newport Beach advised people to "avoid the Balboa Peninsula due to street flooding caused by recent storm conditions and elevated tides".
It also urged people not to drive through flooded streets. Bulldozers have been shoring up the beach to try and prevent further flooding.
With additional reporting by Simon King.

The Pentagon awarded $350M to a firm tied to a senior DOD official
Experts expressed shock at a $281 million contract that was no-bid, enormous for consulting work, and set up as an OTA deal.
Among a cadre of Wall Street executives brought into the Pentagon during President Donald Trump’s second term, George K. Kollitides II has emerged as a powerbroker with a broad mandate to improve procurement of weapons and critical minerals.
The longtime partner at the private equity firm Alvarez & Marsal Capital has framed his tour of duty in government as a service to the country. But the work he’s leading has also been a boon to his old friends in the private sector, government procurement records show.
In April, months after Kollitides had started work at the Pentagon, he was listed on a securities filing as continuing to work for his old company as a senior adviser. Two months later, the Defense Department finalized a $281 million no-bid consulting contract with an affiliate firm, Alvarez & Marsal Federal, to advise Kollitides’ new Pentagon office, the records show.
That contract, large for consulting work even by Defense Department standards, is the second in a pair of deals that since December have awarded almost $350 million in military spending to the firm — about five times more than Alvarez & Marsal entities had received from all U.S. agencies combined in the two decades before Trump returned to office, according to federal spending data. Both of those contracts have been for work connected to Pentagon offices where Kollitides is the head or has a senior role.
The deals remain shrouded in secrecy, records show, because they were signed under an unusual contracting method the Defense Department uses to fund experimental weapons — work A&M has never claimed to do. They have begun to send unprecedented sums of taxpayer money to a company that boasts helping government agencies create a “customer-centric culture” and that is deeply intertwined with the private equity firm where Kollitides was a partner for almost 10 years. The two partner firms tag-team investment deals and share back-office support, company documents and federal filings show.
Kollitides was still working with A&M Capital when the deals were signed. It’s unclear if he will benefit financially from the windfall of military spending on A&M consulting. His employment at the Pentagon is under a special classification that allows him to keep his financial disclosures confidential.
Ethics experts said it’s generally illegal for executive branch officials to play a role in awarding contracts that would have a direct impact on their own finances, unless they were granted a waiver.
“It looks way too cozy to be legitimate. I think taxpayers should be appalled,” said Virginia Canter, a former federal government ethics lawyer. “There are a million consulting firms in D.C. and New York. Why would you sole-source this contract? They’re not sending replacement parts for a ship that is sinking.”
After ProPublica sent questions to the Pentagon, Kollitides and both A&M entities early this week, A&M Capital said Kollitides had just stopped working there days earlier.
In a statement, A&M Capital said it is a “separately capitalized and separately managed firm from the Alvarez & Marsal consulting business” and its “management and employees have no involvement in the day-to-day operations of the consulting business, and vice versa.” The firm said that none of Kollitides’ work for it related to the “defense industry, the Department of War or Mr. Kollitides’ government service.”
The Alvarez & Marsal consulting business did not answer any of ProPublica’s questions, including how it became aware of the possibility that it could seek the $281 million no-bid contract and what services it is providing to Kollitides’ Pentagon team. The Wall Street Journal on Thursday reported the existence of some of the Alvarez & Marsal contracting.
“We are proud to serve clients across all industries, and all levels of government,” the company said in a statement. “The common denominator is always the same: we help solve difficult problems.”
Kollitides did not respond to questions about whether he played a role in A&M securing contracts to work for his office, but a Pentagon spokesperson replied for the department and on Kollitides’ behalf saying they both followed all applicable rules.
“The Department of War maintains a rigorous, multi-layered ethics framework that includes financial disclosure reviews, divestitures where appropriate, and screening to prevent conflicts of interest,” Deputy Pentagon Press Secretary Jacob Bliss wrote in an email. Kollitides, he added, “is in full compliance with all ethical laws and regulations. Any claims otherwise are false.”
There is widespread bipartisan agreement that the Pentagon’s procurement systems are in need of radical reform and private-sector know-how could help the country better secure supply lines and accelerate the development of new weapons to ensure the military is prepared to fight future wars.
But current and former defense officials say the massive spending for connected consultants is a reflection of a changed Defense Department under Trump. They say a clubby and politicized culture has taken hold in a wing of the Pentagon controlled by Kollitides and other former Wall Street executives recruited by Steve Feinberg, the billionaire private-equity titan who is now the deputy defense secretary. It’s an operation, they say, that favors people and companies that have close ties to the administration.
This year, ProPublica reported that the Office of Strategic Capital, a unit at the Pentagon that Kollitides helps lead, granted a small North Carolina startup linked to Donald Trump Jr. a $620 million loan after a top aide to the president intervened on the company’s behalf. A group of Democratic lawmakers accused the office of “a staggering level of corruption and influence peddling.”

Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.
Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.
But German police were already closing in on him.
After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.
Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime â attacking civilian infrastructure â allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".
Both he and his country have denied any involvement.
Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.
It was 02:03 am on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.
There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 â not yet in action, but already full â and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas.
Both have been inoperable ever since.
Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers.
They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda.
Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.
As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow.
Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure.
But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise.
They went on following the forensic crumbs.
Eventually they led to Ukraine.
The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services.
In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich.
That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy.
He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada â all dated after the Nord Stream attacks.
But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected.
Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him.
By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert.
Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs.
The saboteurs
None of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions.
But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them.
"Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that."
Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe.
That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it.
Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution.
"Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out.
The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution.
Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence.
"At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained.
Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned".
Germany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far.
Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.
He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation.
Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him.
Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning.
He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver.
But he is a civilian.
Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.

The Omani co-pilot who allegedly attempted to hijack a Flydubai plane started a "drift towards extremism and terrorism" while studying in Australia, United Arab Emirates officials say.
UAE Attorney-General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi also alleged the pilot - widely named as Hamam al-Hammami - was last week trying to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's airport in a "suicide attack".
He wounded the captain in the cockpit with the emergency crash axe before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew on the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight was able to land the aircraft in Saudi Arabia.
Melbourne university RMIT earlier confirmed the pilot had studied there but left before completing his engineering qualification.
According to Shamsi, interrogations of the 29-year-old pilot revealed he had been inspired by al-Qaeda's 11 September attacks in the US in 2001.
"The findings indicated that signs of his drift towards extremism and terrorism first emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia," the attorney-general was quoted as saying by the UAE's state news agency Wam on Friday.
"During that period, he was influenced by takfiri [radical] ideology through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks."
The Wam report also said the pilot had told investigators "he had prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach".
"He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim," Wam said.
The Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported the man was issued an Australian student visa in 2014 and studied in the country in 2015-17, before leaving.
This week, the Sydney Morning Herald unearthed tweets from al-Mammami's now-deleted X account in which he referred to his five years spent studying abroad in Australia, Britain, and New Zealand, as "the golden years of my religious commitment".
More than 170 passengers and crew were on board flight FZ1073 on 30 September.
In the days after the incident, Australian authorities confirmed they were looking into the man's links to Australia.
The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team - made up of the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Victoria Police and the country's security agency ASIO - said it was "investigating the man's links to Australia".
Indian co-pilot Capt Smit Machchhar has been hailed a hero after managing to unlock the cockpit door while being violently attacked with an axe, allowing passengers to get in and take control of the aircraft.
Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by Flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv.
Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views.
He was later hired by UAE-based Flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials.
Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country.

US President Donald Trump has once again made complaints that he did not receive the Nobel Peace Prize, calling this year's decision "disgraceful and embarrassing".
The prize was awarded to former International Criminal Court judge Navi Pillay on Friday. Hours after the announcement, Donald Trump told a rally he had "never heard" of the "mystery person".
"This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway" he said, adding "we will not forget".
Trump has been outspoken about his desire to win the prize, and made similar criticisms in 2025 when it was awarded to Venezuelan opposition leader MarÃa Corina Machado.
Last year, Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re explained to Trump it was an independent committee based in Norway, not the Norwegian government, which decides who will receive the prize.
Speaking to his supporters at a rally in Syracuse, New York, the US president repeated claims that he had settled eight wars and was "about to settle or win two more", without providing evidence.
"The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilisation," he said.
Pillay, a former UN human rights chief and International Court of Justice judge, was recognised "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.
The South African's work had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted", said the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee JÃ¸rgen Watne Frydnes.
Shortly afterwards, the 85-year-old reacted to the news from Nuremberg's Palace of Justice by saying "it must be a joke" and thanked those who had gathered to applaud her.
"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked.
Last year, the president openly expressed his displeasure at missing out on the prize, with the White House accusing the committee of placing "politics over peace".
In January, Machado gifted her medal to Trump during a meeting at the White House, which she said was in recognition of his commitment to her country's freedom.
Trump said on social media that the move was "a wonderful gesture of mutual respect".
The Nobel committee later clarified that the prize was not transferable.
"Once a Nobel Prize is announced, it cannot be revoked, shared, or transferred to others," it said in a statement. "The decision is final and stands for all time."

US country music star Ella Langley has said she had to cancel her sold-out concert in Tulsa, Oklahoma on Friday night, due to a "serious security threat".
The singer made what she called the "incredibly difficult" decision around two hours before the show at the 19,000-seater arena was due to start.
In a post on Instagram, the 27-year-old said the threat involved "the safety of my fans, the venue staff and my team".
Cpt Richard Meulenberg from Tulsa Police Department said a person had called saying "great harm" would be done at the event with "shots fired and bombs."
He stated his team had checked the venue at BOK Center several times before the show and "could not find any threat".
"The event was ready to go," he added, saying officers with sniffer dogs did a sweep of the arena again after the phone call was made.
"We could not find a credible threat," he said, stressing that the person who had made the call "disrupted this entire event" for thousands of Langley fans.
The star - who did not give any further details - also apologised to her fans, saying additional information regarding ticket refunds "will be shared as soon as possible".
BOK Center issued its own statement, saying that "the safety and well-being of everyone involved is our absolute priority, and after careful consideration, we have determined that the show cannot proceed.
"We understand the disappointment this news brings and apologise to fans who planned to attend."
In September, Langley's country smash Choosin' Texas overtook Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You to become the longest-running number one single in US chart history.
Its success helped the singer from Alabama to sweep the Academy of Country Music Awards in May.

For more than six years, asbestos has been washing up with the tide, turning one of Plymouth's handful of swimming spots into the centre of a growing environmental mystery.
Mount Batten Beach has been fenced off since the summer, and access restricted to two other areas on the peninsula.
It comes after tests in April and July found asbestos fibres in sand samples at levels that could pose a risk to health if inhaled, Plymouth City Council said.
Inhaling the fibres can increase the risk of serious diseases - including lung cancer - decades after exposure.
The first discovery came in 2019 when 500kg (1,100lb) of material containing the toxic substance was removed from the shoreline, which sits on Plymouth Sound in one of the South West's most popular holiday destinations.
In total, more than 1.5 tonnes of material containing asbestos, external, including both white and the more dangerous blue varieties, has been cleared from the beach and nearby sites.
Residents and experts believe the material may be coming from roofing and construction waste linked to the former RAF Mount Batten base, where coastal erosion is thought to be exposing the buried material.
The closure has left swimmers, business owners and residents wondering when, or even if, the beach will reopen, and how it looks against the backdrop of Plymouth Sound being named the UK's first National Marine Park., external
City councillor Grace Stickland, who has been bathing at Mount Batten for several years, said dozens of people regularly gathered for swims throughout the year, with festive dips attracting as many as 80 participants.
"It was a really popular little beach and everybody loved it," she said.
"All the swimmers feel as though they've been evicted from their homes."
Stickland said older swimmers and people with mobility issues particularly valued Mount Batten because of its accessibility, adding that the closure was "breaking up" a community that had grown around the beach.
The National Marine Park in Plymouth Sound has faced a number of challenges in the past, including hundreds of old tyres being discovered on the seabed and sewage spills.
Yet the asbestos contamination problem has proved difficult to solve.
When asbestos was first discovered in 2019, the council temporarily closed the beach and expected the amount of material washing ashore to decrease over time but that has not been the case.
"Our beach collections have shown that the amount of material washing up on the beach hasn't shown any real decline," a council spokesperson said.
Earlier testing suggested the risk was low. Warning signs were installed and visitors were advised to avoid parts of the beach where asbestos fragments had been found.
But council officials described the latest results as a "new and worrying development".
Although two rounds of testing have found no evidence of airborne asbestos on the beach, the discovery of fibres in the sand was enough to trigger the closure.
Professor Steve Maddern, Plymouth's director of public health, said shutting the beach had been a last resort.
"We understand the disappointment this will cause but the latest sand samples are concerning and we must prioritise the safety of the public," he said in July.
While the beach remains closed, attention has turned to the question: Where is the asbestos coming from?
Residents have long suspected the source could be the former RAF Mount Batten site, which occupied the peninsula for much of the 20th Century before closing in 1992.
During its heyday it was one of Britain's most important flying boat bases, with Sunderland aircraft carrying out anti-submarine patrols and sea rescue missions during World War Two.
Today little remains beyond memorials and historic seaplane hangars.
Maritime archaeologist Mallory Haas, director of the Ships Project CIC in Plymouth, said she believed asbestos-containing roofing materials from the RAF base had been buried and were now being exposed through coastal erosion.
"If you look at what's on the beach, and if you also look at the deposits behind the staircases when you walk down to the beach, you can see it eroding out of the land there," she said.
She added: "It's Britain's Ocean City, the UK's first National Marine Park and it's an MPA [Marine Protected Area].
"It should be some of the most protected waters around."
Asbestos and health risks
The properties of asbestos made it an ideal material for use in a number of products, including insulation material for buildings, boilers and pipes; car brakes and floor tiles, insulating board to protect buildings and ships against fire; asbestos cement for roofing sheets and pipes.
Due to the risks to health following inhalation exposure to asbestos the importation of blue and brown asbestos has been banned in the UK since 1985.
This ban was extended to include white asbestos in 1999.
Asbestosis is a rare but serious lung condition that affects people exposed to asbestos. It cannot be cured but treatment may improve the symptoms.
Symptoms include:
- shortness of breath
- persistent cough
- wheezing
- extreme tiredness
- pain in your chest or shoulder
- in more advanced cases, swollen fingertips
It can take 20 to 30 years after being exposed to asbestos before symptoms appear.
There are sometimes no symptoms.
The advice is to visit a GP if you have symptoms of asbestosis and think you have been exposed to asbestos.
Sources: UKHSA, external and NHS, external
Local MP Rebecca Smith has been pressing the council for answers; arguing the closure is having a significant impact on sea swimmers, watersports users, businesses and the wider community.
More than 140 people attended a public meeting about the issue, while a petition has been handed to Parliament calling for urgent action to reopen the beach.
The Conservative MP for South West Devon questioned why the problem had still not been resolved more than six years after asbestos was first discovered.

- Published
Barrels of chemicals left at an approved development site have been removed and testing carried out, a developer has said.
The Islip Fuel Depot in Oxfordshire is a former RAF and Esso fuel storage and transfer facility and has had outline planning permission approved to build residential and affordable homes.
Concerns were raised after campaigners discovered about 40 barrels of firefighting foam liquid, which contains PFAS - a group of chemicals often dubbed forever chemicals, had been left at the site for decades.
Developer, Newcore, said it had already identified the potential contamination and that "this potential risk and any contamination identified will be cleaned up immediately."
The depot previously supplied fuel to the former RAF Upper Heyford, around five miles north, which is suspected to be the source of forever chemical, or PFAS, contamination from firefighting foam.
Images show the barrels to be manufactured by Angus Fire Armour, that settled a legal battle out of court with residents in Yorkshire, after claims they had been exposed to PFAS near the company's foam manufacturing plant.
CEO of Newcore, Hugo Llewelyn, who took over the site in 2012, said it plans to regenerate the site with 50% affordable housing and that it was made aware of the barrels "in recent weeks" and had them removed in a "responsible and professional manner".
"Whilst firefighting foam containers were present on site from the MOD's operation back in the 20th Century, we do not believe it was ever deployed; the containers were sealed; and successive surveys have confirmed that there is no "pathway" for it to cause pollution," he added.
Mr Llewelyn disputes the quality of the testing carried out by campaigners.
"A 'pressure group' has trespassed unlawfully to obtain a questionable sample from this site to demonstrate that in the secured area of the site that was purposefully designed to accommodate foam for firefighting purposes, which is likely to contain PFAS, does, according to their findings, contain PFAS.
"I'm not sure there is anything to be surprised about here," he said.
He added that a Phase 1 assessment of the site last year had already identified the potential for contamination and that, "the specification for the Phase 2 investigation has therefore been designed to specifically address this potential risk and any contamination identified will be cleaned up immediately".
The Environment Agency's Chemical Compliance team had contacted the site owners to ensure that the drums are properly managed.
Campaigners from Gallos Brook community group, who have been regularly testing for PFAS in the area, took a sample of soil near the storage area which they claimed is "likely the highest level of soil contamination measured anywhere in the UK."
The group said the sample, which was analysed by a UKAS certified laboratory, came back as having 3.74325 micrograms of PFAS per kilo. PFOS - a particular forever chemical - was found in their testing to be 205 times higher than the safe limit for residential land use.
Llewelyn disputed the testing carried out by campaigners and produced his own results which he claimed were taken from the same area, as part of the Phase 2 investigations.
He said these produced a total level of 0.0641micrograms per kilo of PFAS, roughly 98% lower than results by the campaigners, and were "the accurate results of our professional testing."
The BBC has not been presented with the official lab results to verify these independently.

They came in their thousands from near and far - men, women and children lined up on a Kentucky riverfront for the public hanging of a black man convicted of raping and killing an elderly white widow.
It was 14 August 1936 in Owensboro, Kentucky, a sweltering Friday in the middle of a legendary heat wave. Some slept overnight near the gallows to preserve their spots. Others held "necktie" parties the previous evening, arriving hungover as teenagers sold popcorn and soda to the spectators.
By the execution time of 5am, the crowd had swelled to an estimated 20,000.
That's when Rainey Bethea, an orphan in his 20s, stepped up to the gallows - sentenced to death after allegedly confessing to robbing, raping and killing Lischia Edwards, 70.
The previous afternoon, he'd eaten a last meal of fried chicken, pork chops, mashed potatoes, pickled cucumbers, cornbread, lemon pie and ice cream.
Many of those gathered - including press from as far away as Chicago and New York - came to see the rumoured "Lady Executioner;" the local sheriff had died four months earlier, and his widow became the unlikely female replacement. She declined to pull the trip lever herself, however, and it was hired hangmen who instead sent Bethea to his death.
That moment marked the last high-profile public hanging in America. The circus surrounding Bethea's death embarrassed many in Kentucky, and the governor outlawed public executions 18 months later.
By then, most states had abolished capital punishment in view of the masses as societal attitudes sought more humane and private methods. Another hanging was attended by a few hundred in Missouri in 1937, but that was lesser known and marked America's final public execution - until now.
A little more than 90 years after Bethea's killing, US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that the military would publicly execute Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 unarmed fellow soldiers in 2009 at the Fort Hood military base in Texas.
The Pentagon followed up by saying the execution by firing squad would be live-streamed.
"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said.
University of Colorado professor emeritus Michael Radelet, a long-time scholar of capital punishment, was shocked.
"I never imagined [another] public execution," he told BBC.
He noted how public support for the death penalty in general has been steadily declining; it was 80% in 1994, for example, but now stands at 52%.
"It's gone down precipitously, especially when you give the alternative of life without parole," he said.
It's too soon to know what the American public thinks of the idea of livestreaming an execution. But it's nearly certain that millions or more will tune in.
With Hegseth's announcement, Radelet said, "the justification for the death penalty becomes entertainment â¦ bring your popcorn, invite your friends".
Sonya Lea, who just last year published a book about Bethea's execution, "felt absolute horror for our descendants" when she heard of the announced firing squad livestream.
"What they called it in 1936 was a carnival of sadism," she said. "That we now have the technology that can make it go wider than the 20,000 people who showed up â¦ to witness in Owensboro, Kentucky, it just makes it even more horrific."
Lea's grandparents were teenage newlyweds among that 1936 crowd. She only found out after her grandmother's 2002 death, when she read an account her late grandma had given detailing how they were close enough to hear Bethea's neck snap.
The author's subsequent years of research taught her that many Kentuckians were "haunted" by that execution.
"I really thought, with all my heart, that we had put this in the rearview mirror, this level of grotesquery that only a few countries in the world engage in - Iran, North Korea, Afghanistan," she said. "Are we now, as the United States of America, considering ourselves to be part of that kind of government? It's just horrific."
But the polarisation and rhetoric in American politics may have, in some way, perhaps set the stage for such an announcement, said Kurt Gray, a social psychology professor at Ohio State University.
"Some Americans might thirst for blood, but I think a lot of Americans don't, and, if anything, I think a lot of other Americans are just kind of maybe desensitised," he said. "So it's not like they're cheering a public execution; they're just like, 'Oh, yeah, I guess that's where we're at now.'"
Other research indicates that Hegseth and the administration may be reading the country wrong.
Garen Wintemute, director of the Violence Prevention Research Program at the University of California, Berkeley, said survey data points to a declining appetite for violence in the US.
"This morning, the chair of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops labeled this [livestream execution announcement] as barbaric," he said. "And I think he speaks for a lot of people."
"I think it's this: A public execution is not who we are," he added. "It's not who we aspire to be as a country."
Vice-President JD Vance, a Catholic, has said he would not be watching the execution.
President Donald Trump dodged the question of whether he'd tune in himself - but confirmed he approved the decision to livestream Hasan's death.
"I really don't care how he goes as long as he goes," Trump said. "And I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."
