It is 06:00 and I'm meeting drone pilot Pete Short for a dawn patrol in the Cairngorms National Park.
It is a job he has been doing for almost three months, since a huge wildfire tore through this landscape in July.
The flames which swept across the hillsides are gone. From where we are standing, there is little to suggest there is still a fire here at all.
But that is exactly what we have come to find.
After a bumpy drive into the woodland, Pete launches a thermal drone into the early morning sky.
I am given a job too: keeping the aircraft in sight while he studies the images being sent back to his screen.
"Every week I hope that I find none," he tells me. "On the last thermal flight I did we found eight."
It doesn't take long.
"We might have something here," Pete says, as a white glow appears on the thermal image beneath a tree.
Three months after the fire first ignited, heat is still being detected beneath the ground.
We make our way towards the coordinates identified by the drone, and at first, there is almost nothing to see.
Then we feel it.
The soil is warm. A rock Pete picks up from the ground is, too.
Nearby, after scraping away a thin layer of earth, smoke begins to rise.
"It's really now cooking away," Pete says.
"Without the thermal technology we would be totally blind to this."
Fire beneath the ground
The wildfire began in the middle of July and burned across about 3,300 hectares â 33 sq km â of land, according to the Cairngorms National Park Authority.
At the height of the emergency, five experienced drone pilots were brought together to provide aerial information to the agencies fighting the fire.
Pete describes it as one of the most challenging environments he has ever flown in, with "multiple walls of flame", personnel and vehicles moving around the site and helicopters operating overhead.
Now the challenge is different.
The dramatic flames have disappeared, but hot spots can continue to burn beneath the earth.
Each one found by the drones is reported to the land manager. They send teams who can dig into the ground and douse it with water.
For Ben Jones, senior site manager for the RSPB at Abernethy, knowing exactly where to send those teams has been crucial.
"We've been fighting this fire for over two months now and obviously we've got limited resources in terms of the number of people we have and we can't send everybody out everywhere all the time," he says.
"So we really need to know where these specific hot spots are - where we should be sending people - so that they can be as efficient as possible."
And despite the arrival of colder, wetter weather, the remaining fires cannot simply be ignored.
"Each of these hot spots has got the potential to reignite a larger fire," Ben says.
A landscape transformed
Walking through the forest, the scale of what happened is almost haunting.
Tree trunks are blackened and charred. The acrid smell of fire still hangs around. Large areas of the forest floor have been scorched.
But look closely and there are splashes of colour.
Green shoots are emerging. Fungi is growing. I even spot a small yellow flower shooting up from the blackened ground.
Dr Sarah Henshall, head of conservation at the Cairngorms National Park Authority, says it is too early to know the full ecological impact of the fire.
"Some of that will be incredibly quick, some of it will take years, decades, or even beyond our lifetime," she says.
"It will recover, but we just don't know what that's going to look like yet."
And the drones that helped during the fire - and are still searching for what remains of it - are being given another job.
Pete is programming them to repeatedly fly exactly the same routes over the damaged landscape.
Using predetermined waypoints, photographs and video can be taken from the same positions month after month and year after year, allowing conservationists to build up a picture of how the landscape changes.
"This standard drone route will have exactly the same route flown month by month, year by year and visually it's going to give us some amazing information about how it's recovering," Sarah says.
There could be another role for the tech too - spotting future fires before they have a chance to spread.
Pete believes getting a view above the tree canopy quickly could prove critical.
"It's those moments before a wildfire gets out of control that could be critical to stopping it before it gets out of hand," he says.
Back on the ground, our patrol has found another hot spot.
Again, there is almost nothing visible from a distance. But guided by the drone, we find the precise spot.
Beneath a thin layer of earth, it is hot and the smoke becomes obvious after we stoke the soil.
Another location to report. Another fire for the ground teams to extinguish.
Above us, the forest is already showing its first signs of life but below our feet, the last of the fire is still burning.

WHITTED, Fla.—When Ann Jones runs her kitchen faucet, the water flows clear only some of the time. Sometimes the water is brown. Fill a pitcher, and the water is the color of iced tea.
Jones, 81, is a gentle woman who has lived most of her life in this unincorporated historically Black community of 52 residents southeast of Orlando. She can recall, as a teen, glimpsing the Ku Klux Klan burn crosses not far from her childhood home, as her family drove past.
Through the years the community has held firmly to its heritage and the close bonds its neighbors share, even as the outer bounds of metro Orlando have crept closer. Recently several new developments have sprung up around the outskirts of the tiny neighborhood, all of them connected to the local water system and offering clean drinking water flowing from their taps.
In Whitted, residents rely on well water, and testing they requested from the Florida Department of Health has confirmed at least some of the wells are contaminated with arsenic and PFAS/PFOS, so-called “forever” chemicals associated with cancer, cardiovascular disease, developmental problems in children and infants, diabetes, immune system disruption and neurological damage. A $2.3 million effort to connect the community to the local water system has moved slowly since the funding was announced in 2024, an issue Osceola County Commissioner Ricky Booth, who represents Whitted, acknowledged.
“Those new developments pay for those services to come in,” he said. “Hearing from the residents, my position has been let’s get them hooked up to city water. It seemed like the right thing to do, and that’s why we’ve been fighting so hard to get it done.”
Jones, who lives with her husband in a tidy home painted bright white, does not drink the tap water. Every two weeks two five-gallon jugs of water and three 24-packs of bottled water are delivered to the house, and a neighbor helps lift and empty the jugs into several pitchers the couple uses for drinking and cooking. The couple bathes in the water, but Jones throws in some bleach with the whites to ensure the water does not stain the laundry. She estimates the couple spends about $150 a month on bottled water, a situation she considers a legacy of the segregation and racism that historically characterized this part of central Florida.
“We’re not begging or asking for something that no one else has, that is sacred to the white people,” she said. “We deserve to have clean water. It doesn’t matter what race you are. Everybody deserves clean water, to know that they are safe in drinking their water.”
A Landfill, Not a Park
In the late 1800s, a small group of Black families settled among this region’s agricultural and ranch lands and began working the citrus groves and sugarcane fields. They established the St. Luke Missionary Baptist Church, and eventually the tiny house of worship would serve as a spiritual and social center for generations of Whitted families. The Black children attended their own schools, and residents knew better than to go after dark into nearby St. Cloud, which was known as a “sundown town.”
In 1964, a resident named James Whitted, whose relatives helped establish the community and lent their name to it, agreed to lease three acres of his land to Osceola County for a dollar a year for the construction of a park and recreational space for the community’s children, according to records residents obtained recently. Whitted was elderly at the time, could not read or write and suffered from some mental health problems, said Christian Wells, professor of anthropology and director of the Center for Brownfields Research and Redevelopment at the University of South Florida. Whitted did not understand the lease he signed actually allowed for a landfill.
The park never materialized. Shortly afterward the county dug a hole on the property, and trucks began dumping trash there. The action was undocumented and unregulated, and records are scarce. But based on a lease agreement, the property is believed to have operated as a landfill from 1964 to 1975, according to a 2024 report by the Florida Department of Health.
Whole cars were dumped at the site with no concern about leaching, said Emily Walsh, a master’s student in anthropology and public health at the University of South Florida whose thesis project is on Whitted. After the dumping stopped, the county covered the landfill and the site has remained undeveloped since.
In 1966 the county sanitation director expressed concern to the Board of County Commissioners that the waste at the site could pollute the groundwater, contaminating the wells of nearby residents. The sanitation director requested the county dig a ditch around the property, and the board instructed the county engineer to investigate. There is no evidence any such investigation took place, and no precautions were taken, Wells said.
Homes surrounded the landfill on three sides, some of them only a few dozen feet from the site and without even a fence separating the properties. When the county began preparing the site for the dump, clearing trees and moving dirt, the residents thought construction was getting underway on the park, Jones said. The children got excited.
“This was a way into what we thought would be a heavenly life, a fun life,” she said.
After the dumping began, all kinds of garbage was deposited at the site: clothing, food, furniture, paint, pots and pans, toys, windows. Individuals tossed trash on the property, too. The landfill smelled, and rats and raccoons became a problem for nearby residents. Still, the site became an informal recreational space for the children, who would venture onto the property and play, Jones said. But James Whitted was devastated.
“He said, ‘I didn’t designate that as a landfill. I wanted that for the kids for a park,’” Jones said.

From our collaborating partner “Living on Earth,” public radio’s environmental news magazine, an interview by host Steve Curwood with veteran Maine journalist Kevin Miller.
The closely watched race for U.S. Senate in Maine is pitting two environmentally concerned candidates against each other.
Not only do they both have fairly similar green and climate views, they are also both from Aroostook County, the sparsely populated and northernmost region in a state that is 90 percent forested.
Incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, seeking her sixth term in office, comes from a family that dates back five generations in the lumber business and is a political dynasty. Her father and uncle served multiple terms in the Maine state Senate and both her mother and father were mayors of her hometown, Caribou.
Democratic challenger Troy Jackson grew up in a working-class family of loggers in the Allagash region, deeper in the woods and about 75 miles from Caribou. Jackson entered politics as a prominent labor activist in the logging industry and served six years as the president of the Maine state Senate. He got into this U.S. Senate race late, after the winner of the Democratic primary dropped out.
Kevin Miller is Maine Public Radio’s veteran state house and environmental reporter. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
STEVE CURWOOD: Give me a sense of these two candidates: Susan Collins, the Republican, and Troy Jackson, the Democrat.
KEVIN MILLER: Senator Collins has been in office for 30 years. She is one of the more senior Republican members of the Senate. She is a fairly moderate, centrist Republican. There are some people who will probably be yelling right now, saying she’s not a moderate, but when you look at her in the context of where the Republican Party is today, she’s definitely more to the center, and she also describes herself as a deal maker.
Troy Jackson was a state lawmaker for 20-some years. He’s a logger from far northern Maine, and he’s a fairly progressive candidate. He’s been closely aligned with Bernie Sanders. He became candidate after our last progressive candidate, Graham Platner, his campaign imploded because of rape allegations against him from a former girlfriend of his. But Troy Jackson, he’s had a similar approach to policies as Graham Plattner, so he was able to kind of step in and say, “I’m going to carry Graham Platner’s progressive movement,” which had a lot of momentum in Maine before Platner had to step down.
CURWOOD: At one point, you worked as an environmental reporter, so talk to me about climate and environment as a priority for Maine voters in this race. Where does it fall on the list?
MILLER: Not very high, from what we’re seeing from polls and hearing from voters. Environment and conservation issues are always fairly important in Maine, just because it’s a big natural resource state. So many of our industries are tied to natural resources. But, like we’re seeing in a lot of other places around the country, it’s the other issues. It’s affordability. It’s inflation. It’s gas prices. One of the big concerns headed into the election right now, or at least into winter, is Maine is the most heavily reliant state on heating oil. More than 50 percent of houses in the state use heating oil, and heating oil is diesel, pretty much. When the price of diesel and heating oil are up above $6 a gallon, that’s a big concern for people. Affordability issues are probably top of mind for a lot of people.
CURWOOD: How do these candidates come down on environmental issues? Let’s talk about renewable energy to start with.
MILLER: They’re fairly well aligned in some respects, at least on renewable energy. They’re both known as being fairly prominent supporters of the push to convert Maine and other states to more renewable sources. They’re both supporters of wind energy, especially offshore wind. The Gulf of Maine is a very windy place. There have been proposals that were in the works to build large offshore wind facilities there. They have now been kind of put on hold by the Trump administration, and I think Senator Collins has been critical of that. Troy Jackson has certainly been critical of that.
We do have a significant number of land-based wind resources here, and Troy Jackson actually was key when he was the Senate president, key to greasing the skids to build a large wind farm that would stretch from his area of northern Maine down and would be a major generator. That project’s been stalled for other reasons.
One other issue that I think they’re closely aligned on is biomass energy. Some people don’t regard this as renewable energy, or it’s a more controversial source because of its impact on the climate—you’re burning wood, you’re releasing carbon dioxide. So some environmentalists don’t view this as a truly renewable source, but because we are such a heavily forested state, it’s a big issue up here.
On the broader climate issues, Senator Jackson was very prominently supporting our current Democratic governor’s very ambitious climate agenda. He’s not quite as progressive as some people would like him to be. Senator Collins has also been largely supportive of some of these climate issues, but I think it comes down to which candidate the environmental community feels is going to be a bigger advocate on environmental issues, and in this case, certainly hearing from the environmental groups, it’s Troy Jackson.
CURWOOD: Why is that? Is it because it would be part of flipping the Senate to the Democratic majority, which would have a large impact on environmental policy of the federal government? The Trump administration has rolled back almost everything, gotten out of the climate agreements, and in fact, doesn’t believe that climate’s a problem.

An artificial intelligence (AI) agent, developed by Anthropic, went rogue and sent US police a fake tip about an unsolved murder earlier this year, authorities have revealed.
The Philadelphia Police Department said the tip, sent on 18 July, was "flagged as spam" and not passed on for investigation, but it criticised the tech company for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.
In a statement police said that the bogus tip came through a public website where people can share information on unsolved murders, and that the AI agent had written that it may have information on a case, and claimed to have seen "someone matching the description".
It is believed to be the first time an AI agent has sent fabricated information to authorities, but is the latest in a series of incidents involving rogue AI activity, including hacking systems or taking control of platforms.
Citing Anthropic, the police department said the AI agent had been running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites, when it sent the fake tip.
Anthropic discovered the breach on 28 September, more than two months after the message had been sent, and shut down the automatic testing process that was behind it, police said.
But authorities were not notified for another nine days - on 7 October.
"The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge," Philadelphia police said in a statement to local media, external.
"The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable."
The police department added that there were no signs of breaches to any departmental systems, and that its safeguarding processes stopped the fake tip from getting past its spam folder.
But the safeguards "do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide," the police statement said.
Anthropic this week published a report, external detailing multiple types of "unintended" actions its agents have taken.
Organisations that have been impacted also included several US government agencies including the White House, it said.
The US State Department said the AI agent had filed 20 visa applications using a form on its website, but that they were incomplete and not processed, according to reports.
President Donald Trump recently announced an AI taskforce, which he said will coordinate engagement between the government and all parties, including AI companies, consumers, and religious groups.
Earlier this year, a rogue agent by rival tech company, Open AI, hacked an Australian government website and accessed private data on the country's universal healthcare scheme, Medicare.
In another instance, more than 1,200 OpenAI agents went rogue and started unexpectedly communicating, leading to a large group banding together to hack into AI platform Hugging Face.

This story is part of an investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project. Read the other stories here.
In May, the Hellenic Aquaculture Producers Organization gathered in Athens to promote the industry as the future of sustainable food security. Flanked by industry titans, the European commissioner for fisheries and oceans, Costas Kadis, framed aquaculture as a solution to the pressures of climate change, pollution and overfishing. “In the European Union, aquaculture is at the epicenter of our priorities,” he said.
The industry group’s chairman, Apostolos Touralias, went one step further: “Aquaculture is the most sustainable form of animal protein,” he said. “Aquaculture needs less space, less feed, less freshwater. It produces the lowest carbon footprint regarding all other sectors.”
But not everyone agrees with the industry’s assessment of itself.
“The aquaculture industry’s sales pitch is flat wrong,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at the University of British Columbia. The most popular farmed seafood are fed wild fish—the exact livestock aquaculture claims to be saving. That’s accelerating ocean depletion, not slowing it, he explained.
After the 2011 debt crisis, Greece bet its coastal future on the blue economy by mapping out 25 “Areas of Organized Development.” While many of these zones remain in the final stage of legal approval, the plan earmarked potentially exclusive use of almost 60,000 acres of coast to multinational aquaculture firms. Expanding the industry’s footprint 24-fold came with a simple economic pitch: People want more seafood, the limit of what can be viably pulled from the wild is quickly being reached and fish farming is the way to meet the growing demand while slowing the collapse of the oceans.
From the Ionian Sea in the west to the Euboean Gulf in the east, the Greek farmed finfish industry is now the most valuable in the European Union. It’s also the bloc’s top producer of sea bream and sea bass, producing over 120,000 tons annually.
Now accounting for over two-thirds of the nation’s total seafood production, the sustainability argument for fish farming—“grow more, so we can catch less”—is one of the reasons that the $313 billion industry is the fastest-growing food sector in the world.
Yet two-thirds of global aquaculture grows species that are fed fishmeal and fish oil—ingredients made by cooking and pulverizing wild-caught fish. Before it reaches market, a seabass or sea bream at some Mediterranean farms, for instance, eats more than two-and-a-half times its weight in wild-caught fish.
The feed that powers most of this industry comes with a huge variety of other hidden costs, many of them borne by communities far away from Greece or other developed fish-farming economies, according to a wide-reaching investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization based in Washington, D.C.
These costs include the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths and violent protests typically spurred by the horrid stench from fishmeal factories. These social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed.
Some sea bass and sea bream farmed in Greece in recent years were fed fishmeal tied to more than a dozen environmental enforcement actions in U.S. waters between 2018 and 2025, and humpback whale deaths in the Southern Ocean in 2024, according to The Outlaw Ocean Project’s investigation.
About This Investigation
Across five years, The Outlaw Ocean Project carried out an extensive investigation of fishmeal and fish oil. The reporting effort mapped a vast segment of the entire global fishmeal industry, including more than 1,400 fishmeal factories across 64 countries.
The Food for Feed investigation found that the oceans bear an especially heavy and largely invisible burden from the fishmeal and fish oil industry. More than a fifth of wild-caught fish around the world is used for non-human consumption, especially fish feed but also for chickens and pigs.
In Gambia and Mauritania, the series documented how the industry drives food insecurity as fish that once sustained local communities are increasingly being diverted into fishmeal factories for export. In remote islands in Russia’s far east and in China’s Xinjiang region, reporting detailed the use of forced labor on ships, on farms and in factories. In other countries, including India and Peru, this industry was tied to at least 80 incidents of civil unrest, some of them violent, usually in the form of labor strikes and community protests sparked by the water pollution or the stench from factories cooking thousands of tons of decomposing fish. The team also developed Bait to Plate, an online tool that tracks the fishing and seafood industries.
Africa’s Last Colonial State
In Greece, two of the largest aquaculture players have also been sourcing fishmeal from Western Sahara.
Since the mid-1970s, Morocco has militarily occupied Western Sahara, a presence that more than 10 EU Court of Justice rulings and various United Nations resolutions have deemed illegal. Still, Moroccan ships routinely fish in Western Saharan waters, turning their illicit catch into fishmeal in Western Saharan plants, before exporting it to farms globally labeled as Moroccan.
The seafood company Avramar—which controls 70 percent of Greek production and exports to 40 countries—imports raw materials and ingredients from more than a dozen Moroccan companies. Additionally, one of its subsidiary companies, Perseus—which has since been enveloped into Avramar’s larger operations—was receiving shipments of fishmeal from Western Sahara as recently as 2022.

dcfb6fe43d3b.text: President Trump lashed out late Friday night after he once again did not win the Nobel Peace Prize he has openly coveted . Why it matters: The award is Trump's white whale, an honor he talks about frequently and believes he deserves. This year's prize went instead to a former judge of a court Trump has sanctioned and called "rogue" and "evil." Navi Pillay, the winner, reacted to the award by saying world leaders have a "legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war," according to the AP . What he's saying: " I know nothing about this woman, and neither does anyone else! In fact, to the best of my knowledge, no one ever heard of her other than the fact that she, very obviously, hates Israel. I don't know what the woman has done," Trump said in a Truth Social post of nearly 600 words that went up just before midnight on Friday. "I settled 8 Wars, with letters being sent from every President and Prime Minister from the countries that I helped to the Norwegian Nobel Committee, and I'm about to settle, or win, two more, Iran and, Russia/Ukraine," Trump wrote. "They're both happening at breakneck speed but, forget them, it's the 8 that I've already settled, any one of which, in particular, Pakistan and India, would be far more than necessary to win the Nobel Prize. In actuality, I should have won 8 Nobel Peace Prizes, not just 1." Between the lines: Pillay, this year's winner, is a former judge of the International Criminal Court and also the former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. Nobel officials said she received the honor "for her efforts to promote peace and international law." Originally from South Africa, Pillay, 85, also served as chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Zoom in: Trump took aim at that UN association as well. "In all of the Wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations—they were of no help. The United States of America, represented by me, as your President, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn't," he said. The intrigue: Trump also blasted Norway, as he's previously done over Nobel snubs, though the country doesn't award the prize. "This is an indelible stain on Norway, one that will never be forgotten. The Nobel 'Peace' Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of Radical Ideologues who are Anti-Democracy, and Enemies of Civilization!" The bottom line: The president didn't hold back making his case for why he should have won — and why his loss was a personal snub.

1213c45d0006.text: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's announcement that the Fort Hood shooter's execution will be livestreamed reflects a shift toward putting raw, real-world violence on display for unlimited audiences. Why it matters: The Trump administration has made a show of flexing American power, sometimes with grisly footage. Now, it's preparing to make the government's ultimate punishment available for all to see. The big picture: Americans are increasingly encountering shocking images on their phones, often without warning. Graphic footage of Charlie Kirk's assassination spread widely across social media, searing in the brains of social media users — often young ones. Since Oct. 7, 2023, footage from the Hamas attacks and Israel's military campaign in Gaza has circulated online. Some videos have spread from Telegram to social platforms like X , where clips are easy to find. Footage of the August 2025 killing of Ukrainian refugee Iryna Zarutska on a Charlotte train went viral across X, stirring debate about crime and public safety. Trump later said he had watched the video and wished he hadn't. A livestream of Nidal Hasan's execution would be the first known public broadcast of a lawful execution, according to death penalty experts interviewed by Reuters. Public executions are increasingly rare worldwide. In recent years, most have taken place in Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International. Friction point: Tech companies are now facing the question of whether they would allow the Pentagon to livestream the execution on their platforms. Hasan, who killed 13 people in 2009 at the Fort Hood Army base in Texas, is scheduled to be executed on Dec. 3. TikTok and Kick said that livestreaming the event would violate their policies, The Verge reported. YouTube, Meta, X and Twitch did not respond to The Verge's requests for comment. Yes, but: Elon Musk has positioned X, in particular, as a bulwark against internet censorship in the name of free speech. Hegseth's plan is putting the limits of that free-speech philosophy to a new test. The platform defended its decision to keep graphic content of the Kirk shooting on the platform, saying: "We will continue to stand against violence and censorship, ensuring this platform amplifies truth and open dialogue for everyone." After a bishop was stabbed during a livestreamed church service in Australia in 2024, X defied government demands to remove footage of the attack worldwide. Zoom out: Hegseth's announcement raises the prospect of reversing America's nearly century-long retreat from public executions. He justified making the execution public, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." The 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky, which drew 20,000 spectators, is widely considered America's last public execution. A modern-day livestreamed execution could reach billions. The intrigue: Vice President JD Vance questioned Friday whether the execution would actually be livestreamed and said he wouldn't watch if it were. Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) posted : "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainme. …Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent." President Trump told reporters he had approved the decision to livestream the execution. The bottom line: America spent nearly a century moving away from public executions. Now, with real-world violence just a click away, the U.S. government is preparing to show one to the world.

Russia has attacked the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia with five glide bombs, killing at least 15 people including three children, President Volodymyr Zelensky and emergency services have said.
The glide bombs hit residential buildings in the south-eastern city. At least 16 other people were injured in the attack, with more still missing and believed to be under the rubble after the strike on Saturday morning.
Zelensky said 13 other regions had also been hit overnight, adding: "Our responses to [these] Russian strikes will come".
The Russian attacks happened just hours after President Donald Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the US.
Photos and videos from the site of one of the strikes show an apartment block mostly destroyed.
"The ground floor was hit, and the floors above just collapsed," acting Mayor Regina Kharchenko told Ukrainian television, speaking from the scene.
She said more than 80 workers were involved in ongoing search and rescue operations which are expected to continue throughout the day.
The rescuers regularly stop to listen for any noises made by survivors who could be under the rubble.
Kharchenko said Russia had struck at "our very heart" and "our littlest ones" were among those killed, adding that their deaths were "awful grief for their families. For the city."
Zelensky has heavily criticised Trump's diesel deal with Russia, calling it a gift to President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".
More recently, in his response to the overnight strikes, he said "Russia interprets any easing of pressure as a signal that it can supposedly continue the war.
"Russia must understand that the war needs to be stopped, and for that, it must feel its losses," he wrote on X, external.
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months, as the war between the two countries drags on.
Zaporizhzhia is a major regional centre with more than 700,000 residents. It is located less than 10 miles (16 km) from the front line and is frequently attacked by Russian drones and missiles.
The latest strikes on the city comes amid a sharp increase in the number of Russian attacks that are causing higher numbers of civilian casualties.
On Thursday, at least 33 people were killed in another Russian glide bomb attack on two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, in the eastern Donetsk region.
The day before, 22 people including five children died as a Russian missile hit an apartment block in the town of Pryluky, east of Kyiv.
According to the UN, the number of civilian casualties in Ukraine jumped by 55%, external in the first eight months of this year.
Russia has also targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, ramping up attacks every winter since Putin launched a full-scale invasion in 2022.
For its part, Ukraine has attacked Russia's infrastructure - with the latest being strikes on data centres owned by tech giant Yandex.

87dfababcb79.text: Poll after poll spells trouble for GOP candidates — in purple states and deep-red ones alike — but while Democrats see a blue wave coming, some Republicans see a polling mirage. Why it matters: Pollsters worry they're flying partly blind. Even a modest polling error could mean the difference between Republicans retaining control of Congress and President Trump facing Democratic majorities in both chambers. The big picture: Polling Trump voters has long been notoriously difficult. The polls underestimated Trump's support in 2016, 2020 and 2024. Midterm polling has been more accurate, though some still underestimated Republican support in 2022, notes Scott Keeter, senior survey adviser at Pew Research Center. Catch up quick: With less than a month until the midterms, the polls paint a bleak picture for Republicans. The House: Democrats lead Republicans 49.8%-41.9% in the RealClearPolling generic congressional ballot average. Cook Political Report projects Democrats will gain nine to 19 seats, enough to win a narrow majority. The Senate: Cook now sees a potential Democratic net gain of two to six seats. Democrats need four to take control, and Cook just moved the Kansas Senate race into its toss-up column. Trump: The president's approval rating stands at 37.6% in Cook's polling tracker . A recent Economist/YouGov poll found 35% approving and 60% disapproving of his performance. State of play: Research suggests Republicans have become somewhat less likely than Democrats to participate in telephone surveys, and response rates overall have plummeted since the late 1990s, per Pew . "We definitely have more people answering surveys who voted for [former Vice President Kamala] Harris than who voted for President Trump," says Brent Buchanan, a Republican pollster and founder of Cygnal. "But if you're a good pollster, you still get the other people." Pollsters can compensate by giving greater weight to Trump voters or adjusting samples to better reflect the Republican electorate, which skews male, white and working class. Advanced statistical modeling tools can also take a poor sample and make it look like the true electorate, though results may be inaccurate for subgroups like young people or Hispanic voters, Pew's Keeter says. But that has risks: "The adjustment assumes that the Republicans who respond to a poll are similar to the Republicans who don't respond to the poll," Rice University political science assistant professor Matthew Tyler tells Axios. Tyler said weighting GOP respondents more heavily can backfire if those willing to answer polls are also more willing to vote Democratic than the Republicans who never respond. That could inflate the apparent size of a Democratic wave. Between the lines: Predicting who will actually vote can dramatically change the results. YouGov chief scientist Douglas Rivers found Democratic leads ranging from six to 16 points depending on how likely voters were identified in a September survey — and called the 16-point margin "almost certainly an overstatement." The bottom line: Even with the questions about the accuracy of recent polls, most pollsters believe Democrats have the edge heading into Election Day. " I think it's telling that we're hanging our hopes on, 'The polls are wrong,'" Buchanan says. "That's not very strong."

Hundreds of protesters have reportedly been detained in Delhi during the latest demonstration by the Gen-Z led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) over electoral reforms.
The group said its founder Abhijeet Dipke, who began the movement in May after India's Chief Justice likened some jobless young people to "cockroaches", was detained with other leaders shortly after landing in Delhi.
Tens of thousands of security personnel were deployed and roads barricaded ahead of the demonstration, though the CJP insisted it would go ahead.
Delhi Police has not commented on the detentions, but had refused permission for the protest to take place at Jantar Mantar, a landmark in the Indian capital.
The group - who are not registered as a political party in India - are seeking electoral reforms just months before crucial state elections.
It has also demanded the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists - which the Election Commission has denied.
Under Kumar's leadership, India's election commission has undertaken a mammoth exercise to update electoral rolls nationwide - it said this was a routine exercise to weed out dead, duplicate or ineligible voters.
But in many states, the exercise has been shrouded in controversy, with tens of thousands of people alleging they have been wrongly removed.
The CJP - and opposition parties - accuse Kumar of favouring Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in the way the electoral rolls are being updated.
The Election Commission and the BJP have denied this.
Before arriving in Delhi, the CJP's founder Dipke said: "If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail or trying to intimidate us with the fear of imprisonment, you are mistaken."
He and and two other leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained on their flight from Mumbai on Saturday.
The group claimed the three men have been taken to an undisclosed location. Delhi Police have not commented.
Ajinkya Shinde, the CJP's new designated leader while the others are in detention, released a video telling protesters that "if Delhi Police tries to stop you, wherever they stop you will become your Jantar Mantar".
Student activist Neha Bora, who had also been detained by Delhi Police, urged demonstrators to "hold the line".
The large number of protesters expected to descend on Delhi were unable to get anywhere close to Jantar Mantar due to the heavy security presence and road blocks.
Announcements could be heard across the city, asking people to co-operate with the police.
One protester, Sabika Muzaffar, told the BBC she and her mother expected to be detained.
"On the way to the protest site, instead of reciting hymns and verses as we usually do, my mother and I were rote learning our lawyer's number," she said.
She said that showing up to protest was "her way of defending the country and its democracy".
A few minutes after Muzaffar spoke to the BBC she was taken away by police.
Several trains to and from major Delhi stations had been cancelled and dozens of metro stations were closed from Friday night.
Buses packed with detained protesters were seen being driven away from the protest site.
The CJP first emerged as a major protest movement during weeks of demonstrations over the summer demanding education reforms and the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The group stemmed from a joke made by Dipke in response to a remark by India's Chief Justice Surya Kant, who had likened jobless youngsters to "cockroaches". He later said the comments were misinterpreted.
Dipke, who previously worked with the opposition Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), had just completed a master's degree at Boston University when he posted a question on X in May: "What if all cockroaches come together?"
The post went viral, and the CJP was born. Momentum built around the movement which tapped into anger over over unemployment, exam paper leaks and government accountability.
In July, Dipke watched from the stage as the five-week-long protest ended in celebration after the resignation of India's education minister.

A former headmaster of an Islamic boarding school in Indonesia has been named as a suspect in a sexual abuse investigation and detained by police, following a BBC Eye report.
Ahmad Imanuddin Sumar, known to students as Abah, led the Abul Barokat boarding school on the island of Lombok.
Police reopened the case after the BBC World Service revealed accusations of sexual abuse against him, and documented how former students had gathered evidence in an effort to bring the allegations to the authorities.
The story sparked public outrage and led to 12 more former students giving testimony to police.
Warning: This story contains details of sexual assault
The student detectives
Central to the BBC Eye investigation were former students Ziadatur Rahmah, known as Zia, and Sukma Rohana Fajar.
They launched their own investigation after Zia told a former classmate, Yusron Azzahidi, that the headteacher had sexually assaulted her when she was 17. The pair had been star pupils at the school.
By the time Zia confided in Yusron, she was studying in Cairo, Egypt, while he was in Jakarta.
Yusron suggested they gather evidence to support Zia's allegation. Speaking to former classmates, they spoke to Sukma, who alleges that Abah attempted to rape her at the school.
Yusron compiled a seven-page document detailing the allegations, and they gave it to representatives of Nahdlatul Wathan Diniyah Islamiyah (NWDI), the organisation that ran the school.
Thinking the school would support them, the students say that instead, they were pressured to withdraw their accusations.
In a secretly recorded phone call, Abah pleaded with Yusron to protect him and his reputation.
"Cover the shame of your teacher. Everyone makes mistakes, my child," Abah said.
Abah also contacted Zia, who secretly recorded their conversation and shared it with the BBC.
In the recording, Abah is heard apologising, but pleads with her to remain silent.
Following the BBC investigation, Abah held a news conference where he denied all the allegations. He did not deny that the voice heard in the recorded calls was his, but said the recordings were not confessions.
Sukma told the BBC she had been forced to sign a document saying her allegations were lies. She later secretly recorded a conversation with Abah's wife, known to students as Umi. In the recording, Umi tells Sukma that the document was intended to protect "her good name".
The former students eventually resumed their efforts to seek justice, with support from lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has experience in similar cases.
More students come forward
The day after the BBC investigation was published, parents arrived at the school to collect their children, with some travelling from other islands.
One mother said she had begun crying when she heard the news, thinking about her daughter.
"I'm moving her right now," she said. "I absolutely want my child to leave this school."
Yusron said he and Zia, who recently got married, were overwhelmed by the response from former students.
"It was beyond what we expected," he said. "So many people contacted us - on Instagram, WhatsApp. They contacted me and Zia directly, and lots of them were saying, 'I'm a victim too'."
Police interviewed Zia and Sukma, along with the 12 other former students who came forward with allegations of abuse.
"They thought they were the only ones - and it's been really shocking for them to learn, like I did, that they weren't alone," Zia said.
Sukma said she felt relieved and grateful that the allegations are now being taken seriously.
"It's not about revenge. It's more the acknowledgement that what he did was wrong. I'm waiting for the day when he admits that himself," she told the BBC.
Abah has resigned from the school and has said he will respect the legal process.
The BBC contacted Abah and his wife during its original investigation, but they did not respond at the time.
NWDI denied trying to cover up the allegations and said it was investigating them internally. It said it had a duty to protect the organisation from being tarnished by the alleged actions of individuals.
In the wake of the BBC investigation, NWDI vowed to ensure such abuse never happened again and said it would safeguard the rights of students who came forward.

Hundreds of people have taken part in a protest against plans to build a new data centre because of concerns about its effects on the area.
Developers want to construct a complex on a 101 acre site between Caernarfon and Y Felinheli, in Gwynedd, saying it could create more than 900 jobs during construction and 200 permanent roles.
About 300 gathered for a rally in Caernarfon to highlight their opposition. More than 22,500 have signed a petition opposing the plan.
Canolfan Ddata Menai has previously said its proposals would "transform and revitalise the long-derelict" site as well as offer significant employment.
But opponent Ernest Dyson, who lives near the proposed site, said it was "basically the destruction of the most beautiful part of the Menai Strait".
"It is quite incredible it should come to this.
"The people of the area are custodians of it. That's what we must think of," he said.
Liz Saville Roberts, the Plaid Cymru MP for Dwyfor Meirionnydd, said: "We know that we need data centres but they have to be the right size, the right technology and in the right places.
"We need proper regulations and we need to make sure that communities benefit from this.
"We have too long a history in Wales of extractive industries that left nothing behind and have little benefit for communities.
"That mustn't happen again in the 21st Century."
Canolfan Ddata Menai said the project would ensure "continued use" of the surrounding area , including LÃ´n Las Menai cycleway and footpath, and would have "no undue impact" on the Menai Strait and an associated site of special scientific interest (SSSI).

Navi Pillay, the winner of this year's Nobel Peace Prize, has called US sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) "unheard of" and "unacceptable".
The South African former ICC judge was awarded the prize on Friday "for her efforts to promote peace and international law", which paved the way for a "more comprehensive global legal order", the Nobel committee said.
US President Donald Trump expressed his disatisfaction with the pick and hours later the US unveiled sweeping sanctions in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it described as a "rogue" institution.
The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.
Pillay, speaking via video link during an event at the Nobel Peace Center in Oslo on Saturday, said: "There is so much tension and anxiety over the continued existence of international courts, mainly the International Criminal Court in The Hague.
"Most importantly, sanctions have been announced by one country against the judges, just for the judicial orders they issue. This is unheard of, unacceptable."
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio earlier said the sanctions - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans.
The US has already sanctioned 17 ICC judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to inhibit its ability to operate financially.
However, the US has provided a six-month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns.
The Trump administration claims that the ICC is run by what it calls globalists who threaten American sovereignty.
It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The new sanctions, however, do not say that those warrants must be withdrawn before the measures can be lifted.
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar".
The UK joined Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan and the Netherlands in saying they "regret and strongly disagree with" the sanctions.
Pillay, 85, also served as UN rights chief, taking part in high-profile work considering allegations of human rights violations, including in Rwanda, Myanmar and Gaza.
Her early work included defending anti-apartheid activists in South Africa, and on Friday she became the country's fifth Peace Prize winner - following in the footsteps of Nelson Mandela and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.
"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," she joked after receiving the prize, a reference to last year's winner, Venezuelan opposition figure MarÃa Corina Machado, deciding to gift her prize to the US president.
Trump called the announcement of Pillay as 2026's winner "disgraceful and embarassing", and an "indelible stain on the country of Norway".
He has long indicated he thought he should have been awarded the prestigious prize, and was nominated by several allies for it last year.

An international airport in the Saudi capital has been attacked again, reports say, just days after Yemen's Houthi rebels claimed two successful attacks on the hub.
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was evacuated after a loud blast was heard on Saturday, two international news agencies have reported.
More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing to the airport, according to Reuters, citing an eyewitness. Saudi authorities have not commented, while the airport told passengers to check with their airline before travelling there.
The attack comes a day after authorities said three Saudi nationals, including a pilot, were killed in two attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis the day prior.
Another three people were killed in Houthi attacks on two Saudi airports on 6 and 7 October.
They came during a marked escalation in renewed fighting between Yemen's Saudi-backed government forces and the Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west.
The Houthis say they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war.
The conflict worsened after the Houthis seized strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive.
That included the port of Mokha on the Bab al-Mandab Strait, which is the narrowest point of the Red Sea and a chokepoint for global shipping. Yemeni pro-government forces have since said they had "secured" the strait at the southern end of the Red Sea.
A Saudi-led coalition was formed in 2015 after Arab countries joined forces to stop the Houthis taking over Yemen from the country's internationally recognised government.
A temporary ceasefire was brokered in 2022 after years of air strikes and ground fighting led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people, triggering one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
But the informal truce began to unravel in July.
The Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. They said they were retaliating against what they described as a years-long Saudi blockade and for an air strike on Sanaa airport.

A woman has been arrested after injuring three people in the third knife attack recorded at schools in Poland this week.
The 21-year-old used a "dangerous object" to attack a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital Warsaw, police have told news agencies PAP and AP.
It comes a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which killed a female caretaker.
A Warsaw police spokesperson said they could not confirm whether the latest incident was related to the two previous attacks.
Authorities told local media that the 17-year-old injured on Saturday had been taken to hospital, but her condition is not life-threatening. Two other women aged 17 and 24, who had come to submit enrolment documents were also injured, the state news agency reported.
Police told local media that the suspected attacker was a student at the school and initial findings suggest she did not know the three victims.
Schools in Poland had been stepping up security following knife attacks at schools across the country on 7 and 8 October. Polish police said they had arrested 76 people after deploying to schools across the country.
"When it comes to the safety of Polish children and peace in our schools, there is no room for compromise," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said ahead of the operation.
Local media, citing a police spokesperson, reported authorities had information to suggest incidents this past week could be related to an internet challenge.
On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.
A day later, a 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in LeszczydÃ³Å-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.
Interior Minister Marcin KierwiÅski also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".

A drone attack by Sudan's paramilitary forces has killed 41 people in the country's Blue Nile region bordering Ethiopia, a rights group has said.
The strike by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted a camp for displaced people in the state's Abu Shandi area on Friday, Emergency Lawyers said.
The UN Office for the Co-ordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) said it was "appalled by horrifying reports". It said initial reports suggested most of the casualties were women and children.
The Sudanese army and paramilitary forces including the RSF have been locked in a power struggle since 2023, a conflict that has killed hundreds of thousands and displaced more than 14 million from their homes.
It has also created one of the worst humanitarian crises in the world, with millions of people needing medical help.
The army controls much of Sudan's central and eastern regions, while the RSF is headquartered in the western region of Darfur and also controls areas in the south.
Both sides have been accused of using drone attacks.
Ocha said in a statement that the area reportedly struck on Friday had been "under sustained atttack in recent weeks, displacing thousands of civilians and exposing many more to grave harm".

US death row inmate Christa Pike has been discharged from hospital following her botched execution at the end of last month, her lawyers have said.
The 50-year-old murderer has been returned to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years, according to a statement from her lawyers on Saturday.
She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison.
Pike survived two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September, which left her in a critical condition.
Earlier this week, she regained consciousness and began speaking - stunning experts, medical staff and her lawyers.
"She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances," her lawyers said in their statement.
Pike's case is now in uncharted territory as Pike is believed to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.
At a court hearing on Wednesday, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General Will Ayers told the judge he does not know whether the state intends to try to execute her again.
The judge also ordered the state of Tennessee to preserve all evidence related to the failed injections. That evidence could lay the groundwork for a future lawsuit against the state.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for low-income young people.
After Pike survived the two lethal injections, she lost consciousness and was taken to a local hospital.
For days, her legal team believed she was brain dead, and expected her to be taken off life support at any moment.
She eventually woke up and began talking again on Tuesday - her lawyer Randy Spivey said her first words were "Where am I?" and "Who are you?"
At a press conference on Wednesday, Pike's lawyers said she was shackled to the bed and suffering from pneumonia, significant swelling on her arms, and was unable to swallow.
"We don't know the toll all of this will take" on her mental health, Spivey said at the time, noting she felt "angry and confused".
It's not clear the extent of medical care Pike is receiving back at the prison, but her lawyers previously said she faced a "long road to recovery".

60c6e552422f.text: President Trump called Saturday for Ukraine to replace President Volodymyr Zelensky with someone willing to make a deal with Russia to end the war. Why it matters: Trump's attack on Zelensky after the Ukrainian president criticized his diesel deal with Russia signals the most serious crisis between the two leaders since their February 2025 meeting exploded in front of cameras. Driving the news: Trump announced Friday he had reached a deal with Russia to lift sanctions to allow Russian diesel exports to the U.S. and the global energy market. Zelensky, who was surprised by the deal made behind Ukraine's back, attacked the move and told Axios it was "not fair and not honest" and was a "sign of weakness" by Trump and a "birthday gift" to Putin. A U.S. official told Axios later that Trump struck the diesel fuel deal after Zelensky ignored half a dozen U.S. requests to stop attacking Russian oil refineries. What he is saying: Trump said Zelensky could have reached a deal with Russia many times "but chooses not to." "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal," Trump told reporters Saturday. "… And I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president." He said he asked Zelensky to stop attacking Russian oil refineries and claimed Zelensky's actions harmed American farmers. "He better damn well stop," Trump said.

93af3748dade.text: Tennessee inmate Christa Pike was released from the hospital and is back in prison more than a week after she survived the state's attempt to execute her by lethal injection , her attorneys said Saturday. The state called an ambulance and Pike got life-saving care at a local hospital. Pike's attorneys said they believed she was "brain dead" and on life support. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she had been housed for decades. "She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery." Catch up quick: Gov. Bill Lee ordered an independent review to determine how Pike was able to survive the attempted lethal injection. Another execution set for December was called off while that investigation plays out. 68c1e3ecc1d0.text:
- Published
US President Donald Trump has said he thinks "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president" as he responded to Volodymyr Zelensky's criticism of the US diesel deal with Russia.
The Ukrainian president warned a new deal to release millions of tonnes of Russian diesel into the US would provide Moscow with money to continue its war against his nation, calling it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday that Zelensky "wants to make problems for the world" by continuing to authorise attacks on Russian refineries.
"He'd better damn well stop," Trump said, before suggesting Ukraine should "get a new leader who can make a deal".
Russia and Ukraine have recently intensified their strikes, targeting energy-generating and transport facilities, as well as major logistics hubs.
"We said, 'you can do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries', because that's a world problem that's caused," he said.
"He could have made many deals and for some reason, he never does."
The US president confirmed on Friday that an agreement had been reached with Moscow to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April.
Zelensky reacted by saying it would allow Moscow to raise new funds to source new military equipment to continue the war.
He also accused Moscow of taking the deal "to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they keep dropping bombs on cities" following deadly new strikes on Zaporizhzhia.
The Ukrainian president spoke to several allies on Saturday to discuss the latest developments, calling for "real decisions to protect lives in Ukraine" and to protect European security.
A Downing Street spokesperson said UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham had spoken to Zelensky and that the pair had agreed Russia should acquiesce to "an immediate energy ceasefire" and end its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea.
"This would immediately release more energy and food supplies into the global market," the spokesperson added.
News of the US-Russia diesel deal was also met with criticism by EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas, who echoed Zelensky in saying that suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."
She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday.
The deal with Russia is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.
That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
The average price of diesel is currently $6.28 (Â£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA â up from last month's $5.94 average, and $3.68 last year.
Under the deal, Russia would release an initial 300,000 tonnes of diesel "to the American and global marketplace" followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November.
A further million would follow, Trump wrote on Truth Social, and then another 3m tonnes "within a short period of time" â but he noted that this delivery will be "based on the condition of their diesel refineries".
In the past 10 months, Russia experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country due to Ukrainian drones strikes on its oil refineries.
Diesel production in Russia dropped by an estimated 30%, according to the International Energy Agency.
Trump had already called for new elections in Ukraine last December, external, saying Ukrainian voters should have the choice to replace Zelensky.
Since the war broke out in 2022 Ukraine has been under martial law, meaning elections are suspended.

A team of researchers are on their way to a remote island to inspect what they think could be the wreckage of famed aviator Amelia Earhart's plane.
The group, from the US-based Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) and Purdue University, are expected to arrive at Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean by Monday in the hopes of solving the mystery of her disappearance.
The American pioneer vanished while attempting to circumnavigate the globe in 1937, spawning decades of speculation on her fate.
The team are aiming to find what has been called the Taraia Object, first spotted sitting on the edge of a lagoon off Nikumaroro in satellite imagery in 2020.
Purdue University said the object had since been confirmed to have been visible in aerial photography of the area dating back to 1938.
The researchers are currently roughly halfway through their journey to the remote atoll aboard the Marin Mainiku, a Kiribati National Shipping Line vessel.
They departed the capital of Kiribati on Wednesday to begin the 830-mile journey to Nikumaroro, which is also part of the multi-island country.
When they eventually arrive, they will have to navigate through a narrow gap created in the atoll's reef created by the British in 1963 - the last time the island was inhabited.
"Finding Amelia Earhart's Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime," Richard Pettigrew, head of the ALI and the expedition lead, said.
Earhart had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her Electra twin-engine plane when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea on 2 July 1937.
From there, she and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to travel towards Hawaii and then finally back to California.
But her plane vanished without a trace while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote, uninhabited coral island near Nikumaroro, to refuel.
Earhart's disappearance spawned numerous theories - from a simple crash due to fuel exhaustion to more elaborate claims of interference.
The official explanation is that the plane suffered communication problems while the two struggled to find the island, and Earheart eventually crashed into the ocean when she ran out of fuel.
While this version of events is largely accepted, no physical evidence has ever been recovered.
One theory is that Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.
Images of the so-called Taraia Object show what could be the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters.
But some - including rival explorers - have expressed scepticism that this could be a plane, let alone Earhart's.
Ric Gillespie, who specialises in recovering historic aircraft wrecks, told news agency Reuters that the object looked like a tree that had fallen from the atoll into the nearby water.
"I'd love to find that airplane. It ain't gonna happen," he said.
The researchers en route to the island credit Gillespie with previously finding evidence of a human presence on the atoll in the 1930s and forensic analysis of skeletal remains found there in the 1940s they say lend credence to their theory.
But Gillespie suspects Earhart's plane had likely broken apart and its fragments carried into the depths of the Pacific long ago.
Previous attempts to find her Electra have also come up short.
In 2024, a group of researchers said they may have found it lying around 4,877m (16,000ft) below the surface near Howland Island through sonar imaging - but this was later confirmed to be a rock formation.
Similarly, an expedition in 2019, conducted by the marine archaeologist who discovered the Titanic wreck, to investigate a photograph of what might have been a landing gear protruding from the water near Nikumaroro also failed to find anything.

A man has shot and killed eight people, including two children, at a home in the US state of Pennsylvania before appearing to take his own life.
Police were called to a street in the city of Erie on Friday afternoon after witnesses reported seeing a man firing a gun before he entered a home, the Erie News Now outlet reported. Two women were reportedly found dead in the street.
The gunman then barricaded himself inside as police surrounded the building and ordered him to leave, but more gunshots were heard, the outlet reported.
When police entered, several more victims were found along with the gunman , who had an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound.
The nine deaths were confirmed in a statement issued on Saturday by the mayor's office.
"Investigators have determined that all deaths occurred before officers arrived," it said.
"The deaths were not the result of any prolonged standoff or delay in police action."
Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said that "there are no words that can adequately express the magnitude of the loss of life here.
He added that police "will not speculate about a motive or any information that could compromise this investigation".
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said he had offered his administration's "full support following the tragic mass shooting in Erie last night - killing nine of our fellow Pennsylvanians".
"My heart breaks for this family," he said, adding that he and his wife "are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community".
The mayor is expected to hold a press conference on Saturday afternoon.

Four people have died and hundreds of thousands are without power after Hurricane Isaias battered parts of the southern US with powerful winds and heavy rain.
Officials reported two deaths each in the states of Alabama and Florida, which included people who were killed after trees fell on their houses.
At least 600,000 people were without power in several states as of Saturday afternoon, according to poweroutage.us.
Isaias made landfall in Florida on late Friday with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles per hour (168 km/h) before being downgraded to a post-tropical cyclone.
The storm felled trees and damaged houses. Alabama, Florida and Georgia all declared states of emergency ahead of its arrival, while both Florida and Alabama issued mandatory evacuation orders to thousands of people.
Two deaths were reported in Florida's Escambia County. A woman was killed after a tree fell on her house, local Sheriff Chip Simmons said.
Joey Williams told NewsNation his wife had died in the storm. He said they went outside to snap pictures of the damage but, when they went back into their home, a tree fell through the roof and trapped them.
"I was able to squeeze out. My wife didn't make it," Williams told the outlet.
Simmons later reported that a man had died from carbon monoxide poisoning after running a generator in a garage that was not properly ventilated. Four other people who were in the same house were taken to hospital.
Officials had to rescue people in vehicles that were submerged by flood waters. In a post on X, the Florida National Guard shared pictures of a truck stuck in a flood ditch, saying soldiers "stopped, swam to the vehicle and pulled its occupants to safety".
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said flooding was a continued risk and warned of a "very hazardous situation".
In neighbouring Alabama, a sheriff was injured when a tree fell on him as he was responding to a car crash.
"Unfortunately, we have also learned that two Alabamians have lost their lives," Governor Kay Ivey said in a post on X, without giving further details on the circumstances of the deaths.
She also said officials were concerned about "spinoff tornadoes" in the state from the strong winds and heavy rain.
"As we approach the weekend and any travel plans, make sure you have reliable information as conditions develop," she said.
In Charleston, South Carolina, officials asked people to stay home on Saturday night as high tide is expected to reach 7.5ft (2.3m).
"After dark, floodwater is much harder to see, and it's impossible to judge how deep it is from behind the wheel," the city said in a post on Facebook.
The storm is expected to continue to weaken as it travels to the north-east, but the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) warned the Carolinas and Georgia could see floods from up to 10 inches (25cm) of rainfall.
In addition to Isaias, Tropical Storm Rachel is expected to hit southern California later on Saturday, and Hurricane Simon will hit the Pacific coast of Mexico on Sunday.
Hurricane Isaias was the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El NiÃ±o conditions in the Pacific.

Watch: 'Time for Ukraine to get a new president', says Trump
US President Donald Trump has called for new leadership in Ukraine, criticising President Volodymyr Zelensky for striking Russian oil refineries.
"It's time for Ukraine to get a new president" he told reporters.
On Friday Trump announced a deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel, a deal Zelensky described as "a gift" to President Putin.

b50314ac12cc.text: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed Saturday to force a House vote to block Russian oil purchases, challenging President Trump's diesel deal with President Vladimir Putin. Why it matters: Trump has touted the deal as a way to lower fuel prices, but it could also provide revenue for Russia's war in Ukraine. Driving the news: Fitzpatrick, co-chair of the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, said he would introduce the "Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act" and force a vote through a discharge petition. "It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly," Fitzpatrick wrote on X . Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) tells Axios he has "already agreed" to sign the petition. Catch up quick: Trump said Friday Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets, with more shipments to follow. Energy analysts are skeptical the additional diesel will meaningfully lower prices. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal "not fair and not honest," telling Axios it amounted to a gift to Putin. Trump called Saturday for Ukraine to replace Zelensky with a leader willing to reach a deal with Russia. The White House has not yet responded to Axios' request for comment about Fitzpatrick's bill. The big picture: Fitzpatrick is the latest Republican lawmaker to break with Trump in a high-profile way, as the party fights to keep control of Congress amid mounting disapproval of the president. Zoom out: Fitzpatrick is turning to a tactic lawmakers have increasingly used to bypass Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.): a discharge petition, which requires 218 signatures to bring legislation up for a vote without House leadership's approval. Fitzpatrick and Bacon forced a House vote on Ukraine aid and Russia sanctions earlier this year; it passed the House but stalled in the Senate. Reality check: Fitzpatrick has little time to pass the bill before this Congress ends in January. The House isn't scheduled to vote again until after the Nov. 3 midterm. Any legislation that passes the House would still need Senate approval and could face Trump's veto pen. What they're saying: Another House Republican, speaking anonymously to offer their candid thoughts, tells Axios: "Being that Congress won't be in session for another four weeks, any prudent lawmaker would probably not make a commitment to this prematurely." One House Democrat tells Axios that they will personally sign the petition and that "most" of their colleagues probably would as well, but unanimous support from Democrats is not guaranteed. "Leadership may not want people to help him," the Democrat said, though they added that may change after the midterms. Ben Geman contributed.
